# How to get a driving licence in Hyderabad: learner's licence to car licence, step by step

URL: https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/how-to-get-driving-licence-hyderabad.html
Category: Learning to drive · Published 2026-11-17 · Updated 2026-11-17

To get a driving licence in Hyderabad you first get a learner's licence, practise for at least 30 days with it, then pass a practical driving test at an RTA office. The whole process starts online and takes a few weeks if you plan your slots well.

This guide walks through each step for a car (in official language, a "light motor vehicle" or LMV, non-transport). It explains what happens and in what order, but it deliberately leaves out fees and slot rules: those change, and the official websites are the only reliable source for them. Always check the Telangana Transport Department (https://transport.telangana.gov.in) and Parivahan Sarathi (https://sarathi.parivahan.gov.in) before you apply.

## Step 1: check you are eligible

For a private car licence you need to be at least 18 years old. You also need to be able to read and understand traffic signs and rules, because that is what the learner's licence test checks, and you must be physically fit to drive. Most applicants declare their fitness on a self-declaration form; in some cases, for example with certain medical conditions or above a certain age, a medical certificate from a registered doctor is needed. The application form tells you which applies to you.

You apply to the transport office that covers your address. Hyderabad and its surroundings are served by several Regional Transport Offices and Unit Offices, and when you book online you choose from the offices offered for your area.

## Step 2: gather your documents

The exact list is shown on the application portal, and it is worth reading it before you start rather than halfway through. In general terms you will need:

- **Proof of age**, such as a birth certificate, school certificate, passport or another document the portal accepts.

- **Proof of address** in Telangana. If you have moved recently, make sure the address on your document matches where you are applying.

- **A recent photograph and your signature**, usually uploaded in a set size and format.

- **The fitness declaration or medical certificate**, as above.

Aadhaar is widely used on Parivahan Sarathi to fill in your details and, for some services, to verify your identity. Keep the phone number linked to it handy, because one-time passwords are sent to it.

Scan your documents clearly before you begin. Blurred or cropped uploads are a common reason for an application being sent back, which costs you days.

## Step 3: apply for the learner's licence online

Go to Parivahan Sarathi (https://sarathi.parivahan.gov.in) and choose Telangana as your state, or start from the Telangana Transport Department (https://transport.telangana.gov.in) website, which links to the same services. The usual order is:

- Choose the learner's licence application and fill in your personal details.

- Select the vehicle class. For a car this is LMV (non-transport). If you also want to ride a motorbike, you can add that class in the same application.

- Upload your documents, photograph and signature.

- Pay the fee online. The amount is shown on the portal at the time you apply.

- Book a slot for the learner's licence test, if your application route needs one.

Save the application number and print or download the acknowledgement. You will need it for every later step, including the driving test.

## Step 4: pass the learner's licence test

The learner's licence test is a short computer-based test on traffic rules, road signs and safe driving. You read each question and choose the right answer. Depending on the current rules and the option you choose, you may take it at the transport office or online. The portal shows what is available for Telangana when you apply.

The questions are not difficult if you have prepared, but they catch people who have only skimmed the signs. Expect questions such as what a sign means, who has the right of way at a junction, and what to do when an ambulance approaches. Practice tests are available on the official Sarathi portal, and they are the best way to see the real style of question.

Spend most of your preparation time on road signs. Learn the three families (mandatory, cautionary and informatory) and the shapes that tell them apart; our guide to road signs for the learner's licence test (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/road-signs-india-learner-licence-test.html) covers them in one place.

Once you pass, you can download your learner's licence. It is valid for six months.

## Step 5: practise during the waiting period

You must hold your learner's licence for at least 30 days before you can take the driving test. Treat this as training time, not waiting time. While you hold a learner's licence:

- Drive only with a person who holds a valid licence for that class of vehicle sitting beside you.

- Display the "L" sign on the front and back of the car, as the rules require for learners.

- Carry your learner's licence whenever you drive.

Most people in Hyderabad take lessons from a driving school, which also provides a dual-control car. That is the safest way to learn clutch control, real braking and what it feels like when a bus pulls out in front of you. Lessons with a licensed instructor matter much more than any amount of reading.

Between lessons, a simulator can help with the thinking side of driving: keeping left, indicating early, reading signals and junctions. Sawari (https://sawari.airacode.online/about.html) is a free browser simulator built on real Hyderabad roads, and it marks you on the faults that matter, such as running a red light or turning without an indicator. It is practice only, it is not connected to the RTA, and it does not replace a single lesson. Our post on driving in Hyderabad for beginners (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/driving-in-hyderabad-for-beginners.html) suggests an order for building up to busier roads.

## Step 6: book and take the driving test

After the 30 days, and before your learner's licence expires, apply for the driving licence on the same portal using your learner's licence number. Pay the test fee and book a slot at your chosen RTA office. Slots in Hyderabad can be busy, so book as soon as you are ready rather than at the last moment.

On the day, bring:

- Your learner's licence and the application acknowledgement.

- The original documents you uploaded, in case they are checked.

- A suitable car with valid registration, insurance and pollution certificate, and "L" plates. Many people use their driving school's car. Check with the office whether you need to bring one and what is accepted.

The test itself checks whether you can control the car safely and follow the rules. The format depends on the office: some use dedicated test tracks with marked lanes, others may test you on a set course. Ask your driving school, or the office, what format your office uses so you can practise for it. Our RTA driving test tips (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/telangana-rta-driving-test-tips.html) explain what examiners generally look for and the mistakes that most often lead to a fail.

Do not drive alone before you hold a full driving licence. Driving on a learner's licence without a licensed person beside you is against the rules, and your insurance may not cover you.

## Step 7: receive your licence

If you pass, your driving licence is issued and sent to your address, and you can usually see its status on Parivahan Sarathi. Digital copies held in DigiLocker or the mParivahan app are accepted as valid documents in India, which is useful if you leave the plastic card at home.

If you do not pass, you can apply to take the test again. The portal explains when you can rebook. Use the gap to work on whatever the examiner pointed out, and remember that your learner's licence must still be valid on the day.

### A quick checklist

- Confirm you are 18 or older and gather proof of age and address.

- Apply for the learner's licence online, upload documents and pay.

- Prepare road signs and rules, then pass the learner's licence test.

- Take lessons and practise for at least 30 days with "L" plates and a licensed person beside you.

- Apply for the driving licence, book a test slot and take the test.

- Check the status and download a digital copy once it is issued.

When you want to rehearse junctions, signals and lane discipline between lessons, you can try a route in Sawari (https://sawari.airacode.online/play.html) straight from your browser.

## Frequently asked questions

**What is the minimum age for a car driving licence in Telangana?**
You must be at least 18 years old to apply for a learner's licence for a car (a light motor vehicle). The same age applies across India.

**How long must I wait after my learner's licence before the driving test?**
You must hold the learner's licence for at least 30 days before you can take the driving test. The learner's licence stays valid for six months, so book your test within that window.

**Can I apply for a learner's licence online in Hyderabad?**
Yes. Applications start on Parivahan Sarathi or through the Telangana Transport Department website, where you fill in the form, upload documents, pay and book a slot. Check the official sites for which steps can be completed fully online.

**Where do I take the driving test in Hyderabad?**
At the Regional Transport Office or Unit Office you choose when you book your slot. Hyderabad has several offices; the Telangana Transport Department website lists them.

---

# Road signs in India explained for the learner's licence test

URL: https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/road-signs-india-learner-licence-test.html
Category: Learning to drive · Published 2026-11-17 · Updated 2026-11-17

Road signs in India fall into three families, and you can tell them apart by shape and colour before you can read a word: red circles give orders, red triangles give warnings, and blue rectangles give information. Learn the families first, then the individual signs, and the learner's licence test becomes much easier.

The signs used across India follow the same national system, so what you learn for the test in Hyderabad applies anywhere in the country. This guide covers the families, the signs that come up most often, road markings and hand signals. For official practice questions, use the learner's licence practice test on Parivahan Sarathi (https://sarathi.parivahan.gov.in).

## Mandatory signs: the red circles

Mandatory signs, also called regulatory signs, are instructions. Ignoring one is an offence. Most are circular.

### Prohibitory signs

A circle with a red border, usually on a white background, tells you something is not allowed. Where there is a red diagonal bar across a symbol, it is forbidden. Common examples:

- **No entry**: a red circle with a white horizontal bar. You must not drive in from your side.

- **One way** signs, which work with no entry signs to show the permitted direction.

- **No overtaking**, **no U-turn**, **no left turn** and **no right turn**.

- **No parking** and **no stopping or standing**, which have a blue background with red border and bars.

- **Horn prohibited**, often near hospitals and schools.

- **Speed limit**: a number in a red circle is the maximum speed in kilometres per hour.

- Limits on **width, height, length and weight**, shown as a number with a symbol.

### Compulsory signs

A solid blue circle with a white symbol tells you what you must do: compulsory turn left, compulsory ahead, keep left, compulsory cycle track, and so on. A common LL test trap is mixing up "no left turn" (red border, bar across the arrow) with "compulsory turn left" (blue circle, white arrow).

### Two signs with their own shapes

The **STOP** sign is a red octagon. It means stop completely at the line, look, and only go when the way is clear. Slowing down is not enough.

The **GIVE WAY** sign is a triangle pointing downwards with a red border. It means let traffic on the main road go first, and stop if you need to.

These two have unique shapes on purpose: you can recognise them from behind, or covered in dust, or in the dark.

## Cautionary signs: the red triangles

Cautionary or warning signs are triangles pointing upwards, with a red border, a white background and a black symbol. They do not order you to do anything specific; they tell you a hazard is coming so you can slow down and get ready. Examples you will see in Hyderabad and in the test:

- **Bends**: left, right, hairpin and a series of bends.

- **Junctions**: crossroads, T-junction, Y-junction, side road on the left or right, and roundabout ahead.

- **Narrow road** or **narrow bridge** ahead.

- **Pedestrian crossing**, **school ahead** and **men at work**.

- **Steep ascent** and **steep descent**.

- **Slippery road**, **loose gravel** and **falling rocks**.

- **Speed breaker** or hump ahead.

- **Cattle** and **animals crossing**.

- **Level crossing**, guarded or unguarded.

Speed breakers deserve a special mention for Hyderabad drivers: they are everywhere, not always signed, and often painted with yellow and black stripes. Our post on speed breakers and speed limits (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/speed-breakers-speed-limits-hyderabad.html) covers how to approach them.

## Informatory signs: the blue rectangles

Informatory signs are rectangles, usually blue, sometimes green on highways. They help rather than instruct. Examples:

- **Direction and place signs**, showing which lane or turn leads where.

- **Parking**: a white P on blue.

- **Hospital**, **first aid post**, **fuel station**, **eating place** and **rest area**.

- **No through road** and **U-turn** signs at median openings.

A useful rule for the test: if a sign is rectangular and blue, it is almost always information. If it is circular, it is an order. If it is a triangle pointing up, it is a warning.

Make flashcards with the symbol on one side and the meaning on the other, and sort them into the three families before you learn the details. Grouping by shape is faster than memorising a long list.

## Road markings

Paint on the road is as much a part of the rules as signs on poles, and the LL test asks about it.

- **Broken white centre line**: you may cross it to overtake or turn when it is safe.

- **Continuous centre line**: do not cross it to overtake.

- **Double continuous lines**: never cross them.

- **Lane lines**: broken lines divide lanes going the same way. Stay within your lane and indicate before you change.

- **Stop line**: a solid line across your lane at a junction or signal. Stop behind it, not on it.

- **Zebra crossing**: black and white stripes where pedestrians cross. Slow down, and stop for people waiting or crossing.

- **Arrows** painted in a lane show the directions that lane is for. Get into the right lane early.

India drives on the left, so on a two-way road you keep left of the centre line. On a dual carriageway with a median, you use the lanes on the left of the median and overtake on the right.

## Signals, hand signals and the traffic police

### Traffic lights

Red means stop behind the line. Amber means stop, unless you are so close that stopping would be unsafe. Green means go if the way is clear, still giving way to pedestrians who are already crossing. A green arrow lets you go only in the direction it shows. A flashing amber means proceed with caution.

### Driver hand signals

The test sometimes asks about the hand signals drivers use, mostly for when indicators fail. With your right arm out of the window:

- Arm stretched straight out: I am turning right.

- Arm rotated in an anticlockwise circle: I am turning left.

- Arm stretched out, palm down, moved up and down: I am slowing down.

- Arm raised straight up: I am stopping.

### Traffic police

A traffic police officer's directions override signals and signs. In broad terms, a raised hand with the palm towards you means stop, and a beckoning wave means come on. Watch the officer, not the light, when someone is directing traffic. The Hyderabad Traffic Police (https://www.htp.gov.in) publish guidance and notices for the city.

## How signs appear on the LL test

The learner's licence test is computer-based. Sign questions usually show a picture and ask what it means, or describe a situation and ask which sign applies. A few tips:

- Read every option. Wrong answers are often close: "no parking" against "no stopping", "no left turn" against "compulsory turn left".

- Use shape and colour to rule out options before you look at the symbol.

- Do the official practice test on Sarathi several times; it uses the real style of question.

- Learn the rules alongside the signs: right of way, giving way to emergency vehicles, and what to do at an uncontrolled junction.

Our step-by-step guide to getting a driving licence in Hyderabad (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/how-to-get-driving-licence-hyderabad.html) explains where the LL test fits in the whole process.

### Seeing signs in context

Signs make more sense when you see them on a real road. In Sawari (https://sawari.airacode.online/features.html), a free browser simulator on real Hyderabad routes, you drive through signals with stop lines and zebra crossings, over striped speed breakers and past U-turn signs at median openings, with the current speed limit shown on the dashboard. The debrief tells you when you ran a red or went over the limit. It is a practice aid only, not an official resource, and it does not cover every sign in the question bank. For the test itself, the official practice questions are what count.

## Frequently asked questions

**What are the three types of road signs in India?**
Mandatory (or regulatory) signs, which you must obey; cautionary (warning) signs, which tell you about a hazard ahead; and informatory signs, which give directions and information.

**What shape are mandatory road signs in India?**
Most are circles. A red-bordered circle usually forbids something, such as no entry or no overtaking, while a blue circle tells you what you must do, such as compulsory turn left. The STOP sign is a red octagon and the GIVE WAY sign is a downward-pointing triangle.

**Are road signs part of the learner's licence test?**
Yes. The learner's licence test includes questions on traffic signs as well as rules of the road. Learning the shapes and colours of each family of signs makes most questions straightforward.

**What does a solid white line in the middle of the road mean?**
A continuous centre line means you should not cross it to overtake. A broken line may be crossed when it is safe to do so. Double continuous lines must never be crossed.

---

# Telangana RTA driving test tips: how to prepare and pass in Hyderabad

URL: https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/telangana-rta-driving-test-tips.html
Category: Learning to drive · Published 2026-11-17 · Updated 2026-11-17

The RTA driving test in Hyderabad is short, and most people who fail it do so for the same handful of reasons: rolling back, touching a marker, forgetting to indicate or check mirrors, or simply letting nerves take over. These Telangana RTA driving test tips cover what examiners look for and how to practise so the test feels routine.

A note before we start: test formats vary between offices and change over time. Some RTA offices use dedicated test tracks with marked lanes; the details of each track, and how it is scored, are best learned from your driving school or the office itself. This post sticks to what is true of any fair driving test, and it is not an official guide. For the current rules, check the Telangana Transport Department (https://transport.telangana.gov.in) website.

## What examiners look for

An examiner is not looking for a racing driver. They want evidence that you can handle the car on your own without putting anyone at risk. In practice that comes down to five things.

### Control

Smooth starts, smooth stops, and steady low-speed steering. In a manual car this means clutch control: moving off without stalling or jerking, and holding the car on a slope without rolling back. Jerky, hurried movements suggest you are not in control even if you finish the course.

### Observation

Checking your mirrors before you move off, before you change direction and before you slow down. Looking over your shoulder before pulling out. Examiners notice whether your head and eyes move, not just whether you avoided something.

### Signalling

Indicating in good time before every turn or change of position, and cancelling the indicator afterwards. A signal that comes after you have started turning tells the examiner you forgot.

### Following the rules

Keeping left, obeying signs and markings, stopping fully where you must, and keeping to a sensible speed. If you are tested on a road or a course with signals, a stop line means the front of your car stops behind it.

### Composure

Mistakes happen. What matters is what you do next. If you stall, put the handbrake on, restart calmly and carry on. Panicking after a small mistake often causes a bigger one.

## Common reasons people fail

Driving schools and instructors in Hyderabad tend to name the same faults again and again. None of them are about knowledge; they are about habits.

- **Rolling back or stalling on a slope.** If your office tests a start on an incline, this is the classic fail. Practise the handbrake start until it is boring.

- **Touching a line, kerb or marker.** On a marked course, going outside the lines or knocking a pole usually counts heavily. This is a matter of slow speed and reference points, not luck.

- **No mirror checks.** Many learners do look, but only with their eyes and too quickly to be noticed. Make the check deliberate.

- **Late or missing indicators.** Indicate before you brake and turn, not during.

- **Going too fast in tight spaces.** Speed makes every manoeuvre harder. Creep. There is no prize for finishing quickly.

- **Not following the examiner's instruction.** Listen to the whole instruction before you move. If you did not hear it, ask them to repeat it.

- **Paperwork problems.** An expired learner's licence, a car without valid documents or missing L plates can stop the test before it starts.

Ask your instructor to give you a mock test on the same kind of course, marked as strictly as the real one. Hearing "that would have been a fail" in a lesson is much cheaper than hearing it on the day.

## A four-week practice plan

You must hold your learner's licence for at least 30 days before the test, which fits neatly with a four-week plan. Adjust it around your lessons; the point is steady practice rather than cramming. (If you have not got your learner's licence yet, start with our guide to getting a driving licence in Hyderabad (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/how-to-get-driving-licence-hyderabad.html).)

### Week 1: the car

Get to know the controls with your instructor in a quiet place. Seat and mirror adjustment, moving off and stopping, clutch control at walking pace, steering hand positions. Do not hurry onto busy roads.

### Week 2: habits

Build the routine you will use on test day: mirrors, signal, manoeuvre. Every turn, every time. Practise stopping smoothly at a line. On quieter roads, work on keeping a steady position on the left of your lane. Our post on indicators and lane discipline (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/indicators-and-lane-discipline.html) goes into this in more detail.

### Week 3: the manoeuvres

Find out what your office tests and practise exactly that. If it includes reversing between markers, parking in a marked bay or a start on a slope, set up something similar with your instructor and repeat it many times. Pick reference points on the car, such as where a line meets the edge of the bonnet or the mirror, so you are not guessing.

### Week 4: test conditions

Do full mock tests. Drive the course start to finish without coaching, then talk through what went wrong. Practise at the time of day your slot is booked if you can. In the last few days, do less, not more: you want to arrive calm and rested.

## Where a simulator fits in

A driving simulator cannot teach clutch control, the bite point, or how hard to press a real brake pedal. It cannot test you on an RTA track. What it can do is drill the decisions that become habits, at home, as often as you like.

Sawari (https://sawari.airacode.online/features.html) is a free browser simulator on real Hyderabad roads. It drives on the left with a right-hand-drive car and an automatic gearbox, and it logs faults as they happen: no indicator before a turn, running a red light, speeding, drifting right of the centre line, leaving the road, collisions and taking speed breakers too fast. The debrief at the end lists each one with advice. Repeating a route until the debrief is clean is a good way to make "signal before every turn" automatic.

Be clear about what it is: practice only. It is not affiliated with the RTA, its routes are not test routes, it has no mirrors, and its score means nothing to an examiner. Use it between lessons, never instead of them. Our guide to free online driving simulators in India (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/free-online-driving-simulator-india.html) explains more about what simulator practice can and cannot do.

## On the day of the test

- Check your documents the night before: learner's licence, application acknowledgement, originals of what you uploaded, and the car's papers if you are bringing it.

- Arrive early. Rushing in late is a poor start to a test of calm driving.

- Adjust your seat and mirrors before you start, even in a familiar car. Examiners often watch this.

- Put your seatbelt on before you start the engine.

- Drive the way you have practised, a little slower if anything.

- If you make a mistake, keep going. Small errors are not always a fail; giving up is.

Never drive alone on a learner's licence to "get extra practice" before the test. Always have a person holding a valid licence beside you and L plates on the car.

## If you do not pass

It is common to fail a driving test the first time, and it is not a judgement on whether you will be a good driver. Ask what went wrong, write it down, and practise that specific thing. The portal explains when you can book again. Check that your learner's licence will still be valid on the new date, because it lasts six months from issue.

Once you have your licence, the real learning starts on real roads. When you want to rehearse a busy route before you drive it, you can open Sawari in your browser (https://sawari.airacode.online/play.html) and try it first.

## Frequently asked questions

**What is checked in the RTA driving test for a car?**
The examiner checks that you can control the car smoothly and safely, follow the rules, use your indicators and mirrors, and complete the manoeuvres set at that office. The exact format depends on the RTA office, so ask your driving school or the office beforehand.

**What are the most common reasons for failing the driving test?**
Typical reasons are rolling back or stalling, touching a boundary or marker, not checking mirrors, forgetting to indicate, and losing control at low speed. Nerves cause many of these, which is why repeated practice of the exact manoeuvres helps.

**Can I take the driving test in an automatic car?**
Rules and office practice on this can change, so check with the Telangana Transport Department or your RTA office before you book. Whatever car you use, it must be roadworthy, registered, insured and show L plates.

**Does practising on a driving simulator help with the RTA test?**
It can help with habits such as indicating, keeping left and stopping at the line, but it cannot teach clutch control or the feel of a real car. Use it alongside lessons with a licensed instructor, not instead of them.

# Defensive driving tips for India: the habits that keep you out of trouble

URL: https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/defensive-driving-tips-india.html
Category: Road skills · Published 2026-11-23 · Updated 2026-11-23

Defensive driving in India comes down to a few habits: keep a buffer of space around your car, stay at least three seconds behind the vehicle ahead, scan far ahead and to the sides, assume others will make mistakes, and slow down for the conditions. In mixed traffic the space keeps getting filled, so the skill is rebuilding it calmly, again and again.

Most crashes are not caused by one dramatic error. They happen when a small mistake by one road user meets a driver with no time or space to react. Defensive driving is about always leaving yourself that time and space. This guide adapts the standard habits to Indian roads, with Hyderabad examples.

## What is the space cushion, and how do you keep one in Indian traffic?

The space cushion is a buffer of empty road around your car, in front, behind and to the sides, that gives you somewhere to go if something goes wrong.

In a city full of scooters and autos you will never have a perfect empty box around you, and that is fine. The habit is to notice when the cushion has gone and quietly rebuild it:

- **In front:** this is the space you control best. Ease off when someone cuts in, rather than closing up to stop them.

- **To the sides:** avoid sitting right beside a bus or truck, or level with a car in the next lane for long periods. Drop back or move ahead so you have an escape route.

- **Behind:** you cannot control a tailgater, but you can give yourself a bigger gap in front so that you never have to brake hard.

- **At a stop:** stop where you can still see the rear tyres of the car in front touching the road. That leaves room to steer round it if it breaks down or rolls back.

## How big a gap should you leave to the vehicle ahead?

Leave at least a two-second gap in good conditions, and three seconds or more in traffic, rain or at night; this is the most important single defensive habit.

The Motor Vehicles (Driving) Regulations, 2017 say a driver must keep enough distance from the vehicle ahead to stop safely if it slows or stops suddenly, and must increase that distance in rain and other bad weather. The regulations do not give a figure, so drivers use a time-based rule of thumb. The current regulations are listed on the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways legislation page (https://morth.gov.in/en/Motor-Vehicle-Legislation).

- Pick a fixed point ahead, such as a lamp post, a metro pillar or a road sign.

- When the rear of the vehicle in front passes it, start counting: "one thousand and one, one thousand and two, one thousand and three".

- If your front bumper reaches the point before you finish, drop back.

A time gap works at any speed because the distance grows as you go faster. Someone will often slip into the gap you leave. Let them, and drop back again; arriving one car-length later costs you nothing.

| Situation | Suggested minimum gap |
|---|---|
| Dry road, good visibility, light traffic | 2 seconds |
| Normal city traffic | 3 seconds |
| Behind a bus, truck or auto that may stop suddenly | 3 seconds or more, and stay out of its blind spot |
| Rain, wet roads, night or a new driver | 4 seconds or more |

These are common driving-school guidelines, not legal limits.

## Where should you be looking?

Look far ahead, not at the bumper in front of you, and keep your eyes moving across the whole scene every few seconds.

- **Look 10 to 15 seconds ahead.** Watch the brake lights two or three vehicles in front, the signal at the next junction and the traffic building up near a U-turn opening. You will slow early and smoothly instead of braking late.

- **Scan the edges.** Pedestrians stepping off the footpath, a scooter leaving a side lane, a parked car's door, a dog, an auto pulling out from the kerb. In Hyderabad most surprises come from the left edge.

- **Check your mirrors** every five to eight seconds, and always before you slow down, change lanes or turn. Our guide to indicators and lane discipline (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/indicators-and-lane-discipline.html) explains the mirror, signal, move routine.

- **Do not stare.** Fixing your eyes on one hazard means you miss the next one.

## Why should you assume other road users will make mistakes?

Because some of them will, and if you have already planned for it, their mistake does not become your crash.

This is not about blaming others. It is about reading what might happen and having an answer ready. Some patterns worth expecting on Indian roads:

- An auto or bus will stop, or pull out, without signalling.

- A two-wheeler will pass on your left as you turn left.

- A vehicle will come the wrong way along the edge of a divided road to reach a nearby U-turn.

- A pedestrian will cross between stationary cars in a jam.

- Someone will jump an amber or red light at a junction.

When you see a likely hazard, take your foot off the accelerator and rest it over the brake. This "covering the brake" cuts your reaction time without slowing you much. Our guide to sharing the road with autos, buses and two-wheelers (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/sharing-the-road-autos-buses-two-wheelers.html) goes deeper into each type of road user.

Make yourself predictable too: indicate early, change lanes gradually and avoid sudden braking unless you have to. The Driving Regulations also tell drivers not to brake suddenly without a compelling reason when someone is following.

## How do you choose a safe speed for the conditions?

The speed limit is the maximum, not the target; a safe speed is the one at which you can stop within the distance you can see to be clear.

- **Busy streets and markets:** crawl. People and vehicles can appear from anywhere.

- **Rain:** slow down well before the water. Wet roads lengthen stopping distances and water hides potholes. See our monsoon driving guide (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/monsoon-driving-hyderabad.html).

- **Night:** drive at a speed that lets you stop within the reach of your headlights, and watch for unlit vehicles and dark clothing.

- **Speed breakers:** many are poorly marked, so slow down where they are likely, such as near schools, hospitals and junctions.

Speed limits vary by road and are posted on signs; our guide to speed breakers and speed limits in Hyderabad (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/speed-breakers-speed-limits-hyderabad.html) covers them.

## How do you stay safe at junctions and when you are tired?

Junctions are where paths cross, so slow down, cover the brake and check every direction even on a green light; and never drive when you are drowsy.

### Junctions

- Get into the right lane early, before the junction, not in it.

- On a fresh green, look left and right before moving off. Red-light runners are most common in the first seconds after the change.

- When turning left, check the mirror and the blind spot for two-wheelers squeezing through on your left.

- At unsignalled junctions, edge forward slowly until you can see, and give way when in doubt.

### Fatigue

Tiredness slows reactions in much the same way as alcohol, and a few seconds of microsleep at highway speed is enough to cross into another lane. Warning signs include yawning, heavy eyelids, missing an exit and drifting in your lane.

- Plan a break every two hours or so on long drives, and share the driving if you can.

- Avoid driving in the hours when you would normally be asleep.

- If you feel drowsy, stop somewhere safe and rest. Opening the window or turning up the music does not fix it.

## Can you practise defensive habits in a simulator?

You can practise the scanning, signalling and junction habits, though not the feel of real braking. Sawari is a free browser driving simulator on five real Hyderabad routes, with an automatic car and traffic that keeps left. It runs on a phone with an on-screen steering wheel, a tablet, a laptop or a PC.

It checks keep-left, indicators, signals and speed breakers, and the debrief at the end lists every fault, including collisions. It has no mirrors and no weather, so it cannot train mirror checks or wet-road gaps. It is practice only. Try Cyber Towers to Jubilee Hills (https://sawari.airacode.online/play.html?route=hitec-city) in heavy traffic and see how many junctions you get through with a clean record.

Never use a hand-held phone while driving. The Driving Regulations prohibit it, and it destroys every habit on this page.

## Frequently asked questions

**What is defensive driving?**
Defensive driving means driving so that you can avoid a crash even when other road users make mistakes. In practice it is a set of habits: keeping space around your car, looking well ahead, expecting the unexpected and adjusting your speed to the conditions.

**What is the three-second rule in driving?**
Pick a fixed point such as a pole. When the vehicle ahead passes it, count three seconds; if you reach the point before you finish, you are too close. It is a rule of thumb, not a legal figure, and you should allow more in rain, at night or behind trucks and buses.

**Is defensive driving possible in Indian traffic?**
Yes, though it looks different from a textbook. Gaps get filled by two-wheelers, so the aim is not a perfect empty space but a buffer you keep rebuilding, plus a constant habit of scanning and covering the brake when something might move into your path.

**Is there a law about following distance in India?**
Yes. The Motor Vehicles (Driving) Regulations, 2017 require drivers to keep enough distance from the vehicle ahead to stop safely if it slows or stops suddenly, and to increase that distance in bad weather. The law does not set a number of seconds or metres.

# How to overtake safely in India: the rules and the technique

URL: https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/how-to-overtake-safely-india.html
Category: Road skills · Published 2026-11-23 · Updated 2026-11-23

To overtake safely in India, pass on the right, only where you can see the road ahead is clear, never across a solid centre line, on a bend, at a junction or near a pedestrian crossing, and indicate before you pull out and before you move back left. If you have any doubt, do not overtake.

Overtaking is one of the riskiest manoeuvres in driving, because for a few seconds you may be on the wrong side of the road. This guide sets out what the law says, based on the Motor Vehicles (Driving) Regulations, 2017, and then the technique, with notes for two-lane highways and trucks.

## Which side should you overtake on in India?

On the right. India drives on the left, so the normal rule is to overtake on the right of the vehicle you are passing.

The Driving Regulations allow passing on the left only in a few situations:

- on a road with two or more marked lanes in your direction, where you can pass safely within your lane;

- when the driver ahead has signalled and is turning right or making a U-turn;

- when passing a stationary vehicle, as long as it is safe.

On multi-lane city roads such as those in Hyderabad, traffic often moves at different speeds in different lanes, and that is not the same as weaving left and right around one car to get ahead. Keep to your lane and change lanes only with a signal and a clear mirror. Our guide to indicators and lane discipline (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/indicators-and-lane-discipline.html) covers lane changes.

## When is overtaking illegal?

Overtaking is not allowed whenever the road ahead is not clearly visible and free, and in a list of specific places set out in Regulation 14 of the Driving Regulations.

| Do not overtake | Why |
|---|---|
| When the traffic situation ahead is not clear | You cannot judge whether you can complete the pass |
| Where a sign prohibits overtaking | A mandatory sign; ignoring it is an offence |
| Across a continuous single or double solid centre line | Solid lines mark places where crossing is unsafe |
| On a bend or corner, or where an obstruction blocks your view | Oncoming traffic can appear with no warning |
| At junctions, intersections and pedestrian crossings | Vehicles turn and people cross in your path |
| Where the road narrows or the number of lanes reduces | There may not be room to move back in |
| On a narrow culvert | No space to escape |
| In a school, hospital or construction zone indicated by signs | Children, patients and workers on or near the road |
| If it would get in the way of oncoming traffic | You must never force oncoming vehicles to brake or swerve |

The regulations also say you must not exceed the speed limit while overtaking. You can find them on the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways legislation page (https://morth.gov.in/en/Motor-Vehicle-Legislation), listed as G.S.R. 634(E), 23 June 2017.

### Solid and broken centre lines

A broken centre line means you may cross it to overtake when it is safe. A continuous solid line, white or yellow, single or double, means you must not cross it to overtake. The regulations also tell drivers not to drive over a solid longitudinal line or a painted traffic island except to get round an obstruction.

## How do you overtake safely, step by step?

Use a clear, unhurried routine every time: decide, check, signal, pass briskly, and move back only when you have left a safe gap.

- **Ask whether you need to.** If the vehicle ahead is only a little slower, or a turn-off is close, stay behind.

- **Hang back.** Keep a good following gap. Sitting close behind a truck hides the road ahead and leaves you no room.

- **Look ahead.** Move slightly right within your lane to see past the vehicle. Check for oncoming traffic, junctions, bends, crossings, signs and solid lines.

- **Check mirrors and blind spot.** Make sure nobody is already overtaking you, and look for a two-wheeler on your right.

- **Signal right.** Indicate in good time. On open roads outside built-up areas, the regulations say you may give a short horn note or a brief headlight flash to warn the driver ahead.

- **Pass briskly.** Accelerate firmly but within the speed limit. Do not hang alongside the vehicle.

- **Signal left and move back** once you can see the whole front of the vehicle you passed in your interior mirror. Do not cut in.

- **Cancel the indicator** and settle back to your normal speed.

If a vehicle appears ahead while you are passing and you are not sure you will make it, abort: ease off, signal left and drop back behind the vehicle you were passing.

## How do you overtake trucks on a two-lane highway?

With more space and more time than you think you need, because trucks are long, block your view and move around in the wind and on uneven roads.

- **Drop well back first.** From further back you can see past the truck and you are visible in its mirrors.

- **Do not trust a truck's right indicator as a signal to pass.** Drivers sometimes use it to mean "go ahead", but it may simply mean the truck is turning right. The Driving Regulations tell drivers not to use the right indicator to invite others to overtake, so treat a blinking right indicator as a turn.

- **Allow for length.** A loaded truck, or two trucks close together, can take far longer to pass than a car.

- **Watch for a second vehicle overtaking from the other direction** at the same moment. On busy state highways this is common.

- **Be extra wary at dusk and at night**, when it is hard to judge the speed of oncoming headlights.

Divided highways and expressways are much safer for overtaking, because there is no oncoming traffic in your carriageway. Even there, slow trucks usually keep left and you pass on the right. If you are planning a long trip, our guides to driving Hyderabad to Vijayawada (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/hyderabad-to-vijayawada-drive.html) and the Outer Ring Road (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/hyderabad-outer-ring-road-guide.html) cover the roads.

## What should you do when someone is overtaking you?

Keep left, hold your speed or ease off a little, and let them move back in front of you.

The Driving Regulations say the driver of a vehicle being overtaken must not increase speed or prevent the overtaking vehicle from returning to the left side. In practice:

- Stay towards the left of your lane.

- Do not speed up or race the vehicle beside you, even if it irritates you.

- If the overtaking driver has misjudged an oncoming vehicle, slow down to give them a gap to move into.

- Do not start an overtake of your own while you are being overtaken.

The same thinking applies in town when someone cuts in: drop back and rebuild your gap. Our guide to defensive driving in India (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/defensive-driving-tips-india.html) covers that habit.

## Does Sawari let you practise overtaking?

Only in a limited way. Sawari is a free browser driving simulator on five real Hyderabad city routes, with an automatic car and traffic that keeps left. It runs on a phone with an on-screen steering wheel, a tablet, a laptop or a PC. The debrief lists faults such as a missing indicator, drifting right of the centre line, red lights and collisions, which helps with signalling and lane discipline when you pass slower traffic on city roads.

It has no mirrors and no highway routes, so it cannot teach you to judge oncoming traffic on a two-lane road. It is practice only. Try Banjara Hills Road No. 1 (https://sawari.airacode.online/play.html?route=banjara-hills) with heavy traffic to practise changing lanes around buses and autos.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is overtaking from the left allowed in India?**
Generally no; you should overtake on the right. The Motor Vehicles (Driving) Regulations, 2017 allow passing on the left only in limited cases, such as on a multi-lane road with marked lanes, when the vehicle ahead has signalled and is turning right or making a U-turn, or when passing a stationary vehicle safely.

**Can you overtake across a solid white or yellow centre line?**
No. The Driving Regulations prohibit overtaking by crossing a continuous single or double solid centre line. A broken line means you may cross it when it is safe and clear.

**Where is overtaking not allowed?**
Overtaking is prohibited where the road ahead is not clear, where signs prohibit it, across a solid centre line, on bends and corners or where your view is blocked, at junctions and pedestrian crossings, where the road narrows, on narrow culverts and in signed school, hospital or construction zones.

**What should you do when someone is overtaking you?**
Keep left, hold a steady speed or ease off slightly, and do not speed up or block the overtaking vehicle from moving back in. The Driving Regulations specifically say the driver being overtaken must not increase speed.

# What to do after a car accident in Hyderabad: a step-by-step guide

URL: https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/what-to-do-after-car-accident-hyderabad.html
Category: Road skills · Published 2026-11-23 · Updated 2026-11-23

After a car accident in Hyderabad, first make the scene safe and switch on your hazard lights, then call 112 if anyone is hurt or the road is blocked. Help the injured without moving them unless they are in danger, report the accident to the police, take photos, swap details and tell your insurer as soon as you can.

Accidents are frightening, and it is easy to forget what to do. This guide gives the steps in order, along with what the law says about helping victims, as of November 2026. It is general information, not legal advice; if your accident is serious, speak to the police and, if needed, a lawyer.

## What should you do in the first few minutes?

Stop, make yourself and the scene safe, and check whether anyone is hurt; everything else can wait.

- **Stop the car.** Do not drive away from an accident you are involved in, even a minor one.

- **Switch on the hazard lights** and, if you have one, place a warning triangle well behind the car.

- **Switch off the engine** and apply the handbrake. If there is a smell of fuel, keep everyone away from the car and do not smoke.

- **Get out on the safe side**, away from moving traffic, and stand behind a barrier or on the footpath. On a flyover or the Outer Ring Road, traffic is fast, so do not stand between vehicles.

- **Check for injuries**, in your car first and then in the other vehicles. Look for pedestrians and two-wheeler riders who may have been thrown clear.

- **Move the cars only if** nobody is hurt, the damage is minor and the cars are blocking traffic. Take photos first.

Stay calm and polite. Arguments after an accident can escalate quickly, especially if a crowd gathers. If you feel unsafe, stay in your locked car and call 112.

## Which emergency number should you call in Telangana?

Call 112. It is Telangana's single emergency number for police, ambulance and fire, and it works from any phone.

Telangana Police moved its emergency response to 112 under the national Emergency Response Support System, and launched an upgraded 112 platform at the Telangana Integrated Command and Control Centre in Hyderabad in August 2026, replacing the old practice of calling Dial 100 for the police. The 108 ambulance service continues to run in Telangana, so you can also call 108 for an ambulance.

| Number | What it is for |
|---|---|
| 112 | All emergencies: police, ambulance and fire |
| 108 | Emergency ambulance |

When you call, give the exact location: the road name, the nearest landmark, flyover or metro station, and which direction you were travelling. Say how many people are hurt and whether anyone is trapped or unconscious.

## How can you help the injured, and are you protected?

Help as far as you safely can and get medical help fast; the law protects people who help accident victims in good faith.

### Basic help

- **Do not move an injured person** unless they are in immediate danger, such as from fire or traffic. Moving someone with a neck or back injury can make it worse.

- **Talk to them** and keep them calm and warm.

- **Press firmly on heavy bleeding** with a clean cloth.

- **Do not give food or water** to a seriously injured person.

- **Do not remove a rider's helmet** unless they cannot breathe.

### Good Samaritan protection

Section 134A, added to the Motor Vehicles Act in 2019, says a Good Samaritan, someone who helps in good faith and voluntarily, without expecting a reward, is not liable in any civil or criminal action for injury or death of the victim caused by their negligence in giving emergency help. The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways then notified rules for Good Samaritans on 29 September 2020 (G.S.R. 594(E) (https://morth.nic.in/sites/default/files/notifications_document/GSR%20594%28E%29%2029th%20September%202020%20Good%20Samaritan.pdf)). Under them:

- no police officer or other person can force you to give your name, address or other personal details;

- if you only informed the police or took the victim to hospital, you cannot be put through further requirements by the police or the hospital;

- hospitals must display a charter of Good Samaritans' rights, and give you an acknowledgement if you ask for one;

- being a witness is voluntary.

The government's Rah-Veer scheme (https://morth.nic.in/sites/default/files/Scheme-Guidelines-on-RahVeer.pdf) also rewards a Good Samaritan who saves the life of a victim of a serious road accident with Rs 25,000. In addition, a central scheme, now called PM RAHAT, provides eligible accident victims with cashless treatment of up to Rs 1.5 lakh for seven days at designated hospitals; calling 112 can link the victim to one.

These protections are for bystanders. If you are the driver involved, the law still requires you to stop, try to get medical help for anyone injured and report the accident.

## When do you need to report the accident to the police?

If anyone is injured or killed, the accident must be reported to the police; for damage only, a report is often still wise.

Under Section 134 of the Motor Vehicles Act, a driver involved in an accident in which someone is injured, or third-party property is damaged, must take reasonable steps to get medical attention for the injured, give the police the information they ask for and report the accident at the nearest police station if no officer is present. Not doing so is an offence.

In practice, police who attend will note the details, and in an injury case a First Information Report (FIR) is usually registered at the police station that covers the area. Ask for the FIR number or a copy, because your insurer and any compensation claim will need it. In Hyderabad, the city is policed by the Hyderabad, Cyberabad and Rachakonda commissionerates; the Hyderabad Traffic Police (https://www.htp.gov.in) site has contact details.

For a small scrape with nobody hurt, the drivers often agree to settle it themselves. That is your choice, but it means you cannot easily claim on insurance later if the other driver changes their mind, so think before you skip the police.

## What evidence should you collect?

Photos, details and names, collected calmly at the scene, make everything that follows easier.

- **Photos** of both cars from several angles, the damage up close, number plates, the road layout, signals, skid marks and any road signs, before the cars are moved if possible.

- **The other driver's details:** name, phone number, vehicle number, and their insurer and policy number if they will share it.

- **Witnesses:** names and phone numbers of anyone who saw it and is willing to help.

- **Dashcam footage**, if you have a dashcam. Save the clip before it is recorded over.

- **Notes:** the time, place and what happened, written down while you remember it.

Do not admit fault or sign anything at the scene beyond what the police ask for. Stick to the facts.

## How do you make an insurance claim?

Tell your insurer as soon as you can, follow its process, and do not start repairs until it says so.

- Call your insurer's claim helpline or use its app, and get a claim number.

- Keep the documents it asks for ready. These usually include your policy, registration certificate, driving licence and, for injury or theft cases, the FIR.

- Let the insurer's surveyor inspect the damage, usually at a network garage for cashless repair.

- If another vehicle was involved and someone was injured, a third-party claim goes through the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal, so inform your insurer straight away.

Our guide to car insurance basics in India (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/car-insurance-basics-india.html) explains third-party and comprehensive cover. Most accidents can be avoided with a bigger gap and earlier braking; see our defensive driving tips (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/defensive-driving-tips-india.html).

## Can a simulator help you avoid accidents?

It can help you build the habits that prevent many of them. Sawari is a free browser driving simulator on five real Hyderabad routes, and its debrief lists every fault, including collisions, red lights, missed indicators and speed breakers taken too fast. It runs on a phone with an on-screen steering wheel, a tablet, a laptop or a PC. It does not simulate crashes or what to do after them, and it is practice only. Try Tank Bund Road (https://sawari.airacode.online/play.html?route=tank-bund) at night with traffic on.

## Frequently asked questions

**What number do I call after an accident in Hyderabad?**
Call 112, Telangana's single emergency number, which connects to police, ambulance and fire services. The 108 ambulance service also continues to operate in Telangana. Both are free to call from any phone.

**Will I get into trouble for helping an accident victim?**
No. Section 134A of the Motor Vehicles Act protects Good Samaritans who help in good faith from civil and criminal liability, and the 2020 Good Samaritan rules say you cannot be forced to give your name or address and need not stay at the hospital if you only brought the victim in.

**Do I need to file an FIR for a minor car accident?**
If anyone is injured or killed, the accident must be reported to the police. For minor damage only, many people settle between themselves, but your insurer may ask for a police report before it pays a claim, so check your policy before deciding.

**How soon should I inform my insurance company after an accident?**
As soon as you reasonably can, ideally the same day. Policies set their own notice periods and documents, so read yours, and do not get the car repaired before the insurer has had a chance to inspect it unless it tells you to go ahead.

---

# Driving on flyovers in Hyderabad: ramps, lanes, merging and gradients

URL: https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/driving-on-flyovers-hyderabad.html
Category: Road skills · Published 2026-11-17 · Updated 2026-11-17

Driving on flyovers in Hyderabad is mostly simple: you pick the right lane before the ramp, hold a steady speed, keep your distance and never stop. Most mistakes happen in the last hundred metres before a ramp, when drivers realise too late that they wanted the road below.

## Hyderabad's flyovers at a glance

Hyderabad has built a lot of elevated road. The best known is the **PV Narasimha Rao Expressway**, about 11.6 km of elevated road on pillars from Mehdipatnam towards Aramghar. It carries traffic over the busy roads below and links the city with the road to Rajiv Gandhi International Airport at Shamshabad.

Most of the city's flyovers are shorter: single or double spans that lift through traffic over a busy junction, with a service road and signal below for traffic that wants to turn. Many newer ones were built under the state's Strategic Road Development Plan, especially across the IT corridor around HITEC City and Gachibowli.

Then there are bridges that are not flyovers but drive like them, such as the Durgam Cheruvu cable bridge between Madhapur and Jubilee Hills. The same rules apply on all of them.

## Choose your lane before the ramp

A flyover splits the road in two. The ramp takes you up and over the junction; the service road beside it takes you down to the signal, where you can turn. Once you are on the wrong one, there is no way across.

- **Know where you are going** before you reach the junction. If you want to turn at it, you almost always want the road below. If you are going straight through, you usually want the ramp.

- **Read the overhead and roadside signs.** They tell you where the flyover lands, and that is not always obvious.

- **Move across early.** Check, signal, and change lanes well before the point where the ramp and service road divide. Our guide to indicators and lane discipline (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/indicators-and-lane-discipline.html) covers how.

- **Never cut across the chevrons.** The striped wedge at the start of the ramp is there because vehicles do not belong there. If you have missed it, take the road you are on and find another way back.

Do not stop or slow sharply at the split to decide. Traffic behind you expects you to keep moving. A wrong choice costs a few minutes and a U-turn further on.

## Gradients: going up and coming down

Ramps are steeper than most city roads. On the way up, a heavily loaded car, an auto or a lorry will slow down, sometimes a lot. Leave a good gap so you are not forced to stop on the slope. If you drive a manual, be ready to change down a gear early rather than letting the engine labour.

At the top, you often cannot see what is beyond the crest. Traffic may have stopped at the landing, or a broken-down vehicle may be just over the top. Do not overtake approaching a crest, and keep your speed down until you can see the way ahead.

On the way down, gravity is on your side, which is the problem. Ease off the accelerator early and let your speed settle before the landing, because there is often a junction, a bus stop or a speed breaker soon after the bottom of the ramp. Watch for brake lights on the road ahead.

### Curves on elevated roads

Some flyovers curve as they turn over a junction, and those curves can be tighter than they look from the approach. There is no verge to run onto and only a parapet beside you. Slow down before the curve, not in it, and respect any speed limit posted on the flyover itself.

## Merging at the landing

The end of a flyover is a merge: you rejoin traffic from the service road, often with buses and autos pulling in at the same point. Some flyovers also have slip roads joining part way along.

- Coming off the flyover, stay in your lane, look left for vehicles from the service road and be ready to take turns.

- Joining from a slip road, build up speed on the slip, signal right, look over your shoulder and fit into a gap. Do not stop at the end of the slip unless the traffic forces you to.

- If you are on the flyover and see someone trying to merge, ease off a little or move right if it is safe. A smooth merge helps everyone behind you too.

## No stopping, no reversing, no photos

Flyovers usually have no hard shoulder and no footpath worth the name. A stopped car blocks a live lane on a road where nobody expects it. Do not stop for any reason except a real breakdown or emergency, and never stop to take photos or enjoy the view. The cable bridge in particular draws people at night for pictures; enjoy it from the footpaths and viewpoints meant for that, not from the carriageway.

If you do break down, switch on your hazard lights, get everyone out on the side away from traffic if it is safe to do so, and call for help. Never reverse back down a ramp because you went up the wrong one.

Restrictions differ between flyovers. Some are closed to certain vehicles, some are closed at certain hours, and the police often close flyovers on special nights such as New Year's Eve. Always check the signs at the foot of the ramp.

### Night and rain

Elevated roads catch more wind and can feel exposed in heavy rain. Water also runs down ramps and collects at the bottom, where it hides potholes. Slow down, leave a longer gap and use dipped headlights. Our posts on night driving (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/night-driving-hyderabad-tips.html) and monsoon driving (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/monsoon-driving-hyderabad.html) have more.

## Practising flyovers in Sawari

Sawari is a free browser driving simulator on real Hyderabad roads, built from OpenStreetMap with real elevation data, so its flyovers rise and fall the way the ramps do. The Cyber Towers to Jubilee Hills route (https://sawari.airacode.online/routes.html#hitec-city) is the one to practise on. It runs from Cyber Towers past Inorbit Mall, across the Durgam Cheruvu cable bridge and along Road No. 36, with flyover ramps, lane choice before the bridge and merging traffic at Inorbit Mall.

- **Follow the blue band.** It shows your lane and tells you early whether you want the ramp or the road below. Turn-by-turn directions, with an optional voice, give you the next instruction in time.

- **Signal lane changes** with `Q` and `E`. The indicator cancels itself after the turn, and a missed signal before a route turn shows up in your debrief.

- **Feel the gradient.** The car's physics include weight transfer, so you will notice it slowing on the way up and running on as you come down. Watch the speed limit sign on the screen and ease off before the landing.

- **Take the wrong ramp?** Press `R` to return to the route. There is no reversing back down in real life, so treat it as a lesson about planning your lane earlier.

Try it in the driver's seat (`C`) with traffic set to Busy or Dense, then read the debrief, which lists every fault with advice. Start the HITEC City drive here (https://sawari.airacode.online/play.html?route=hitec-city), and read our HITEC City to Jubilee Hills route guide (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/hitec-city-to-jubilee-hills-drive.html) before you go.

## Frequently asked questions

**How long is the PV Narasimha Rao Expressway?**
It is about 11.6 km long, an elevated road on pillars running from Mehdipatnam towards Aramghar and the road to the airport.

**Can I stop on a flyover in Hyderabad?**
No, apart from a genuine breakdown or emergency. Flyovers have no hard shoulder, so a stopped car blocks a lane where following traffic does not expect it. Never stop for photos.

**Which lane should I use on a flyover?**
Pick your lane before the ramp: the flyover carries through traffic, the service road below takes you to the junction. Once on the flyover, keep left unless overtaking, and move across early for the exit you need.

**Are two-wheelers allowed on Hyderabad flyovers?**
Rules differ between flyovers and change from time to time, and some flyovers are closed at certain hours. Check the signs at the ramp before you go up.
