# How to drive at roundabouts in India: give way, go clockwise, signal your exit

URL: https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/roundabouts-how-to-drive-india.html
Category: Road skills · Published 2026-11-17 · Updated 2026-11-17

To drive at roundabouts in India, remember three things: go round clockwise, give way to traffic already on the roundabout, which comes from your right, and signal left as you leave. The rest is choosing the right lane and keeping an eye on the two-wheelers that cut inside you.

## How a roundabout works in left-hand traffic

A roundabout, often called a rotary or a circle in India, is a junction where every vehicle travels round a central island in the same direction. Because India drives on the left, that direction is clockwise: you turn left onto the roundabout and the island stays on your right the whole way round.

A roundabout replaces the question "who goes first across the junction?" with a simpler one: "is there a gap?" Everyone flows the same way, at low speed, and nobody has to cross oncoming traffic. That is why roundabouts work well, provided drivers follow the same few rules.

In India you will meet everything from a small painted circle in a colony to large rotaries around a statue or monument. Some busy ones are controlled by signals or by traffic police at peak hours. When they are, follow the lights or the officer, not the general rules below.

## Approaching and giving way

### Slow down early

Look for the roundabout sign and the road markings, and slow down well before the entry. Pick your lane on the approach (see the next section) and signal if you need to.

### Give way to the right

As you reach the entry, look right. Traffic already on the roundabout, coming from your right, has priority. Wait for a gap that lets you join without making anyone brake. Look left too, because pedestrians often cross at the entry and exit, and riders sometimes come the wrong way round the edge.

Do not stop on the roundabout itself to let people in, unless traffic is at a standstill. A driver who stops unexpectedly on the circle confuses everyone behind them.

### Join smoothly

Once there is a gap, go. Hesitating at the line and then lunging into a smaller gap is how most roundabout bumps happen. If you are unsure, wait for the next one.

## Choosing a lane and signalling

Think of the roundabout as a clock face, with you arriving at six o'clock. Your exit decides your lane and your signal.

| Where you are going | Approach lane | Signal |
|---|---|---|
| First exit (left, about nine o'clock) | Left lane | Left on the approach, and keep it on as you leave |
| Straight on (about twelve o'clock) | Left lane, or as marked | No signal on the approach; left after you pass the exit before yours |
| Right (about three o'clock) or full circle | Right lane | Right on the approach; left after you pass the exit before yours |

Lane arrows painted on the approach override this pattern, so follow them where they exist. On a single-lane roundabout, which is common in India, there is only one lane to choose: the signals still matter.

### Going round

If you are going right or all the way round, keep to the inside, near the island, until you are nearly at your exit. Then check left, signal left and move out towards the exit. Do not cut straight across the outer lane, because a vehicle may be there.

### Leaving

Signal left just after you pass the exit before yours. That tells drivers waiting at your exit that you are leaving, so they can join safely, and tells the driver behind what you are doing. Leave in the lane that lines up with your exit, and watch for pedestrians crossing the road you are entering.

## What makes Indian roundabouts tricky

The rules above are the textbook. On the road, you will need a few more habits.

- **Two-wheelers take the inside line.** Scooters and motorbikes often go round close to the island regardless of their exit and then cut across to leave. Before you move left to exit, check your left side and blind spot.

- **Not everyone gives way.** Some drivers treat the roundabout as "first to the gap" rather than giving way to the right. Be ready for it, and do not insist on your priority.

- **Buses and lorries need room.** Large vehicles take up more than one lane on a tight circle. Do not drive alongside them on the roundabout.

- **Autos stop anywhere.** Shared autos pick up and drop passengers at roundabout exits. Expect a stopped auto just after you leave.

- **Pedestrians cross at the edges.** Busy market roundabouts have people walking across the entries and exits, and sometimes over the circle itself. Keep your speed low.

If you miss your exit, do not brake or swerve. Go round again. A second lap costs a few seconds and nobody minds.

## The Charminar as an example

The road round the Charminar in Hyderabad's Old City is a good example of a roundabout that is never quite textbook. The monument sits in the middle of four roads, and traffic runs round it with the Charminar on its right. Around it you have shops, stalls, parked two-wheelers, autos, handcarts and a lot of people on foot.

Here the general rules still apply, but slowly: walking speed is often right. Give way to traffic already circling, keep a steady line close to the island if you are going more than halfway round, and signal left in good time before your exit. Expect pedestrians to cross between vehicles, and two-wheelers to appear on both sides of you.

In real life, vehicle access around the Charminar has been restricted as the area has been made more pedestrian-friendly, so the roads open to traffic and the times they are open can change. Follow the signs and the traffic police on the day. For more on the area, read our Charminar and Old City driving guide (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/charminar-old-city-driving-guide.html).

## Practising roundabouts in Sawari

Sawari is a free browser driving simulator on real Hyderabad streets, and its hardest route, Charminar and Pathergatti (https://sawari.airacode.online/routes.html#charminar), takes you up Charminar Road, round the Charminar itself and north along Pathergatti Road. It is 2.1 km long with nine turns, tight streets, stalls and autos close to the kerb, and parked two-wheelers.

- **Follow the blue band** round the monument. It shows the legal direction of travel, and going against a one-way road is logged as a fault.

- **Signal your exit.** Press `Q` for left and `E` for right before the turns on the route. The indicator cancels itself after the turn, and if you forget, the debrief records it with the advice to signal at least 30 m before turning.

- **Keep it slow.** Collisions with vehicles, pedestrians, walls and buildings are all logged. So is leaving the road, which happens quickly on a tight circle.

- **Look before you go.** Use the driver's seat view (`C`) and drag the mouse to look right before you join, the way you would turn your head. The game has no mirrors.

Start with traffic on Light or Normal, then work up to Dense. If you leave the route, press `R` to return to it. Drive the Charminar route here (https://sawari.airacode.online/play.html?route=charminar), and when you are done, read the debrief: every fault comes with advice. For more on signalling, see our guide to indicators and lane discipline (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/indicators-and-lane-discipline.html).

## Frequently asked questions

**Which way do you go round a roundabout in India?**
Clockwise. India drives on the left, so you turn left onto the roundabout and travel round it clockwise, keeping the central island on your right.

**Who has right of way at a roundabout?**
Traffic already on the roundabout. As you arrive, give way to vehicles coming from your right, and join only when there is a safe gap.

**Do I need to indicate at a roundabout?**
Yes. Signal left as you approach if you are taking the first exit, signal right if you are going more than halfway round, and signal left just after you pass the exit before the one you want.

**What should I do if a roundabout has traffic lights or a police officer?**
Follow the lights or the officer. They override the usual give-way rule, and many busy Indian rotaries are controlled this way at peak hours.

---

# Hyderabad traffic rules: the ones that matter most on the road

URL: https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/hyderabad-traffic-rules-guide.html
Category: Road skills · Published 2026-11-17 · Updated 2026-11-17

Hyderabad traffic rules are the national Motor Vehicles Act rules, enforced by Hyderabad Traffic Police with cameras, checkpoints and e-challans. This guide covers the ones that decide whether your daily drive is safe and legal: keeping left, signals and stop lines, belts and helmets, phones, drink driving, lanes, free lefts, zebra crossings and emergency vehicles.

We have left out fine amounts on purpose. They change, and the point is not the money. If you want the current figures, check with Hyderabad Traffic Police or the Telangana Transport Department.

## Keep left, and never drive on the wrong side

India drives on the left. On a two-way road without a median, stay left of the centre line unless you are overtaking or turning right. On a divided road, use your own carriageway and nothing else.

Wrong-side driving is one of the most common and most dangerous habits in the city. A rider who saves two hundred metres by going against traffic to reach a U-turn is head-on to everyone coming the right way. Do not do it, and expect others to: watch the median edge and the kerb side for scooters coming towards you, especially near U-turn openings and colony entrances.

On one-way roads, the arrow signs and the flow of traffic tell you the legal direction. If you have gone the wrong way, stop safely and turn round. Do not carry on "just to the next turn".

## Signals, stop lines and zebra crossings

### Red, amber and green

Red means stop behind the stop line. Amber means stop too, unless you are so close that braking hard would be unsafe. Amber is not a signal to speed up. Green means you may go if the junction is clear, so do not drive into a box you cannot get out of.

Many Hyderabad junctions have countdown timers. Use them to plan a smooth stop, not to race the last few seconds. Some junctions are also run by a traffic police officer, especially at peak hours. When an officer is directing traffic, their hand signals override the lights.

### The stop line is the line

Stop with your front bumper behind the white stop line, not on it and not past it. Stopping on the zebra crossing forces people on foot into the moving traffic. Stop-line violations are something the police actively photograph at signals.

### Zebra crossings

The black and white stripes belong to pedestrians. Slow down as you approach one, be ready to stop for anyone stepping out, and never overtake a vehicle that has stopped at a crossing: it may have stopped for someone you cannot see.

## Belts, helmets, phones and drink driving

### Seat belts

Wear your seat belt from the first metre of every trip, and make sure your passengers do too, in the back as well as the front. Children should be properly restrained, not on someone's lap.

### Helmets

On a two-wheeler, both the rider and the pillion must wear a proper helmet, fastened. A helmet hanging from the mirror or perched unbuckled on the head does nothing in a fall. Hyderabad Traffic Police photograph helmetless riders and issue e-challans for it, so this is one of the most enforced rules in the city.

### Phones

Do not hold or use your phone while driving or riding. That includes reading messages at a red light, because the light changes and your attention is still on the screen. If you use navigation, mount the phone, set the destination before you move and let the voice guide you. If you must make a call, pull over somewhere safe and legal first.

### Drink driving

The legal limit is very low: 30 mg of alcohol per 100 ml of blood. Hyderabad Traffic Police run breath-test checks, often at night and at weekends. The only safe plan is not to drink at all if you are driving. Book a cab, use a designated driver or leave the car at home.

## Lanes and overtaking

Where lanes are marked, drive within one, not across two. Choose your lane early for the turn you want, and move across only when you have checked and signalled. Weaving from lane to lane in slow traffic gains almost nothing and causes a lot of scrapes.

Overtake on the right, not the left. Do not overtake near junctions, on bends, on the approach to a zebra crossing, or where a solid centre line tells you not to. Keep to the left when you are not overtaking, so faster traffic can pass you safely.

Use your indicators before every turn and every lane change. Our guide to indicators and lane discipline (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/indicators-and-lane-discipline.html) goes into how early to signal and how to pick a lane on Hyderabad's wide roads.

## Free lefts, U-turns and giving way

### Free left turns

At many signalled junctions in Hyderabad, the left turn is "free": a slip lane or a sign lets left-turning traffic go even when the main light is red. Two rules follow from that.

- Only treat a left turn as free where it is signed or clearly built as one. If it is not, wait for the signal like everyone else.

- If you are going straight or right, do not stop in the left lane and block the free left. Traffic police treat blocking it as an offence, and it holds up everyone behind you.

Even on a free left, give way to pedestrians crossing the slip lane and to traffic already on the road you are joining.

### U-turns

Many junctions in the city no longer allow a right turn. Instead, you go straight or left and use a U-turn opening in the median further along. Make U-turns only where they are allowed, from the right of your carriageway, and slowly. Our post on U-turns in Hyderabad (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/u-turns-in-hyderabad.html) explains how to take them safely.

### Emergency vehicles

When you hear a siren or see flashing lights from an ambulance or fire engine, help it through. Move left as far as you safely can, slow down or stop, and do not follow closely behind it to jump the traffic. Since the 2019 amendments to the Motor Vehicles Act, failing to give way to an emergency vehicle is a specific offence. Never move into a junction on red to make space unless it is clearly safe.

## E-challans, documents and the cameras

Most traffic offences in Hyderabad are now caught on camera rather than at a checkpoint. Signal cameras, roadside cameras and officers with handheld cameras photograph the vehicle and the number plate, and an e-challan is raised against the registered owner. You often find out only when you check online or when you sell the vehicle.

You can look up challans against your vehicle number on the official Hyderabad Traffic Police e-challan site (https://echallan.tspolice.gov.in). Pay or dispute them only through official channels, and ignore messages or links that ask for payment from anywhere else.

Carry your driving licence, registration certificate, valid insurance and pollution certificate. Digital copies held in the official DigiLocker or mParivahan apps are accepted. Keep your number plate clean, readable and in the standard format, because the cameras need to read it as much as the police do.

Rules and enforcement change. When a sign, a road marking or a traffic officer tells you something different from this guide, follow the sign, the marking or the officer.

## Practising the rules in Sawari

Sawari is a free browser driving simulator on real Hyderabad streets. It is not a replacement for lessons, but it is a safe place to build the habits above before you need them on the road.

- **Keep left:** the blue route band shows your lane, and the game logs a fault if you drift right of the centre line or go the wrong way on a one-way road.

- **Signals:** running a red light is a fault, and crossing the line on amber earns a warning.

- **Indicators:** press `Q` for left and `E` for right before each turn. They cancel themselves after the turn, and a missed signal shows up in your debrief.

- **Speed:** the limit sign at the bottom right of the screen changes with the road. Speeding and taking speed breakers too fast are both faults.

- **Pedestrians and traffic:** set the traffic level from None to Dense, and practise leaving room for pedestrians and for buses and autos that stop without warning.

At the end of each drive the debrief lists every fault with advice on how to avoid it. A good first drive is Tank Bund Road (https://sawari.airacode.online/routes.html#tank-bund), which has no turns to make, followed by Banjara Hills Road No. 1 (https://sawari.airacode.online/play.html?route=banjara-hills) for busy junctions. Switch to the driver's seat with `C` to get used to seeing the road from the right-hand side of the car. When you are ready for more, read our guide to driving in Hyderabad for beginners (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/driving-in-hyderabad-for-beginners.html).

## Frequently asked questions

**How do I check if I have an e-challan in Hyderabad?**
Hyderabad Traffic Police publish e-challans online. Search by your vehicle number on their e-challan website, and pay or contest them through the official channels only.

**Is a helmet compulsory for the pillion rider in Hyderabad?**
Yes. Indian law requires both the rider and the pillion on a two-wheeler to wear a protective helmet, and Hyderabad Traffic Police enforce it for both.

**Can I turn left on a red signal in Hyderabad?**
Only where a free left is signed or marked at that junction. Everywhere else, a red light means stop for every direction, including left.

**Do rear-seat passengers need to wear seat belts?**
Yes. Seat belts are meant for everyone in the car, front and back. Make it a habit that nobody rides without one, whatever the trip.

# Indicators and lane discipline: how to signal and choose lanes in Indian traffic

URL: https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/indicators-and-lane-discipline.html
Category: Road skills · Published 2026-11-17 · Updated 2026-11-17

Good indicators and lane discipline make you predictable, and in Hyderabad traffic predictable is safe. Signal early, before you brake or move, pick your lane well before the junction, overtake on the right and stay in your lane rather than weaving through gaps.

## Why signalling matters so much in Indian traffic

An indicator is a message to everyone around you: the car behind, the scooter filtering up beside you, the pedestrian waiting to cross, the auto driver deciding whether to pull out. In dense traffic, nobody can read your mind, and nobody has much space to react.

It is easy to stop signalling because others do not. Do it anyway. The one rider who sees your indicator and holds back is the one you would otherwise have hit. Signalling also makes you think about your own plan a few seconds earlier, which tends to make the rest of the manoeuvre smoother.

An indicator does not give you the right to move. It tells people what you would like to do. You still have to check that the space is there and that others have seen you.

## When and how early to indicate

### The order: check, signal, then move

Use the same order every time:

- **Check** your mirrors and, for a lane change, look over your shoulder into the blind spot. Two-wheelers sit there constantly.

- **Signal** in good time, so people see it before you change speed or position.

- **Position** the car in the lane you need.

- **Slow down** for the turn, and check again just before you turn.

- **Turn**, and make sure the indicator goes off afterwards.

### How early is early enough

In city traffic, aim to have the indicator on at least 30 metres before the turn, and more on faster roads. Signal before you start braking, so the driver behind knows why you are slowing. If you signal at the same moment you turn, the signal has told nobody anything.

Do not signal too early either. If there is a side road or a petrol pump entrance between you and your turn, wait until you have passed it, or someone may pull out thinking you are turning into it.

### When to signal

- Every left and right turn, including into a gate or parking.

- Every lane change, including moving out round a parked bus.

- Pulling away from the kerb and pulling in to stop.

- Before a U-turn (right indicator), and at roundabouts as you approach and leave.

Hazard lights are for a stopped or broken-down vehicle, not for going straight through a junction or for driving in rain.

## Choosing the right lane

On Hyderabad's wide arterials, such as the roads through HITEC City and up to Jubilee Hills, the lane you are in decides where you can go. Get it wrong and you either make a late, dangerous cut across or miss your turn.

### The general pattern

- **Left lane:** turning left, the free left at a signal, slower vehicles, buses and autos stopping.

- **Middle lanes:** going straight on.

- **Right lane:** turning right, U-turns at the median, and overtaking.

Always follow lane arrows painted on the road and overhead signs where they exist, because they override the general pattern. Near flyovers, lanes split between the ramp and the service road well before the junction. Our guide to driving on flyovers (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/driving-on-flyovers-hyderabad.html) covers that in detail.

### Plan two junctions ahead

If you know the route, move into the right lane a few hundred metres before you need it, while traffic still has gaps. If you are using navigation, listen for the instruction early. If you end up in the wrong lane, go where that lane goes and find a way back. A missed turn costs a few minutes. A last-second swerve across three lanes can cost far more.

## Overtaking on the right

In India you overtake on the right. Before you pull out:

- Make sure you can see far enough ahead, and that there is no oncoming traffic on an undivided road.

- Check behind you: someone may already be overtaking you.

- Signal right, move out smoothly, pass with a good gap, then signal left and move back in only when you can see the vehicle you passed clearly behind you.

Do not overtake near junctions, on bends, on the approach to a zebra crossing, near a speed breaker or where a solid centre line forbids it. Never overtake a vehicle that has stopped at a crossing.

Passing on the left is the classic Hyderabad move, and it causes many crashes because nobody is looking for you there. The exception is when the vehicle ahead has signalled and moved out to turn right: then you can pass it on the left with care.

## Stay in your lane, do not weave

In slow traffic, the lane next to you always seems to move faster. Usually it is an illusion, and changing lanes over and over gains seconds at most. Each change also puts you across someone else's path, often a two-wheeler you have not seen.

Some simple habits help:

- Keep the car centred in your lane, not straddling the line.

- Leave a gap of at least a couple of seconds to the vehicle in front, so you are not forced to swerve when it brakes.

- When a bus pulls into a stop ahead, slow down early rather than diving into the next lane at the last moment.

- Let merging traffic in, one at a time. Zip merging works only if people take turns.

- If someone cuts in front of you, ease off and let them go. Arguing with your horn will not get you there faster.

Expect scooters and motorbikes to filter between lanes. You cannot control that, but you can make yourself predictable for them: steady speed, steady lane, clear signals. Our post on sharing the road with autos, buses and two-wheelers (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/sharing-the-road-autos-buses-two-wheelers.html) has more on reading their moves.

## Practising signals and lanes in Sawari

Sawari, the free browser driving simulator on real Hyderabad roads, checks your indicators on every route turn. Press `Q` for the left indicator and `E` for the right. Like a real car, the indicator cancels itself after the turn, so you only need to remember to switch it on.

The game expects the indicator to be on well before the turn: if it was not on in the approach, the debrief records "No indicator before a turn" with the advice to signal at least 30 m before you turn. U-turns count as right turns. Gentle bends that only bear left or right are not checked, just as you would not normally signal to follow the road round a curve.

Lane discipline is checked too. The blue route band shows your lane; drift right of the centre line on a two-way road and you get a fault for driving on the wrong side, and going against a one-way road is a fault of its own. Collisions are logged with what you hit, which is a good prompt to leave more space.

The best route for this is Cyber Towers to Jubilee Hills (https://sawari.airacode.online/routes.html#hitec-city), with ten turns, flyover ramps and merging traffic at Inorbit Mall. Start it here (https://sawari.airacode.online/play.html?route=hitec-city), set traffic to Busy or Dense, and drive it in the driver's seat (press `C`). The game has no mirrors, so drag the mouse to look over your shoulder, the same way you would turn your head. If you leave the route, press `R` to return to it. Then read the debrief and work on the faults it lists, one at a time.

For the rules behind all this, see our guide to Hyderabad traffic rules (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/hyderabad-traffic-rules-guide.html).

## Frequently asked questions

**How far before a turn should I use my indicator?**
Early enough that people behind and around you can react: at least 30 metres in slow city traffic, and more at higher speeds. Signal before you brake and before you move across.

**Is it legal to overtake from the left in India?**
The rule is to overtake on the right. Passing on the left is only acceptable when the vehicle ahead has signalled and moved to turn right, or when lanes of slow traffic are simply moving at different speeds.

**Should I indicate when changing lanes on a straight road?**
Yes. Every lane change needs a check over your shoulder and an indicator first, even when the road looks empty. Two-wheelers appear in gaps very quickly.

**Why does my indicator switch off by itself?**
Most cars cancel the indicator when the steering wheel straightens after a turn. A small lane change may not turn the wheel far enough, so check that it has gone off.

# Monsoon driving in Hyderabad: waterlogging, potholes and braking in the rain

URL: https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/monsoon-driving-hyderabad.html
Category: Road skills · Published 2026-11-17 · Updated 2026-11-17

Monsoon driving in Hyderabad means heavy bursts of rain, roads that turn into streams within minutes, and potholes you cannot see under the water. The safest approach is slower speeds, much bigger gaps, and a willingness to turn back or wait it out.

## What the monsoon does to Hyderabad roads

The rains usually arrive in June and can carry on well into October. Hyderabad's heaviest rain often comes in short, intense downpours rather than steady drizzle, and that is what causes the trouble: drains cannot take the water fast enough, and it collects on roads.

- **Waterlogging.** Low-lying stretches, dips under bridges and roads beside lakes and nalas can fill quickly.

- **Underpasses.** These are the lowest point of the road by design, so water runs into them. They can go from passable to dangerous in a short time.

- **Hidden potholes and open drains.** Water hides everything: a pothole, a broken edge, a missing drain cover. Rain also breaks up the road surface, so new potholes appear through the season.

- **Slippery surfaces.** The first rain after a dry spell lifts oil and dust off the road and makes it very slippery. Painted lines, metal covers and speed breakers are slippery too.

- **Traffic jams.** Waterlogging on one main road pushes traffic onto others, and journeys can take far longer than usual.

## Before you set out

- **Ask whether the journey is necessary.** In a heavy downpour, waiting an hour is often faster and always safer.

- **Check for advisories.** The traffic police and city authorities often post waterlogging and diversion updates on their official channels during heavy rain. The Hyderabad Traffic Police (https://www.htp.gov.in) is a good place to start.

- **Check your wipers.** Blades that smear or judder should be replaced before the season, not during it.

- **Check your tyres.** Worn tread cannot clear water from under the tyre, which is what causes aquaplaning. Check the pressures too.

- **Check your lights.** In heavy rain you need to be seen. Make sure the headlights, tail lights, brake lights and hazard lights all work.

## Driving on wet roads

### Slow down and double your gap

On a wet road your tyres have less grip, so it takes much longer to stop. Leave at least twice the gap you would in the dry, and more behind buses and lorries, whose spray blinds you. Brake earlier and more gently.

### Be smooth with everything

Sudden braking, sharp steering and hard acceleration are what make a car slide on a wet road. Make every input gentle, and slow down before bends and turns, not in them.

### Aquaplaning

When you drive fast through standing water, the tyres can ride up on a film of water and lose contact with the road. The steering suddenly goes light, and the engine may rev as the wheels spin. If it happens:

- Ease off the accelerator. Do not brake hard.

- Hold the steering straight and steady.

- Wait for the tyres to grip again as the car slows; you will feel the steering come back.

The best cure is prevention: slow down well before any patch of water, and avoid driving through puddles at speed.

### Visibility: wipers, demisting and lights

- Use your wipers at a speed that keeps the screen clear, and switch on the headlights in heavy rain, even in the day.

- To clear misted glass, turn on the air conditioning and aim the fan at the windscreen, or use the demist setting. A window open a crack also helps.

- Keep the inside of the windscreen clean; a dirty screen mists faster and glares more at night.

- Do not drive with hazard lights on while moving in normal rain, as other drivers cannot see when you signal. Use them if you have stopped or are crawling in very poor visibility.

Rain at night is the hardest combination of all. Our night driving guide (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/night-driving-hyderabad-tips.html) covers glare and seeing in the dark.

### Look after the people around you

Two-wheeler riders in the rain have poor grip, wet visors and often no protection from your spray. Give them more room, do not splash pedestrians and people waiting at bus stops, and expect people to run across the road to get out of the rain. Our guide to sharing the road (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/sharing-the-road-autos-buses-two-wheelers.html) has more on two-wheelers and buses.

## Waterlogged roads and underpasses

This is where people get into real trouble. Water is heavier and stronger than it looks, and you cannot see what is under it.

- **If you cannot see the depth, do not go in.** Watch another vehicle like yours cross first. If the water reaches higher than about the middle of its wheels, or you cannot tell, find another way.

- **Never enter moving water.** Even shallow flowing water can push a car sideways.

- **Be very wary of underpasses.** If an underpass has water in it during heavy rain, do not drive in. The water in the middle is usually deeper than at the edges, and it can rise while you are inside.

- **If you must cross shallow water,** go slowly and steadily in first gear, keeping the engine running at a steady speed so water does not get pushed up into the exhaust. Do not stop in the middle. Do not create a bow wave that pushes water into other cars or onto people.

- **Test your brakes afterwards.** Wet brakes work poorly. Press them gently a few times once you are through, to dry them.

If your car stalls in water, do not try to restart it: water in the engine can wreck it. Switch on your hazards, get out if the water is rising and you can do so safely, and call for help. A car can be replaced; you cannot.

## When not to drive

Sometimes the right decision is to stay put. Do not drive if:

- There is a heavy downpour in progress and the trip can wait.

- Authorities have issued a warning to stay indoors or avoid travel.

- Your route depends on an underpass or low road that floods.

- Your wipers, lights or tyres are not in good condition.

- You are new to driving and have never driven on a wet road; start with light rain and an empty road, with an experienced driver beside you.

## Practising in Sawari before the rains

To be clear: Sawari (https://sawari.airacode.online/play.html) has no rain or weather. The roads are always dry, there is no standing water, and grip does not change. You cannot learn aquaplaning or waterlogged roads in it.

What it can help with is the habits that make wet driving safer: keeping a long gap behind the vehicle in front, braking early and smoothly, signalling before every move and keeping to your lane. The debrief records collisions, speeding, red lights and missed indicators, so you can see which habits need work. Choosing the driver's seat view (`C`) gives a cockpit view closer to what you see through a real windscreen.

Try a drive with Dense traffic and set yourself a rule of never coming within a long gap of the car ahead. If you can finish a route like Cyber Towers to Jubilee Hills (https://sawari.airacode.online/routes.html#hitec-city) that way with no collisions, you are building the habit that matters most on a wet road.

Sawari is for practice only. It does not replace lessons with a licensed instructor, and nothing in it prepares you for real flood water. When in doubt, wait it out.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is it safe to drive through a flooded road?**
Only if you can clearly see how deep it is and it is shallow, ideally by watching a similar car cross first. If you cannot judge the depth, or the water is moving, turn back and find another way.

**What should I do if my car stalls in water?**
Do not try to restart it, because water drawn into the engine can cause serious damage. Switch on the hazard lights, get out safely if the water is rising, and call for help or a tow.

**How do I stop my windscreen misting up in the rain?**
Turn on the air conditioning with the fan aimed at the windscreen, or use the demist setting. Opening a window a little also helps, and a clean inside screen mists less.

**Does Sawari have rain?**
No. The simulator has no rain or weather. It can help you practise gaps, signals and lane discipline, but wet-road driving has to be learnt on the road, carefully.

---

# Night driving in Hyderabad: headlights, high beam and staying alert after dark

URL: https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/night-driving-hyderabad-tips.html
Category: Road skills · Published 2026-11-17 · Updated 2026-11-17

Night driving in Hyderabad is calmer in some ways, with less traffic, and harder in others: you see less, others see you less, and people are tired. Most of it comes down to good use of your headlights, lower speed and a careful eye for anything without lights.

## Why night driving is different

In daylight you see the whole road at once. At night you see what your headlights and the street lamps show you, and everything else is guesswork. Distances are harder to judge, dark objects disappear against dark roads, and the glare of oncoming lights can blind you for a moment.

Traffic changes too. Main roads empty out, so speeds go up. Lorries and goods vehicles that cannot enter parts of the city in the day are often on the roads at night. And late in the evening you share the road with people heading home from work, from weddings and from parties, some of whom have been drinking.

## Headlights: low beam, high beam and when to use each

### Switch on early

Put your headlights on at dusk, not when it is fully dark. The point is not only for you to see, but for others to see you. A grey car in the evening light is very hard to pick out.

### Low beam in the city

On lit city roads, low beam is right almost everywhere. It lights the road ahead without dazzling people coming the other way or the driver in front, who sees your lights in the mirror.

### High beam etiquette

High beam is useful on dark roads with nobody around: an unlit stretch on the edge of the city, a highway at night. The rules of courtesy are simple:

- Dip to low beam as soon as you see an oncoming vehicle.

- Dip when you come up behind another vehicle, even a two-wheeler.

- Do not use high beam on lit city roads at all.

- A quick flash is a way to warn someone or signal at a blind bend, not a weapon.

### When you are dazzled

If an oncoming vehicle has its high beam on, slow down, look at the left edge of your lane rather than into the lights, and hold your line. Flashing back only blinds both of you. If you are dazzled badly, slow right down until your eyes recover.

### Keep your glass and lights clean

Dust on the windscreen scatters light from oncoming headlights and makes glare much worse. Clean the windscreen inside and out, and keep your headlight lenses clean. Check that both headlights, the tail lights and the brake lights work.

## Things you cannot see: unlit vehicles and people

The biggest night danger in the city is something with no lights at all.

- **Unlit vehicles.** Bicycles, handcarts, some autos and two-wheelers with failed lamps, and lorries parked at the edge of the road without any reflectors or hazard lights. A dark lorry parked on a dark road is one of the hardest things to see.

- **Pedestrians.** People in dark clothes walking in the road where the footpath is broken or blocked, and people crossing between lamp posts, in the darker gaps.

- **Wrong-way riders.** At night, a single headlight coming towards you on your side of the road could be a two-wheeler riding the wrong way along the edge.

- **Animals.** Stray dogs and sometimes cattle lie on or beside the road, especially on quieter stretches.

- **Road hazards.** Unpainted speed breakers, potholes, diversions and dug-up road for works are all harder to see at night. Our guide to speed breakers and speed limits (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/speed-breakers-speed-limits-hyderabad.html) covers the clues to look for.

The defence for all of these is the same: drive at a speed that lets you stop within the distance you can see. If your lights show you only a short stretch of road, that speed is lower than you think.

## Fatigue

Tiredness slows your reactions in the same way alcohol does, and it creeps up on you. Warning signs include heavy eyes, yawning, drifting in your lane, missing a turn or not remembering the last stretch of road.

- Do not start a long night drive after a long day if you can avoid it.

- On a long drive, take regular breaks, get out of the car and walk around.

- If you feel sleepy, stop somewhere safe and rest. Cold air, loud music and talking only buy a few minutes.

- A passenger who stays awake and talks to you helps, but is not a substitute for rest.

## Drink-driving checks

Hyderabad Traffic Police regularly run drink-driving checks at night, especially on weekends, with officers stopping vehicles and using breath analysers. Drink-driving is a serious offence under the Motor Vehicles Act, and the penalties can include fines, prison and losing your licence. The simplest rule is not to drink at all if you are driving. Book a cab, use a driver or let a sober friend take the wheel.

If you are stopped at a check, pull over where the officers direct you, keep your licence and documents ready and follow instructions calmly. For current rules, see the Hyderabad Traffic Police (https://www.htp.gov.in).

Never drive after drinking, even "just one". It affects judgement before you feel it, and the people most at risk are the ones on foot and on two-wheelers around you.

## Practising night driving in Sawari

In Sawari (https://sawari.airacode.online/play.html) you pick the time of day before you start: Morning, Midday, Evening or Night. In Evening and Night, the street lamps come on, with warm pools of light on the road below them, windows light up in the buildings, and every vehicle in the traffic shows white lamps in front and red ones behind. The sky, fog and light change with the hour, so distances feel shorter and the road beyond the lamps fades into the dark. The features page (https://sawari.airacode.online/features.html) shows how the different times look.

Your headlights come on by themselves in Evening and Night, and you can switch them off and on with `L`. Try a stretch with them off and you will see how much they matter, even under street lamps. Your brake lights glow brighter when you brake, as on a real car.

The game has one headlight setting, so there is no high beam to practise dipping, and every AI vehicle has working lights, unlike the real road. What it is good for is getting used to judging gaps, speed breakers, junctions and signals in the dark before you do it for real. The Necklace Road (https://sawari.airacode.online/routes.html#necklace-road) route at night, round the lake, is a gentle first drive; the Old City is a harder one. For rain at night, read our monsoon driving guide (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/monsoon-driving-hyderabad.html) too.

Sawari is for practice only. It does not replace lessons with a licensed instructor, and it cannot show you everything a real dark road hides.

## Frequently asked questions

**When should I use high beam?**
Only on dark roads with nobody coming towards you and nobody close in front. Dip to low beam as soon as you see an oncoming vehicle or come up behind someone, and on lit city roads low beam is all you need.

**What should I do if an oncoming driver dazzles me with high beam?**
Slow down, look towards the left edge of your lane rather than at the lights, and keep going straight until they have passed. Do not flash your high beam back at them, as that leaves two blinded drivers.

**How do I stay awake on a late drive?**
Do not start a long drive tired. If you feel your eyes closing, your head nodding or you cannot remember the last few minutes, stop somewhere safe and rest. Open windows and loud music do not fix tiredness.

**Does Sawari have a night mode?**
Yes. Choose Night or Evening as the time of day before you start. Street lamps, lit windows and every vehicle's lights come on, and you can switch your own headlights on and off with the L key.

---

# Sharing the road in Hyderabad: autos, buses, two-wheelers, cyclists and pedestrians

URL: https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/sharing-the-road-autos-buses-two-wheelers.html
Category: Road skills · Published 2026-11-17 · Updated 2026-11-17

Sharing the road in Hyderabad means sharing it with almost everything: autos, city buses, two-wheelers on both sides of you, cyclists, people on foot and, now and then, a cow. You cannot control any of them, but you can give them space, be easy to read and avoid surprises.

## The basic idea: space and predictability

Mixed traffic works because most people watch each other and adjust. It goes wrong when someone does something nobody expected: a sudden lane change, a hard stop with no reason, a turn without a signal. So the two most useful habits are simple.

- **Leave a gap you could stop in.** Behind anything that might stop suddenly, which in this city is almost everything, leave more room than feels necessary. The space in front of you is the only space you control.

- **Do things slowly and signal them early.** Indicate before you move, not as you move. Change position gradually, so the rider beside you sees the car drifting and has time to react.

Our guide to indicators and lane discipline (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/indicators-and-lane-discipline.html) goes into the signalling side in more detail.

## Autos

Auto-rickshaws are small, light and nimble. They turn in a tight space, fit through gaps a car cannot, and stop wherever someone waves at them. That makes them hard to predict.

- **Expect a stop at any moment.** An auto with a passenger looking out, or an empty auto slowing near a group of people, is about to pull over. Hang back.

- **Watch the front wheel.** An auto's single front wheel shows its intention early. When it turns, the auto turns, often sharply.

- **Do not squeeze them.** Autos are easily unsettled by a car passing close. Give them the same room you would give a two-wheeler.

- **Look for autos waiting at junctions and stands.** They pull out into small gaps. Be ready for one to nose out in front of you.

## City buses and lorries

TGSRTC city buses (many people still call them TSRTC buses) are long, heavy and slow to stop. Their drivers cannot see everything around them.

### When a bus stops

Buses pull in to stops, and sometimes stop short of them in traffic. When one does, people step off into the road, and others run across to catch it. Slow right down as you approach a stopped bus, and look under and around it for feet and for anyone stepping out from its front. Only pass when you can see the road ahead and leave a good margin.

### When a bus pulls out

A bus leaving a stop swings out across the lane. If it has signalled and started to move, let it go. You will lose a few seconds; arguing with a bus is a fight you do not want to win.

### Blind spots and turning

Do not sit right beside the back corner of a bus or lorry, and do not try to go up its inside as it turns left. Long vehicles cut in at the back as they turn, and the gap closes quickly. If you cannot see the driver's mirror, the driver probably cannot see you.

## Two-wheelers

Scooters and motorbikes are a large share of Hyderabad traffic, and they move differently from cars. They filter between lanes, pass on the left and on the right, move to the front at signals and squeeze through any gap.

- **Check mirrors and over your shoulder before every move.** Before turning left, especially, look down the left side of the car. A scooter can arrive there in the seconds between your mirror check and your turn.

- **Open your door carefully.** When parked, look behind before opening the door on either side.

- **Do not close a gap to block them.** It is tempting, but a rider forced to brake hard in a narrow gap is in danger. Keep your line and let them through.

- **Watch for riders who are not watching you.** Riders on phones, riders carrying loads or a passenger with a child, and riders looking back over their shoulder all react more slowly.

- **Expect wrong-side riders.** On some roads, two-wheelers ride against the traffic along the edge to avoid a long U-turn. Look both ways at side roads even on a one-way street.

## Cyclists, pedestrians and animals

### Cyclists

Cyclists are slower than everything else and often ride close to the edge, where the road is broken or the drain covers are. Pass them wide, not at speed, and do not cut in sharply in front of them to turn left. At night, many bicycles have no lights at all.

### Pedestrians

Footpaths are often blocked by parked vehicles, stalls or construction, so people walk in the road. They cross wherever they need to, not just at zebra crossings. Near markets, bus stops, metro stations, schools and places of worship, assume someone will step out. Slow down, make eye contact where you can, and stop for people on a zebra crossing.

### Cattle and dogs

Cows and buffaloes still wander on some roads, particularly on the edges of the city and in older neighbourhoods, and stray dogs are common everywhere. Cattle can move slowly and then suddenly. Slow down well before them, pass at a walking pace and do not use a long horn blast, which can make them bolt in any direction.

## Using the horn well

The horn is a way of saying "I am here", not "get out of my way". A short tap is useful when someone is about to step or pull out without seeing you, or on a blind bend. Holding the horn down does not make traffic move faster, and it startles the people and animals you most need to stay calm.

Respect no-horn zones, which are signed near hospitals and some schools. And treat a horn from behind as information, not an insult: someone wants you to know they are there.

## Practising mixed traffic in Sawari

In Sawari (https://sawari.airacode.online/play.html) you can set the traffic from None to Dense. At Dense there are about 80 vehicles around you, and the mix is drawn from what you see on Hyderabad roads: hatchbacks, sedans, SUVs, autos, mini trucks, buses and a large share of scooters and motorbikes. The features page (https://sawari.airacode.online/features.html) lists the details.

The two-wheelers filter past slower vehicles on their right, so you will have bikes coming up beside you in queues. The AI drivers keep a following gap, stop at red lights, give way where their paths cross, slow for speed breakers and stop for people stepping across side-road mouths. Now and then one of them has a moment of inattention and there is a real collision ahead, which is a fair test of whether you left enough room. Larger vehicles like buses and lorries keep to the bigger roads.

Pedestrians walk the footpaths and cross the mouths of side roads, and hitting one counts as a collision in your debrief. There is a horn on `H` and hazard lights on `X`. The traffic does not move aside for the horn, which is honest: on the real road, it usually does not either.

The game does not include cyclists or animals, so those you have to learn on the road. A good way to start is the Charminar and Pathergatti (https://sawari.airacode.online/routes.html#charminar) route with traffic on Medium, then raising it as your gaps and signals become a habit. Our Old City driving guide (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/charminar-old-city-driving-guide.html) describes that route.

Sawari is a practice tool. It does not replace lessons with a licensed instructor, and real traffic will always be less predictable than any simulation.

## Frequently asked questions

**How do I deal with two-wheelers overtaking on both sides?**
Assume there is always a two-wheeler beside you, check your mirrors and over your shoulder before any move, signal early, and change position slowly. Most problems come from sudden moves, not from the bikes themselves.

**What should I do when a city bus stops ahead?**
Slow down and expect passengers to step off into the road and others to run for the bus. Only pass if you can see the road ahead is clear and you can leave plenty of room, and watch for the bus pulling out again.

**Is it rude to use the horn in Hyderabad?**
A short tap to let someone know you are there is normal and useful. Long or repeated blasts do not clear the road and only add stress. Do not use the horn in no-horn zones such as near hospitals.

**Why do autos stop so suddenly?**
Autos pick up and drop passengers wherever they are hailed, so they may brake, swerve to the kerb or turn without much warning. Keep a bigger gap behind an auto than behind a car.

---

# Speed breakers and speed limits in Hyderabad: how to take humps and read the limit

URL: https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/speed-breakers-speed-limits-hyderabad.html
Category: Road skills · Published 2026-11-17 · Updated 2026-11-17

Speed breakers are part of almost every drive in Hyderabad, and speed limits change from road to road. The short version: slow down early for humps, roll over them gently, and take your limit from the posted sign rather than from the traffic around you.

## Why speed breakers matter so much here

On a main road you may go several kilometres without a hump. Turn into a colony road and you can meet three in a few hundred metres: one just after the junction, one outside a school, one in front of a temple or an apartment gate. They are there because people walk on these roads, children cross them and two-wheelers come out of side lanes without looking.

Taking a breaker too fast does more than shake the passengers. It can scrape the underside of a low car, knock the alignment out, damage tyres and suspension, and on a two-wheeler it can throw the rider. It also tends to happen at exactly the places where people step into the road.

## Speed breakers, humps and rumble strips

### Speed breakers and humps

Most breakers in the city are a raised hump across the full width of the road. Well-maintained ones are painted with yellow (or white) and black stripes and have a warning sign before them. Some are wide and gentle; others are short and steep, almost like a kerb laid across the road. You cannot always tell which kind it is until you are close, so slow down first and judge it as you approach.

### Rumble strips

Rumble strips are groups of low raised bands laid across the lane, usually before a junction, a sharp bend, a toll gate or a stretch where the road changes. You feel a rapid vibration and hear a hum. They are a warning, not a barrier: they are telling you that something ahead needs a lower speed.

### Unmarked breakers

The ones that catch people out have no paint and no sign. The stripes may have worn away, the hump may be new, or it may have been put up locally. At night or in the rain, an unpainted breaker is very hard to see. Some clues help:

- Vehicles ahead suddenly dipping, braking or bouncing.

- Two-wheelers moving to the very edge of the road, where some humps are lower or have a gap.

- A slight shadow or ridge across the road surface, especially in low morning or evening sun.

- Schools, hospitals, temples, mosques, colony gates and junctions on residential roads.

## How to take a speed breaker properly

- **Brake before the hump, not on it.** Do your slowing in a straight line while the car is still on flat road. Braking hard on the hump itself pushes the nose down into it.

- **Come off the brake just before the front wheels reach it.** This lets the front suspension rise and the car rolls over more softly.

- **Go over at a crawl, straight on.** Keep the steering straight so both front wheels meet the hump at the same time. Taking it at an angle twists the car and is uncomfortable on a steep hump.

- **Hold a steady, gentle throttle as the rear wheels cross.** Then pick up speed smoothly once you are clear.

- **Watch your mirrors and the vehicle behind.** Brake progressively so whoever is following has time to slow down too. A sudden stop for a hump you saw late is a common cause of rear-end knocks.

If the car is heavily loaded or sits low, slow down even more, and use the flattest part of the hump if there is one. Do not swing into the oncoming side to find it.

Two-wheelers often ride over the edge of a breaker or squeeze past it near the kerb. Expect them beside you at the hump and leave them room.

## Speed limits: read the sign, not the traffic

There is no single speed limit for all of Hyderabad. Different roads carry different limits, and the limit is shown on a round sign with a red border and the number in the middle. That sign is what counts, whatever speed the cars around you are doing.

Some things to keep in mind:

- **Limits are lower where people are.** Near schools, hospitals, markets and busy shopping streets you will often see lower posted limits, and even where there is no sign, the sensible speed is lower.

- **Flyovers and expressways are not a free-for-all.** They may carry a higher limit than the road below, but they also have merges, ramps and sudden queues. See our guide to driving on flyovers (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/driving-on-flyovers-hyderabad.html).

- **The limit is a maximum.** In heavy traffic, in rain, at night or on a narrow colony road, a safe speed may be well below it.

- **Speed is enforced.** The traffic police use speed cameras and checks on many roads. Check the Hyderabad Traffic Police (https://www.htp.gov.in) website for current rules rather than relying on hearsay.

If you are learning, it helps to get into the habit of glancing for a limit sign every time you join a new road, the same way you check your mirrors. Our Hyderabad traffic rules guide (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/hyderabad-traffic-rules-guide.html) covers the other signs you will meet.

## Practising speed breakers and limits in Sawari

Sawari (https://sawari.airacode.online/play.html) is a free browser driving simulator set on real Hyderabad roads, and it checks both of these habits.

### Speed breakers in the game

Breakers appear as humps painted in yellow and black stripes across the road, mostly on two-way colony and side roads, often just after a junction. OpenStreetMap has almost none of the city's breakers mapped, so their positions are estimated by rule to match how these roads usually look; the about page (https://sawari.airacode.online/about.html#data) explains what is mapped and what is estimated. You feel each one as a jolt through the car.

The game advises taking breakers at about 15 km/h. If you cross one faster than 22 km/h, it is logged as a fault, with your speed, and it appears in your debrief at the end of the drive. The AI traffic slows for breakers too, so you will see cars ahead brake for them, which is a good reminder to look for the cue.

### Speed limits in the game

The current limit is shown on the dashboard at the bottom right of the screen. It comes from the maxspeed tag in OpenStreetMap where a road has one; where it does not, the game uses a default for the type of road, lower on residential and service roads than on main roads. These defaults are the game's own choices for practice, not official limits, so on a real road always go by the sign.

Driving more than a few km/h over the limit for a couple of seconds counts as speeding, and the debrief tells you the speed and the limit. A good exercise is to drive a route with the traffic set low and try to finish with no speeding and no breaker faults at all. The Banjara Hills Road No. 1 (https://sawari.airacode.online/routes.html#banjara-hills) route, with its climb and side roads, and the narrow streets of the Old City are both useful for this.

Sawari is for practice only. It does not replace lessons with a licensed instructor, and real roads have breakers, potholes and limits the game does not know about.

## Frequently asked questions

**How slowly should I go over a speed breaker?**
Slow enough that the car rolls over it without a jolt, which for most humps means walking to jogging pace. Sawari suggests about 15 km/h and records a fault above 22 km/h, but a steep or broken breaker may need you to go slower still.

**What is the speed limit in Hyderabad?**
There is no single figure for the whole city. Limits depend on the road and are shown on posted signs, and they are lower near schools, hospitals and busy markets. Always follow the sign in front of you and the traffic police.

**Why are some speed breakers not painted?**
Paint wears off, and some humps are built by residents or contractors without markings or warning signs. On colony roads, treat every junction and every school or temple gate as a place where a breaker may be waiting.

**Are rumble strips the same as speed breakers?**
No. Rumble strips are a series of low raised bands that make the car vibrate and hum to warn you of a hazard ahead, such as a junction or a curve. They are not meant to stop you, but they tell you to slow down.

---

# U-turns in Hyderabad: how to use median openings safely

URL: https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/u-turns-in-hyderabad.html
Category: Road skills · Published 2026-11-17 · Updated 2026-11-17

U-turns in Hyderabad are part of everyday driving. On many main roads you cannot turn right at the junction any more: you go straight on, find the next opening in the median and turn back. Done well it is calm and safe. Done badly it is where cars meet two-wheelers head-on.

## Why Hyderabad uses U-turns instead of right turns

A right turn at a signalled junction needs its own phase of the lights, and every second given to right turners is a second taken from traffic going straight. On busy corridors the traffic police have closed many of these right turns. Traffic going right continues through the junction, or turns left, and then makes a U-turn at a median opening a short distance away.

The result is fewer signal phases and smoother through traffic, but it moves the tricky part of the turn to the U-turn itself. A U-turn opening has no lights. You decide when it is safe, and so does everyone else.

The layouts change from time to time as junctions are redesigned. If a right turn you used to take is now closed, look for the signs telling you where the nearest U-turn is.

## Finding the right opening

Not every gap in the median is a U-turn. Some are for emergency vehicles, some are pedestrian crossings and some were simply cut by people who did not want to drive further. Use openings that are clearly meant for turning:

- A U-turn sign before or at the opening is the clearest sign it is allowed.

- A red circular sign with a crossed-out U-turn means it is not, wherever the gap is.

- Do not make U-turns at signalled junctions where it is banned, on flyovers, on bridges, or near a bend or the crest of a slope where oncoming drivers cannot see you.

If you miss an opening, go to the next one. Never reverse along the road or cut across a gap that is not meant for traffic.

## Positioning and signalling

### Get to the right early

U-turns are made to the right, from the right-hand edge of your carriageway, alongside the median. Check your mirrors and over your right shoulder, signal right, and move into the right lane well before the opening. In heavy traffic this may mean moving across a few hundred metres early.

Keep the indicator on. It tells the traffic behind you why you are slowing, and tells people waiting in the opening from the other side what you plan to do.

### Slow down and stop in the right place

Slow down gently, with time to spare, so you do not catch out the vehicle behind. If you need to wait, stop close to the median, inside the opening if there is a turning pocket, so traffic can pass you on the left. Do not stop half in the lane and half out. Keep your wheels pointing straight while you wait: if you are hit from behind with the wheels turned, you are pushed into the oncoming traffic.

## Judging the gap and making the turn

This is the part that needs patience. You are about to cross the path of traffic coming the other way, and join it.

- **Look right and far.** Oncoming traffic is coming towards you on the other carriageway, and the lane nearest the median is often the fastest. Wait for a real gap, not half of one.

- **Look left as well.** Riders coming the wrong way along the median edge to reach the same opening are common. So are pedestrians crossing at the gap.

- **Check for vehicles turning from the other side.** Some openings work in both directions. Agree with the driver opposite, by eye contact or by who arrived first, before either of you moves.

- **Turn slowly and steadily.** Use full steering lock early and keep the car moving at walking pace. Aim to finish in the lane nearest the median, then move left when it is safe.

Larger cars, vans and anything towing may not make it round in one go on a narrow opening. Take it as wide as you safely can. If the car will not fit, stop, check all around and reverse only a short way when nothing is moving. If in doubt, find a wider opening or go round the block.

Two-wheelers are the biggest danger at U-turns. They come through small gaps at speed, they filter up on your left while you wait, and they often appear on the wrong side of the road near openings. Look twice for them before you move, and once more as you turn.

## When someone else is making a U-turn

You will often be the driver coming the other way. Watch the median ahead for cars nosing out of an opening and buses trying to turn in one long sweep. Ease off and cover the brake when you see one.

If you are behind someone waiting to turn, do not hoot them into a gap they do not think is safe. Pass them on the left only when they are clearly stopped at the median and there is room.

## Practising U-turns in Sawari

Sawari is a free browser driving simulator built on real Hyderabad roads from OpenStreetMap, and its roads have medians with U-turn openings, each marked with a blue U-turn sign. Necklace Road (https://sawari.airacode.online/routes.html#necklace-road), the lakeside loop round Hussain Sagar, has openings in the median, and it is a gentle road to start on.

None of the five routes is planned around a U-turn, but the game treats one the way a real drive would. If you miss a turn or end up heading against the route, a banner tells you to make a U-turn at the next median opening and to look for the blue U-turn sign. You can also press `R` to return to the route if you would rather not.

A few ways to use it:

- Signal with `E` before you move across and before you turn. The indicator cancels itself once the turn is done. On route turns, the game counts a U-turn as a right turn and records a fault in the debrief if you did not signal.

- Set the traffic level higher, up to Dense, and practise waiting for a real gap. Bikes in the game filter through gaps, so you get used to checking for them.

- Switch to the driver's seat with `C` and drag the mouse to look right before you go. There are no mirrors in the game, so look around the way you would turn your head.

- Take it slowly. A collision with a vehicle or the median is logged as a fault, and driving against a one-way carriageway is too.

Start a drive on Necklace Road (https://sawari.airacode.online/play.html?route=necklace-road), then read the debrief for anything to work on. For the signalling side of it, see our guide to indicators and lane discipline (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/indicators-and-lane-discipline.html), and for reading riders and autos around openings, sharing the road with autos, buses and two-wheelers (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/sharing-the-road-autos-buses-two-wheelers.html).

## Frequently asked questions

**Why are there so many U-turns in Hyderabad?**
On many busy roads the traffic police have closed right turns at junctions so the signal can give more time to through traffic. Drivers who want to go right continue a little further and turn back at a median opening instead.

**Which indicator should I use for a U-turn in India?**
The right indicator. In left-hand traffic you make a U-turn to the right, from the right-hand edge of your carriageway, close to the median.

**Can I take a U-turn anywhere there is a gap in the median?**
No. Only use openings meant for turning, usually marked with a U-turn sign, and never where a no U-turn sign is posted, at a signal that forbids it or on a flyover.

**What if my car cannot make the U-turn in one go?**
Take the turn as wide as the opening safely allows. If it still will not fit, stop, wait until it is clear and reverse a short distance only when you are certain nothing is coming.

---

# Hyderabad driving glossary: 60 road, traffic and licence terms explained

URL: https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/hyderabad-driving-glossary.html
Category: Hyderabad roads · Published 2026-11-23 · Updated 2026-11-23

This Hyderabad driving glossary explains about 60 terms you meet on the city's roads, at the RTA and in traffic advisories, from "free left" and "U-turn opening" to ORR, SRDP, HSRP and e-challan. Each definition is short and self-contained, and is correct as we understand it in November 2026.

First, a quick map of who runs what.

| Area | Who is responsible |
|---|---|
| Driving licences and vehicle registration | Telangana Transport Department, through its RTA offices |
| Traffic enforcement and challans | Traffic wings of the Hyderabad, Cyberabad, Malkajgiri and Future City police commissionerates |
| City roads, flyovers and parking policy | GHMC and the newer Cyberabad and Malkajgiri municipal corporations |
| Outer Ring Road and metropolitan planning | HMDA |
| National highways | NHAI and the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways |
| Metro | Hyderabad Metro Rail (HMRL) |
| City buses | TGSRTC |

## A to D

**Auto (auto-rickshaw)**: A three-wheeled taxi with a small engine, seating up to three passengers.

**BH series**: The Bharat series registration, a plate in the format "YY BH 1234 AA" for people who move between states for work, so they need not re-register the vehicle in each state.

**Bus bay**: A recess at the kerb where buses are meant to stop. Expect buses to pull out of it.

**Cable bridge**: In Hyderabad, usually the Durgam Cheruvu cable-stayed bridge, which carries traffic over Durgam Cheruvu lake between Jubilee Hills Road No. 45 and the Madhapur and HITEC City side. It opened in September 2020.

**Challan**: An official notice of a traffic offence with a fine to pay.

**Check post**: A name kept by some junctions that were once checkpoints, such as Jubilee Hills Check Post.

**Commissionerate**: A police unit covering a city area, each with its own traffic police. Since December 2025 the Hyderabad region has four: Hyderabad, Cyberabad, Malkajgiri and Future City.

**Cyberabad**: The popular name for the western IT district around HITEC City, Madhapur and Gachibowli, and the name of the police commissionerate that covers it. Since 2026 it is also the name of a municipal corporation.

**Diversion**: A temporary change of route ordered by traffic police for road works, events, rallies or flooding.

**DL**: Driving licence. In Telangana it is issued by the RTA after a learner's licence and a driving test, and a digital copy in DigiLocker or mParivahan is accepted.

## E to H

**e-challan**: A traffic fine issued electronically, often from a camera photo, and linked to the vehicle's registration number. You can check and pay pending e-challans on the Telangana e-challan portal (https://echallan.tspolice.gov.in).

**Elevated corridor**: A long flyover that carries traffic over several junctions in one go, such as the Aramghar to Zoo Park flyover.

**FASTag**: A windscreen sticker with a radio tag that pays tolls from a linked account. It has been mandatory for four-wheelers on national highways since 2021 and is the normal way to pay on the ORR.

**Financial District**: The office district around Nanakramguda and Gachibowli, west of HITEC City.

**Flyover**: A bridge that lifts traffic over a junction or a stretch of road. See our guide to Hyderabad flyovers and underpasses (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/hyderabad-flyovers-and-underpasses.html).

**Free left**: A left turn you may make on red where a sign, a green left arrow or a slip lane allows it. Give way as you turn, and never block the free left lane if you are going straight.

**Future City**: A planned new urban area on the southern side of the Hyderabad region, beyond the ORR. It has had its own police commissionerate since December 2025.

**GHMC**: Greater Hyderabad Municipal Corporation, the civic body for city roads and parking. It was greatly enlarged in December 2025, and in February 2026 the Cyberabad and Malkajgiri corporations were split off from it.

**HITEC City**: Hyderabad Information Technology and Engineering Consultancy City, the IT district in Madhapur built around the Cyber Towers building.

**HMDA**: Hyderabad Metropolitan Development Authority, which plans the wider metropolitan region and built the Outer Ring Road.

**HMRL**: Hyderabad Metro Rail Limited, the state company behind the metro. The Telangana government took full ownership of the Phase I network from L&T in 2026.

**HSRP**: High-security registration plate, a tamper-proof aluminium plate with a hologram and laser-etched code. New vehicles have had them since April 2019, and Telangana ordered them for older vehicles in 2025.

**HTP**: Hyderabad Traffic Police, the traffic wing of the Hyderabad commissionerate, which posts diversions on its website (https://www.htp.gov.in).

## I to O

**IDP**: International Driving Permit, a translation of a licence in a standard format. Foreign visitors use one issued at home with their home licence; see our guide for NRIs and visitors (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/driving-in-hyderabad-for-nris-and-visitors.html).

**Interchange**: A grade-separated junction where you join or leave an expressway by ramps, as at each exit of the ORR.

**IT corridor**: The western belt of office districts, including HITEC City, Madhapur, Kondapur, Gachibowli and the Financial District.

**LLR**: Learner's licence, the first step to a driving licence. It is valid for six months and lets you drive only with a licensed driver beside you and L plates displayed.

**LMV**: Light motor vehicle, the licence class for ordinary cars and jeeps.

**Malkajgiri**: An area in the north-east of the city that gave its name to a police commissionerate (formerly Rachakonda) in December 2025 and to a municipal corporation in 2026.

**Median**: The raised divider down the middle of a road, separating the two directions. Breaks in it are used for U-turns.

**Metro pillar number**: The number painted on each pillar of the elevated metro, used as a landmark for addresses and cab pick-ups.

**MMTS**: Multi-Modal Transport System, the suburban train service run by South Central Railway on the city's railway lines.

**Necklace Road**: The lakeside road along the western and northern shores of Hussain Sagar.

**NH 44**: The national highway that runs through Hyderabad from north to south, carrying traffic towards Nagpur in one direction and Bengaluru and the airport side in the other.

**Old City**: The historic area south of the Musi river around the Charminar, with narrow, crowded streets and markets.

**ORR**: The Outer Ring Road, officially the Nehru Outer Ring Road, a 158 km, eight-lane access-controlled expressway around the city with tolls by distance.

## P to R

**Pathergatti**: The stone-arcaded market street leading north from the Charminar towards the Musi.

**PUC**: Pollution Under Control certificate, proof that a vehicle's emissions passed a test.

**PVNR Expressway**: The PV Narasimha Rao Expressway, an elevated road of about 11.6 km from Mehdipatnam to Aramghar, on the main route to the airport.

**RC**: Registration certificate, the document that proves a vehicle is registered and shows its owner.

**ROB and RUB**: Road-over-bridge and road-under-bridge, which take a road over or under a railway line instead of across a level crossing.

**Rachakonda**: The former name of the police commissionerate covering the eastern side of the city, renamed Malkajgiri in December 2025. The old name still appears on some signs.

**RRR**: Regional Ring Road, a planned second ring road of about 340 km far outside the ORR. As of November 2026 it was not yet built. See our RRR guide (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/hyderabad-regional-ring-road-rrr.html).

**RTA**: Regional Transport Authority, the local office of the Telangana Transport Department for licences, registration and driving tests. Often called the RTO.

**Rumble strips**: Rows of low ridges across the road that make the car vibrate to warn you of a hazard ahead.

## S to T

**Service road**: A slower road alongside a main road or expressway, giving access to buildings.

**Share auto**: A larger auto or small van that runs on a fixed route and picks up several passengers at once.

**Slip road**: A short road that lets traffic leave or join a main road, or turn left, without going through the junction.

**Speed breaker**: Also called a hump, a raised bump across the road to slow traffic, often unpainted.

**SRDP**: Strategic Road Development Plan, a programme to build flyovers, underpasses, road-over-bridges and steel bridges at the most congested junctions.

**Steel bridge**: A flyover built with a steel deck rather than concrete. The best known is the Indira Park to VST steel bridge of about 2.6 km, opened in August 2023 and named after Nayini Narsimha Reddy.

**Tank Bund**: The road along the dam on the eastern side of Hussain Sagar, built in the sixteenth century, linking Hyderabad and Secunderabad.

**TG plate**: A Telangana registration plate. The state code changed from TS to TG for new registrations from March 2024; older TS plates remain valid.

**TGSRTC**: Telangana State Road Transport Corporation, which runs the city's buses. Many people still call it TSRTC, its name before 2024.

**Toll plaza**: A row of booths where tolls are collected, on the ORR and national highways.

**Towing**: Removal of wrongly parked vehicles by traffic police. You pay a towing charge and a fine to recover it.

## U to Z

**U-turn opening**: A break in the median where you turn back to go the other way. On many main roads it replaces the right turn at the junction. See U-turns in Hyderabad (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/u-turns-in-hyderabad.html).

**Underpass**: A road that dips under a junction or another road so traffic can pass without stopping. Low ones can flood in heavy rain.

**Wrong-side driving**: Driving against the flow of traffic, often to avoid a long U-turn. It causes head-on crashes and is fined.

**Zebra crossing**: Black and white stripes marking a pedestrian crossing. Stop before it, not on it, at a red signal.

## See these terms on real roads in Sawari

Sawari is a free browser driving simulator on five real Hyderabad routes: Tank Bund, Necklace Road, Charminar and Pathergatti, Cyber Towers to Jubilee Hills over the Durgam Cheruvu cable bridge, and Banjara Hills Road No. 1. Its roads have medians with U-turn openings, flyovers, metro viaducts, autos and buses, and the debrief lists your faults. It works on phones held sideways with an on-screen steering wheel, tablets, laptops and PCs.

Sawari is for practice only. It does not replace lessons with a licensed instructor. On the road, follow the signs, signals and instructions from the traffic police.

## Frequently asked questions

**What does RTA mean in Hyderabad?**
RTA stands for Regional Transport Authority, the local office of the Telangana Transport Department that issues driving licences, registers vehicles and conducts driving tests. People often use RTA and RTO to mean the same thing.

**What is a free left in Hyderabad?**
A free left is a left turn you may make even when the main signal is red, where a sign, a green left arrow or a separate slip lane shows it is allowed. You must still give way to pedestrians and traffic, and you should never block a free left lane if you are going straight.

**What is the difference between the ORR and the RRR?**
The ORR is the 158 km Outer Ring Road expressway that already loops round Hyderabad. The RRR is the Regional Ring Road, a much larger second ring of about 340 km that is planned far outside the ORR and was not yet built as of November 2026.

**What is SRDP in Hyderabad?**
SRDP is the Strategic Road Development Plan, a programme to build flyovers, underpasses, road-over-bridges and steel bridges at Hyderabad's most congested junctions.
