# Hyderabad e-challan guide: how to check, pay and dispute a traffic challan

URL: https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/hyderabad-e-challan-guide.html
Category: Hyderabad roads · Published 2026-11-23 · Updated 2026-11-23

An e-challan is a traffic fine issued electronically against a vehicle's registration number, usually from a camera photo, and in Hyderabad you check, pay or dispute it on the official Telangana Police e-challan site, echallan.tspolice.gov.in. Search by your vehicle number, check the photo, and either pay online or raise a grievance if it is wrong.

This guide covers how challans are raised in Hyderabad, Cyberabad and the other Telangana police areas, how to look them up, how to pay, what happens if you ignore them and how to dispute a wrong one, as of November 2026. We have left out fine amounts on purpose: they are set by law and change, and the e-challan site shows the exact amount for each challan.

## What is an e-challan?

An e-challan is an electronic notice of a traffic offence, linked to the vehicle's registration number and sent to the registered owner. It replaces the old paper challan written at the roadside, although officers can still issue challans on the spot.

Each challan records the date, time and place, the offence, the amount and, for camera challans, a photo of the vehicle. Hyderabad Traffic Police, Cyberabad, Rachakonda (Malkajgiri) and the other commissionerates in Telangana all feed into the same integrated e-challan system, so one search shows challans from across the state.

### Key facts

- **Official site:** echallan.tspolice.gov.in (https://echallan.tspolice.gov.in), the Telangana Police integrated e-challan system.

- **Who it is issued to:** the registered owner of the vehicle, whoever was driving.

- **How to search:** vehicle number, driving licence number, challan number or mobile number.

- **How to pay:** UPI, debit card, credit card or net banking on the official site.

- **Disputes:** a grievance option on the same site, with reasons such as "Not my vehicle", "Wrong challan" and "Double challan".

- **Official SMS:** the site says genuine e-challan messages come only from a sender header starting "ECHALN".

## How do cameras and police issue e-challans?

Most challans in Hyderabad now come from cameras, not from an officer stopping you. There are three main sources.

- **Junction and roadside cameras.** Cameras at signals and along main roads capture offences such as jumping a red light, crossing the stop line, riding without a helmet and driving on the wrong side.

- **Officers with handheld cameras.** Traffic police photograph offences such as wrong parking, a rider without a helmet, triple riding or a phone in hand, and the photo becomes a challan.

- **Spot challans.** At checkpoints an officer issues a challan with a handheld device, and you can pay there or later. The official site notes a small user charge on spot challans.

Because the challan follows the number plate, a dirty, bent or non-standard plate can lead to wrong readings, and a car sold without transferring the RC can keep collecting challans in the old owner's name. Our guide to TG number plates (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/telangana-tg-number-plates-explained.html) explains the plate format, and our Hyderabad traffic rules guide (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/hyderabad-traffic-rules-guide.html) covers the offences cameras catch most often.

## How do you check an e-challan by vehicle number?

Go to the official e-challan site, enter your vehicle number and the captcha, and it lists every pending challan against that vehicle. Step by step:

- Open echallan.tspolice.gov.in (https://echallan.tspolice.gov.in) in your browser. Type the address yourself rather than tapping a link in a message.

- Choose the vehicle number search and enter the registration number in full, for example TG 09 followed by the series and number. Both older TS and newer TG plates are searched by their own number.

- Enter the captcha and submit.

- Read each challan: date, time, place, offence and amount. Open the photo and check that the vehicle and number plate really are yours.

The same site lets you search by licence number, challan number or mobile number, look up payment receipts and check the penalty points on a driving licence. The national Parivahan e-challan site (https://echallan.parivahan.gov.in) also shows challans for many states.

Check your vehicle every month or two, and always before you sell it or buy a used one. A challan you never knew about is much easier to deal with early.

## How do you pay an e-challan, and what if you do not?

Pay on the official e-challan site by UPI, debit card, credit card or net banking. Select the challans you want to clear, pay, and note the transaction reference number shown at the end. You can download a receipt later from the payment receipt search.

- **If money is debited but the challan still shows as pending,** the site advises waiting 24 hours. If it is still not updated, contact the helpdesk for your commissionerate with the reference number. The site says failed payments are generally refunded within seven working days.

- **Use only official channels.** Telangana Police warn about fake e-challan websites and apps that copy the real one. Never pay through a link that arrives by SMS, WhatsApp or email.

- **Helplines.** As of November 2026 the official site lists helpdesk numbers for each commissionerate, including Hyderabad on 040-27852721 and 040-27852772.

A message saying "your challan is pending, pay now or face court action" with a link is a common scam. Check the challan yourself on the official site before paying anything.

### What happens if you do not pay?

Unpaid challans do not go away, and recent national rules make ignoring them more costly. In January 2026 the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways amended the Central Motor Vehicles Rules on challans and licences. As widely reported, the changes include:

- **A window to act.** A set period, reported as 45 days from issue, to either pay the challan or contest it online with evidence. A challan you neither pay nor contest is treated as accepted.

- **Blocked services.** A vehicle with unpaid challans can be flagged on the national portal, which stops services such as transfer of ownership, change of address and other RTA applications, apart from paying road tax.

- **Licence disqualification.** The Central Motor Vehicles (Third Amendment) Rules, 2026 (G.S.R. 48(E), 21 January 2026) let the licensing authority disqualify a driver for five or more offences within one year, counted from 1 January 2026.

Police can also stop vehicles with many pending challans during special drives. If you are unsure which rules apply to your challan, the official site and the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (https://morth.gov.in) publish the current position.

## How do you dispute a wrong e-challan?

Raise a grievance on the official e-challan site with evidence, as soon as you notice the mistake. Wrong challans usually come from a misread or fake number plate, a vehicle you have already sold, a duplicate of an earlier challan, or a photo that does not show the offence.

- **Find and open the challan** on the official site and look carefully at the photo.

- **Select the grievance option** and choose the reason that fits: not my vehicle, wrong challan or double challan.

- **Add clear remarks**, for example "The photo shows a white hatchback; my vehicle is a grey sedan" or "Vehicle sold on this date; RC transferred".

- **Keep your evidence ready:** RC, a photo of your own number plate, the sale and transfer papers, or proof of where the vehicle was at that time.

- **Note the reference** and watch for the SMS update on the outcome.

If someone is using your number on another vehicle, the site has a separate **fake number plate** complaint, and a **sold out vehicle** option for vehicles you no longer own. Do not simply pay a challan you believe is wrong; once paid, it is treated as settled.

## Have there been challan discount schemes?

Yes, but only as one-off schemes, and none was running as of November 2026. Treat this as history, not a promise of another:

| When | What happened |
|---|---|
| March to April 2022 | A one-time discount on pending challans, started on 1 March 2022 and extended into mid-April 2022. |
| 26 December 2023 to 15 February 2024 | A government order gave discounts on pending challans, with different rates by vehicle type. It was extended twice and ended on 15 February 2024. |
| December 2024 | A viral message claimed a new discount; Hyderabad Traffic Police said it was fake. |

Fake discount messages appear regularly, and they are often a lure to a payment link. A genuine scheme is announced by Telangana Police and the state government and shows on the official site itself.

## Can you practise the habits that avoid challans?

The best way to deal with challans is not to collect them. Most camera challans come from a few habits: stopping behind the stop line, not jumping an amber light, keeping to your lane and parking only where it is allowed. Our Hyderabad parking guide (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/hyderabad-parking-guide.html) covers the last one.

Sawari, a free browser driving simulator on five real Hyderabad routes, scores those same habits. It runs on a phone, tablet, laptop or PC, and the debrief at the end lists every red light, missed indicator and lane fault. It is practice only and cannot tell you about real challans, but a calm run through the signals on the HITEC City route (https://sawari.airacode.online/play.html?route=hitec-city) is a good rehearsal for the cameras.

## Frequently asked questions

**How do I check my e-challan in Hyderabad?**
Open the official Telangana Police e-challan site at echallan.tspolice.gov.in, enter your vehicle registration number and the captcha, and it lists every pending challan with the date, place, offence and photo. You can also search by licence, challan or mobile number.

**How do I pay a Telangana e-challan online?**
Select the challans on the official e-challan site and pay by UPI, debit card, credit card or net banking, then note the transaction reference number. If money is debited but the challan still shows as pending, the site advises waiting 24 hours before raising it with the helpdesk.

**What if I get a wrong e-challan?**
Use the grievance option on the official e-challan site, select the challan, choose a reason such as not my vehicle or wrong challan, and add remarks. Keep evidence such as your RC, photos of your own number plate and proof of where the vehicle was, and note the reference you are given.

**Is there a discount on pending challans in Telangana now?**
As of November 2026 we found no current discount scheme. Telangana ran one-off discounts in 2022 and from December 2023 to February 2024, and police have repeatedly called later discount messages fake, so trust only official police announcements.

---

# Hyderabad parking guide: malls, the Old City, HITEC City, metro stations and street parking

URL: https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/hyderabad-parking-guide.html
Category: Hyderabad roads · Published 2026-11-23 · Updated 2026-11-23

Parking in Hyderabad is easiest in malls, office campuses and paid parking lots, and hardest in the Old City, on busy commercial roads and around hospitals. The safe rule is simple: park only where it is clearly allowed, because traffic police tow and fine wrongly parked vehicles and many fines arrive as camera e-challans.

This guide covers the places drivers ask about most, as of November 2026. We have left out parking rates, because they change often and vary by operator; check the signboard or app at each place.

| Place | What to expect |
|---|---|
| Malls and multiplexes | Basement parking; first 30 minutes free under Telangana rules, with more free time if you show a bill |
| Charminar and the Old City | Very little parking; park further out and walk or take an auto |
| HITEC City and the IT corridor | Campus parking for staff with passes; limited visitor space |
| Metro stations | Parking at some stations, mostly at the ends of lines; paid at Miyapur and Nagole |
| Hospitals | Often full at peak times; drop the patient at the entrance first |
| Main roads | No parking on most arterial roads, flyovers and near junctions; towing is common |

## Is mall parking free in Hyderabad?

Partly. A Telangana government order that came into force on 1 April 2018 sets limits on what malls and multiplexes in Hyderabad can charge:

- **Up to 30 minutes:** no parking fee.

- **Up to one hour:** free if you show a purchase bill from the mall.

- **More than one hour:** free if your bill or movie ticket is worth more than the parking fee; otherwise the normal fee applies.

Not every mall has followed it. GHMC inspection teams found malls charging customers who had purchase receipts and issued notices in 2024, and GHMC has fined malls for illegal parking fee collection. Keep your bill and parking ticket, and if you are wrongly charged, complain to the mall and to GHMC.

Mall basements are tight. Follow the arrows, drive at walking pace with your headlights on, and watch for pillars and people walking between cars. On weekend evenings the queue to get in can back up onto the main road, so arriving early helps.

## Where can you park near Charminar and in the Old City?

Hardly anywhere close by, so plan to park at a distance. The streets around the Charminar, Gulzar Houz, Laad Bazaar and Pathergatti are narrow and crowded, and shoppers and traders have long complained about the lack of parking.

- **The planned car park is not built.** GHMC has planned a multi-level parking complex on the Charminar bus stand and Khilwat Khazana building sites, but as of November 2026 the project was stalled after its tenders drew no response.

- **Festival parking.** During Ramzan and other busy seasons, traffic police have opened temporary parking at places such as the Charminar bus station ground, Khilwat and the Quli Qutub Shah Stadium. Look for the announcements from Hyderabad Traffic Police (https://www.htp.gov.in) before you go.

- **Use an auto for the last stretch.** Parking further out and taking an auto or walking is often quicker than circling the lanes.

If you do drive in, go early in the day and read our Charminar and Old City driving guide (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/charminar-old-city-driving-guide.html) first.

## How does parking work at HITEC City offices and hospitals?

Most large tech parks in HITEC City, Madhapur, Gachibowli and the Financial District have basement or multi-level parking for employees, usually with a pass, a sticker or a tag. Visitor parking is limited, and some campuses ask visitors to register at the gate.

- **Ask your host** whether visitor parking is available before you drive to a meeting.

- **Do not park on the service roads** or outside the gates unless it is signed as allowed. These roads carry heavy traffic at log-in and log-out times and are watched closely.

- **Consider the metro.** The Blue Line serves HITEC City and Raidurg, so driving to a station with parking and riding in can be easier than finding a space in the IT corridor.

### Hospitals

Hospital parking fills up quickly, especially in the morning outpatient rush. If you are bringing a patient, drop them at the entrance first and then look for a space. Never block the ambulance bay or the emergency entrance, even for a minute. At large hospitals on busy roads, a cab or auto may be easier for routine appointments.

## Can you park at Hyderabad metro stations?

At some of them. Parking is mostly at or near the ends of the lines, where stations have more land; many stations in the city centre have little or none.

- **Paid parking** was introduced at Miyapur and Nagole stations in 2024 by the then operator, L&T Metro Rail. The Telangana government took over the Phase I network from L&T in 2026, so check the current arrangements at the station.

- **Nampally** has a fully automated multi-level parking complex built by Hyderabad Metro Rail, opened in January 2026. Cars are moved and stored by machine after you leave them at the entry bay.

- **Do not park under the viaduct** or on the road outside a station unless signs allow it. The roads below the metro are busy and often narrowed by pillars.

Our Hyderabad metro guide for drivers (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/hyderabad-metro-guide-for-drivers.html) explains which lines run where and when park and ride makes sense. Check Hyderabad Metro Rail (https://www.hmrl.co.in) for station facilities.

## What are the rules for street parking in Hyderabad?

Park only where it is allowed, clear of traffic, and never where you block others. In general, do not park:

- where a **No Parking** or **No Stopping** sign applies;

- on a **footpath**, a **zebra crossing** or near a **junction**;

- at or near a **bus stop**, or in a **free left** lane;

- on a **flyover**, a bridge or the **Outer Ring Road**, except in an emergency;

- in front of **gates and driveways**, fire hydrants or hospital entrances;

- **double parked** beside another vehicle.

GHMC runs paid on-street parking at some locations, and its parking policy has generally allowed on-street parking only on wider roads. Where you see attendants, ask for a receipt. Our Hyderabad traffic rules guide (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/hyderabad-traffic-rules-guide.html) covers the wider rules.

### No-parking fines and towing

Traffic police tow cars and two-wheelers parked in no-parking zones or blocking traffic, and photograph wrongly parked vehicles for e-challans. If your vehicle has gone, call the local traffic police station or the Hyderabad Traffic Police helpline to find out where it was taken. You will normally pay a towing charge and a fine. Check pending challans on the Telangana e-challan portal (https://echallan.tspolice.gov.in).

Before you walk away, look back at your car: is it fully off the carriageway, clear of any gate, and not under a no-parking sign you missed? It takes ten seconds and saves a trip to the tow yard.

## Parking tips that save time

- **Decide where you will park before you leave.** Map apps show many paid lots, and choosing one in advance stops you circling.

- **Arrive early** for weekend malls, festivals, cricket matches and the Numaish exhibition.

- **Reverse into bays** where you can. Driving out forwards into a busy lane is safer.

- **Fold your mirrors** on narrow streets and leave room for two-wheelers to pass.

- **Keep valuables out of sight** and lock the car, even in staffed lots.

- **Leave a phone number** on the dashboard in residential areas so a neighbour can call rather than complain.

## Practising crowded streets in Sawari

Sawari does not simulate parking manoeuvres, so it will not teach you to reverse into a bay. What it can help with is driving the crowded approach to places where parking is hard. Its Charminar and Pathergatti route (https://sawari.airacode.online/routes.html#charminar) has narrow streets and busy kerbs, and the debrief lists every fault so you can see where you came too close or went too fast. It runs free in a browser on phones held sideways with an on-screen steering wheel, tablets, laptops and PCs.

Sawari is for practice only. It does not replace lessons with a licensed instructor. On the road, follow the signs, signals and instructions from the traffic police.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is mall parking free in Hyderabad?**
Under a Telangana rule in force since April 2018, the first 30 minutes are free, parking up to an hour is free if you show a purchase bill, and beyond an hour it is free if your bill or movie ticket is worth more than the parking fee. GHMC has warned and fined malls for not following it.

**Where can I park near Charminar?**
There is no large permanent car park right beside the monument, and a planned multi-level parking complex near Charminar had not been built as of November 2026. Most visitors park further out and walk or take an auto, and traffic police open temporary parking grounds during Ramzan and other busy festivals.

**Can I park at Hyderabad metro stations?**
Some stations have parking, mostly at or near the ends of the lines such as Miyapur and Nagole, where paid parking was introduced in 2024. Many central stations have little or none, so check before relying on park and ride.

**What happens if my car is towed in Hyderabad?**
Traffic police tow vehicles parked in no-parking zones or where they block traffic, and you will normally pay a towing charge and a fine to get it back. Contact the local traffic police station or the Hyderabad Traffic Police helpline to find where it was taken.

---

# Hyderabad to Bengaluru by road: the NH 44 drive via Kurnool and Anantapur

URL: https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/hyderabad-to-bengaluru-drive.html
Category: Hyderabad roads · Published 2026-11-23 · Updated 2026-11-23

Hyderabad to Bengaluru by road is roughly 560 to 610 km on National Highway 44, and the drive usually takes nine to eleven hours with short stops. The route runs south past Jadcherla to Kurnool, through Gooty and Anantapur in Andhra Pradesh, and into Karnataka past Bagepalli, Chikkaballapur and Devanahalli.

It is one of the longest drives people regularly make from Hyderabad, and most of it is a four-lane divided highway. This guide covers the route, tolls, stops, the cautions that matter most on a trip this long, and the alternatives, as of November 2026. We have left out toll rates, which NHAI revises, and give distances and times as ranges because they depend on where you start and finish.

## How far is it and how long does it take?

Expect about 560 to 610 km and nine to eleven hours door to door, including short breaks. Starting near Shamshabad and ending in north Bengaluru is at the short end; starting in west Hyderabad and ending in south Bengaluru adds an hour or more of city driving.

| Key fact | Detail |
|---|---|
| Highway | NH 44, mostly four lanes with a central median |
| Distance | About 560 to 610 km, city to city |
| Typical time | About 9 to 11 hours with short stops |
| States | Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka |
| Halfway area | Roughly between Kurnool and Anantapur |
| Tolls | Several plazas, all on FASTag |

## What is the route via Kurnool and Anantapur?

Stay on NH 44 the whole way. The main places, in order:

- **Shamshabad**, past the airport. If you live near the ORR, join NH 44 at the Shamshabad interchange to avoid the city; see our Outer Ring Road guide (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/hyderabad-outer-ring-road-guide.html).

- **Shadnagar and Jadcherla**, the first stretch through Telangana.

- **The Krishna river crossing** and the approach to the state border.

- **Kurnool**, across the Tungabhadra in Andhra Pradesh, a little over a third of the way and the first big city.

- **Dhone and Gooty**, through dry, open country.

- **Anantapur**, the other large city on the route.

- **Penukonda**, then the Karnataka border near Kodikonda.

- **Bagepalli and Chikkaballapur**, where the road climbs gently towards the Bengaluru plateau.

- **Devanahalli**, past Kempegowda International Airport, then into the city via Hebbal.

The last stretch from the airport into Bengaluru is often slow, especially on weekday evenings. Our comparison of Hyderabad and Bengaluru traffic (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/hyderabad-vs-bengaluru-traffic.html) explains why.

## What should you know about tolls and FASTag?

There are several toll plazas between the two cities, all on FASTag, so check your balance before you leave.

- **Without FASTag you pay more.** Since 15 November 2025, a vehicle without a valid FASTag pays 1.25 times the toll by UPI and twice the toll in cash on national highways.

- **Annual pass.** The NHAI FASTag annual pass for private cars covers one year or 200 toll crossings on national highways, whichever comes first. On a route with this many plazas, a return trip uses a lot of crossings, so check whether it suits you on NHAI (https://nhai.gov.in)'s channels.

- **Toll queues** are longest around long weekends and festivals, and at the plazas nearest each city.

## Where should you stop?

Plan two or three real breaks, not just fuel stops, because ten hours at the wheel is tiring. In general terms:

- **Around Jadcherla** for an early breakfast or tea if you leave before dawn.

- **Kurnool** for a proper meal and a rest, since it is a large city with plenty of choice just off the highway.

- **Anantapur** for a second meal or a long break.

- **Fuel stations** along the whole route, many with toilets and food courts. Fill up before the long, emptier stretches between towns.

Carry water, especially in summer, when the Rayalaseema stretch around Kurnool and Anantapur gets very hot. Check tyre pressures, coolant and the spare before you set off.

## Is it safe to drive NH 44, especially at night?

You can drive it at night, but daytime is safer and less tiring. NH 44 carries heavy lorry and sleeper-bus traffic after dark, and night adds hazards you do not see by day:

- **Unlit vehicles.** Tractors, carts and some two-wheelers run without proper lights, and broken-down lorries are often parked on the carriageway with little warning.

- **People and animals.** Villagers cross at junctions and cattle wander onto the road, especially near towns.

- **Glare.** Oncoming high beams across the median dazzle you; look towards the left edge of your lane, not at the lights.

- **Tiredness.** The straight stretches through Rayalaseema invite microsleep, most of all between about 2 and 5 am.

Night crashes here can be severe. In October 2025 a Hyderabad to Bengaluru sleeper bus caught fire after hitting a motorcycle on NH 44 near Kurnool, and around 20 people died. It is a reminder to keep a long gap, slow down for anything unclear in your headlights and never drive while drowsy.

If you must drive at night, share the driving, stop every two hours, keep to the posted speed limits and use dipped headlights when other vehicles approach. Everyone, front and back, should wear a seat belt.

Our night driving tips (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/night-driving-hyderabad-tips.html) cover headlights, glare and tiredness in more detail.

### Habits for the whole drive

By day or night, drive it as a fast divided highway that still has local traffic:

- **Keep left and overtake on the right,** with your indicator on, and move back left once you are well past.

- **Expect wrong-side traffic** near median openings and villages, mainly two-wheelers and tractors.

- **Slow down through towns and junctions,** and well before toll plazas.

- **Follow the posted speed limits,** which change between states and stretches.

- **Watch for works.** NHAI has plans to upgrade parts of NH 44 between the two cities, including bypasses and underpasses around Kurnool, and wider sections near Bengaluru. As of November 2026 several were at the planning or tender stage, so expect diversions in the coming years.

Leaving Hyderabad early, around dawn, usually gets you through Kurnool by mid-morning and into Bengaluru before the evening rush.

## What are the alternatives to driving?

If you do not need a car at the other end, other options are often less tiring:

- **Flights** are the quickest, with many daily flights between the two airports.

- **Train.** The Kacheguda to Yesvantpur Vande Bharat Express, running since September 2023 via Mahbubnagar, Kurnool City and Anantapur, takes a little over eight hours. Many overnight trains also run.

- **Bus.** Government and private sleeper buses run overnight.

- **Split the drive.** An overnight stop in Kurnool or Anantapur turns one long day into two easy ones.

For shorter trips, see our Hyderabad to Vijayawada guide (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/hyderabad-to-vijayawada-drive.html) and our list of weekend road trips from Hyderabad (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/weekend-road-trips-from-hyderabad.html).

## Can you practise for the drive?

Only the city part. Sawari, a free browser driving simulator, has five real Hyderabad city routes and no highways, so it cannot show you NH 44. It does train the habits that matter at both ends of the trip: lane discipline, indicating, judging gaps and driving in heavy mixed traffic, including at night. It runs on a phone, tablet, laptop or PC and is practice only. Try the HITEC City to Jubilee Hills route (https://sawari.airacode.online/play.html?route=hitec-city) at night to rehearse busy junctions under street lights.

## Frequently asked questions

**How long does it take to drive from Hyderabad to Bengaluru?**
Usually about nine to eleven hours for roughly 560 to 610 km, including short stops. The open highway is quick; most of the variation comes from leaving Hyderabad, entering Bengaluru and how long you stop.

**Which highway goes from Hyderabad to Bengaluru?**
National Highway 44, the north-south highway, runs from Hyderabad past Shamshabad and Jadcherla, through Kurnool, Gooty and Anantapur in Andhra Pradesh, and on through Bagepalli, Chikkaballapur and Devanahalli into Bengaluru.

**Is it safe to drive from Hyderabad to Bengaluru at night?**
It is possible, but daytime is safer. At night the highway carries many lorries and sleeper buses, and you meet unlit vehicles, pedestrians and animals, while tiredness builds on the long straight stretches. If you must drive at night, share the driving and stop every two hours.

**What are the alternatives to driving from Hyderabad to Bengaluru?**
Flights are the fastest. By rail, the Kacheguda to Yesvantpur Vande Bharat Express via Kurnool and Anantapur takes a little over eight hours, and many overnight trains and buses also run between the two cities.

---

# Hyderabad to Vijayawada by road: the NH 65 drive, tolls, stops and safety

URL: https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/hyderabad-to-vijayawada-drive.html
Category: Hyderabad roads · Published 2026-11-23 · Updated 2026-11-23

Hyderabad to Vijayawada by road is roughly 270 to 280 km on National Highway 65, and the drive usually takes four and a half to six hours. It is a four-lane divided highway through Choutuppal, Suryapet, Kodad, Jaggayyapeta and Nandigama, with three FASTag toll plazas on the way.

This guide covers the route, the towns, tolls, stops, the safety points that matter on this highway and when to go, as of November 2026. We have left out toll rates, because NHAI revises them; the FASTag app and the toll plaza boards show the current amount. Distances and times are ranges, because they depend on where in each city you start and finish.

## How far is it and how long does the drive take?

Expect about 270 to 280 km and four and a half to six hours of driving, plus your stops. The biggest variable is getting out of Hyderabad: from the western suburbs you cross most of the city, while from LB Nagar or the ORR you are almost on the highway already.

| Key fact | Detail |
|---|---|
| Highway | NH 65, four lanes with a central median |
| Distance | About 270 to 280 km, city to city |
| Typical driving time | About 4.5 to 6 hours, more at festival times |
| Main toll plazas | Pantangi, Korlapahad, Chillakallu |
| Payment | FASTag; without one you pay more |
| State border | Telangana to Andhra Pradesh, after Kodad |

## What is the route from Hyderabad to Vijayawada?

Leave Hyderabad on the Vijayawada highway through LB Nagar and Hayathnagar, cross the Outer Ring Road near Pedda Amberpet, and stay on NH 65 all the way. In order, the main places are:

- **LB Nagar and Hayathnagar**, the slow, busy eastern edge of the city.

- **Pedda Amberpet**, where the highway meets the ORR. Joining from the ORR here avoids the city if you live near another ORR exit; see our Outer Ring Road guide (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/hyderabad-outer-ring-road-guide.html).

- **Choutuppal**, with the Pantangi toll plaza, the first major toll.

- **Narketpally**, where roads branch off towards Nalgonda, followed by the Korlapahad toll plaza.

- **Suryapet**, roughly the halfway point.

- **Kodad**, the last large town in Telangana.

- **Jaggayyapeta** in Andhra Pradesh, with the Chillakallu toll plaza.

- **Nandigama and Kanchikacherla**, then **Ibrahimpatnam** and into Vijayawada across the approach to the city.

Navigation apps sometimes suggest a detour through Bhongir or Khammam when NH 65 is jammed. These are slower two-lane roads in places, so use them only if the main highway is badly blocked.

## What should you know about tolls and FASTag?

All three main toll plazas take FASTag, and you should not travel without a working one. GMR built the four-lane highway and collected tolls from 2012 until mid-2024, when NHAI took over toll collection.

- **Without FASTag you pay more.** Since 15 November 2025, under the National Highways Fee rules, a vehicle without a valid FASTag pays 1.25 times the toll if it pays by UPI and twice the toll in cash.

- **Annual pass.** NHAI sells a FASTag annual pass for private cars, valid for one year or 200 toll crossings on national highways, whichever comes first. If you drive this highway often, compare it with paying per trip on the NHAI (https://nhai.gov.in) or Rajmargyatra channels.

- **Before you leave,** check your FASTag balance and that the tag is active and linked to the right vehicle.

## Where can you stop for food and fuel?

There are plenty of stops, and you rarely go long without a fuel station. In general terms:

- **Dhabas and highway restaurants** line the stretch around Choutuppal, Narketpally and Suryapet, with Telangana and Andhra meals, tiffin in the morning and tea at all hours.

- **Fuel stations** are frequent, and many have clean toilets and space to park. Larger ones near the towns are usually better lit at night.

- **Towns** such as Suryapet and Kodad have more choice if you want to leave the highway, but turning across the median into a town adds time.

- **A good rhythm** is a short break every two hours. Suryapet, near the halfway mark, is a natural place for a longer stop.

Park well clear of the carriageway when you stop, and do not pull up on the shoulder for tea at a roadside stall. Lorries and buses use the shoulder too.

## How do you drive NH 65 safely?

Treat it as a fast highway with village traffic mixed in. The road is divided, but it passes many villages and junctions where people cross, and accidents on this highway are a frequent concern.

- **Keep left and overtake on the right.** Slow lorries often sit in the right lane; do not undertake them on the left at speed.

- **Watch for wrong-side traffic.** Two-wheelers, tractors and even cars sometimes come the wrong way on your side to reach a median opening.

- **Slow down at junctions and villages.** Pedestrians, cattle and two-wheelers cross at median openings, especially near towns.

- **Follow the posted speed limits,** which change along the route, and slow down well before toll plazas, where queues build fast.

- **Keep a long gap** behind lorries and buses so you can see past them and stop in time.

- **Take breaks and do not drive tired.** Microsleep on a straight, familiar highway is a real risk, especially after lunch and late at night.

- **Expect works zones.** NHAI plans to widen most of NH 65 between the two cities to six lanes with service roads. As of November 2026 bids had been invited and work was expected to start in early 2027, so diversions are likely for some years.

Wear seat belts in every seat, front and back. If you break down, get everyone out on the side away from traffic and behind the barrier if there is one, and put the hazard lights and warning triangle on.

Our posts on night driving (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/night-driving-hyderabad-tips.html) and monsoon driving (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/monsoon-driving-hyderabad.html) cover the conditions that make this highway harder.

## When is the best time to drive?

Early morning on a weekday is usually best: leave Hyderabad around dawn, clear the eastern suburbs before the morning rush and reach Vijayawada by late morning.

- **Avoid Sankranti weekends if you can.** In January, huge numbers of people drive home to Andhra Pradesh. In January 2026 the Pantangi toll plaza handled over one lakh vehicles in a day, with delays of two to three hours reported at the toll booths, and the return journey a few days later was just as slow.

- **Long weekends and festivals** such as Dasara bring similar, smaller peaks. Leaving a day early or very early in the morning helps.

- **Avoid late-night driving** if you can. Lorries dominate the highway at night, and tiredness catches up with you.

- **Monsoon** brings heavy rain and poor visibility; slow down and increase your gap.

For other trips out of the city, see our list of weekend road trips from Hyderabad (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/weekend-road-trips-from-hyderabad.html).

## Can you practise for the drive?

Partly. Sawari, a free browser driving simulator, has five real Hyderabad city routes, not highways, so it will not show you NH 65. What it does help with is the city part of the trip and the habits that carry over: lane discipline, indicating before every lane change, judging gaps and keeping calm around buses and two-wheelers. It runs on a phone, tablet, laptop or PC, and it is practice only. A run on Tank Bund Road (https://sawari.airacode.online/play.html?route=tank-bund) in heavy traffic is a fair warm-up for leaving the city.

## Frequently asked questions

**How long does it take to drive from Hyderabad to Vijayawada?**
Usually about four and a half to six hours for roughly 270 to 280 km, depending on where you start in Hyderabad, traffic leaving the city and how long you stop. At festival times such as Sankranti it can take much longer.

**Which highway connects Hyderabad and Vijayawada?**
National Highway 65, a four-lane divided highway that runs from Hyderabad through Choutuppal, Suryapet and Kodad in Telangana and Jaggayyapeta and Nandigama in Andhra Pradesh to Vijayawada.

**How many toll plazas are there between Hyderabad and Vijayawada?**
There are three main toll plazas on NH 65: Pantangi near Choutuppal, Korlapahad between Narketpally and Suryapet and Chillakallu near Jaggayyapeta. NHAI took over toll collection in 2024, and payment is by FASTag.

**Is the Hyderabad to Vijayawada highway being widened?**
Yes. NHAI plans to widen most of NH 65 between the two cities to six lanes with service roads. As of November 2026 bids had been invited and work was expected to start in early 2027, so expect works zones over the next few years.

---

# Hyderabad vs Bengaluru traffic: an honest comparison for people moving between the cities

URL: https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/hyderabad-vs-bengaluru-traffic.html
Category: Hyderabad roads · Published 2026-11-23 · Updated 2026-11-23

Hyderabad traffic is, on average, lighter than Bengaluru's: in the TomTom Traffic Index for 2025, Bengaluru was the world's second most congested city and Hyderabad was 47th. But both cities jam badly at peak hours around their IT districts, and the bigger difference for a driver is road layout: Hyderabad has a complete 158 km expressway ring road, while Bengaluru has a larger metro.

This is a comparison for people moving between the two cities, not a contest. Both are fast-growing tech cities with similar problems, and both are building their way out of them. Figures are the latest we could verify as of November 2026, with their sources.

|  | Hyderabad | Bengaluru |
|---|---|---|
| TomTom Traffic Index 2025, world rank | 47th | 2nd |
| Average congestion level, 2025 | About 55.5% | 74.4% |
| Change from 2024 | Down 1.3 points | Up 1.7 points |
| Expressway ring road | ORR, 158 km, complete loop | No complete loop; NICE Road and parts of the STRR |
| Metro, November 2026 | About 69 km, three lines | Just over 100 km |
| Registered vehicles | Nearly 89 lakh in Greater Hyderabad (early 2026) | Over 1.2 crore (March 2026) |

Vehicle counts use each city's own boundaries, so compare them loosely.

## Is Hyderabad traffic better than Bengaluru?

On average, yes, by a clear margin. The TomTom Traffic Index (https://www.tomtom.com/traffic-index/) for 2025, published in January 2026, ranked Bengaluru second in the world for congestion, behind only Mexico City, with an average congestion level of 74.4%, up 1.7 points on 2024. Hyderabad was 47th, with an average of about 55.5%, a small improvement of 1.3 points.

TomTom also estimated the time a rush-hour commuter loses to congestion in a year: about 168 hours in Bengaluru and about 123 hours in Hyderabad.

Two caveats are worth knowing. First, TomTom measures from connected-car and navigation data, and Bengaluru Traffic Police have said their own data shows travel times close to 10% faster than TomTom reported. Second, a city average hides the roads you actually use. A Hyderabad commute from Kukatpally to the Financial District at 6 pm can feel every bit as slow as a Bengaluru one across Silk Board.

## How do the road networks compare?

Hyderabad's biggest advantage is a complete expressway ring; Bengaluru relies more on arterial roads and flyovers.

### Hyderabad: the ORR and wide western roads

Hyderabad's Outer Ring Road (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/hyderabad-outer-ring-road-guide.html) is a 158 km, eight-lane, access-controlled toll expressway that loops right round the city, linking the IT corridor, the airport and the highways. It lets a lot of traffic avoid the centre altogether. A second, much larger Regional Ring Road of about 340 km is planned but not yet built. Inside the city, the newer western districts have wide roads, many flyovers and long stretches where right turns are replaced by U-turn openings in the median.

### Bengaluru: arterial ring roads and a growing outer network

Bengaluru's Outer Ring Road is an arterial city road with junctions and signals, not an expressway, and the tech parks along it make it one of the busiest roads in the country. The tolled NICE Road links parts of the south and west, the Satellite Town Ring Road far outside the city has opened in sections, and a Peripheral Ring Road has been planned for years but was still at an early stage in 2026.

If you are moving from Bengaluru, do not confuse the two ORRs. In Hyderabad, "take the ORR" means an expressway with ramps, tolls and lane speed limits, not a signalled city road.

## Which city has the better metro?

Bengaluru's metro is now larger. Its Namma Metro passed 100 km in November 2026, when the Pink Line opened, making it the third Indian city after Delhi-NCR and Mumbai to do so. Hyderabad Metro has three lines, Red, Blue and Green, covering about 69 km, all elevated above the main roads; the Telangana government took full ownership of it from L&T in 2026, and a second phase is planned.

For drivers, the practical point is the same in both cities: a metro line nearby makes it realistic to drive part of the way and ride the rest, especially into areas where parking is hard. Our Hyderabad metro guide for drivers (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/hyderabad-metro-guide-for-drivers.html) shows where the lines run.

## When are the peak hours in each city?

Peak hours follow office times in both cities, and the evening peak is usually the worse of the two. In Hyderabad, plan for roughly 8 to 11 am and 5 to 9 pm on weekdays, with the IT corridor busy late into the evening; TomTom measured an average of about 39 minutes for 10 km in Hyderabad's evening rush in 2025. Bengaluru's peaks are similar in timing, and its higher congestion score suggests they are slower on its worst corridors.

Rain makes both cities much worse, as low junctions and underpasses flood. In Hyderabad, Cyberabad traffic police have repeatedly asked IT companies to stagger log-out times on heavy rain days. See our guides to Hyderabad traffic hotspots and peak hours (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/hyderabad-traffic-hotspots-peak-hours.html) and the best time to drive in Hyderabad (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/best-time-to-drive-in-hyderabad.html).

## Is the driving culture different?

Less than people expect. Both cities have dense, mixed traffic, two-wheelers passing on both sides, autos and buses stopping without warning, and loose lane discipline at busy junctions. A few differences stand out to people who move:

- **U-turns.** Hyderabad uses median U-turn openings in place of right turns very widely, so you will often go past your turning and come back.

- **One-ways.** Central Bengaluru has an extensive network of one-way streets; central Hyderabad has some, especially in the Old City, but fewer.

- **Speed on open roads.** Hyderabad's wider western roads and the ORR allow higher speeds, which makes lane discipline and speed limits matter more.

- **Enforcement.** Both cities rely heavily on cameras and e-challans. In Hyderabad, check fines on the Telangana e-challan portal and follow advisories from Hyderabad Traffic Police (https://www.htp.gov.in).

## How do parking and two-wheelers compare?

Both cities are dominated by two-wheelers and short of parking in their busiest districts.

- **Two-wheelers.** In Bengaluru, two-wheelers made up roughly 70% of more than 1.2 crore registered vehicles in March 2026. Hyderabad's fleet is smaller, at nearly 89 lakh vehicles within Greater Hyderabad in early 2026, and is likewise mostly two-wheelers.

- **Parking.** Parking is hard in both cities' old centres and IT districts. In Hyderabad, a state rule limits mall parking fees, with the first 30 minutes free; see our Hyderabad parking guide (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/hyderabad-parking-guide.html).

### Moving with your car

Your driving licence is valid anywhere in India, though you can update the address on it. A car registered in Karnataka needs re-registration in Telangana if you keep it there for more than 12 months, unless it carries a BH series plate. Our guide to TG number plates explains the codes, and the Telangana Transport Department (https://transport.telangana.gov.in) has the current process.

## Getting to know Hyderabad roads in Sawari

If you are moving from Bengaluru, Sawari can help you learn Hyderabad's road layout before you arrive. It is a free browser driving simulator on five real Hyderabad routes, including Cyber Towers to Jubilee Hills over the Durgam Cheruvu cable bridge, Tank Bund, Necklace Road, the Charminar area and Banjara Hills Road No. 1. You meet medians with U-turn openings, flyovers and metro viaducts, and the debrief lists every fault. It runs on phones held sideways with an on-screen steering wheel, tablets, laptops and PCs. Try the HITEC City route (https://sawari.airacode.online/routes.html#hitec-city) first.

Sawari is for practice only. It does not replace lessons with a licensed instructor or real driving experience. On the road, follow the signs, signals and instructions from the traffic police.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is Hyderabad traffic better than Bengaluru?**
On city-wide measures, yes. In the TomTom Traffic Index for 2025, Bengaluru was ranked the second most congested city in the world with an average congestion level of 74.4%, while Hyderabad was 47th at about 55.5%. Individual roads in both cities can be just as slow at peak hours.

**Which city has the bigger metro, Hyderabad or Bengaluru?**
As of November 2026 Bengaluru's Namma Metro is larger, at just over 100 km after the Pink Line opened in November 2026. Hyderabad Metro has three lines covering about 69 km.

**Is Hyderabad's ORR the same as Bengaluru's Outer Ring Road?**
No. Hyderabad's ORR is a 158 km, eight-lane, access-controlled toll expressway right round the city. Bengaluru's Outer Ring Road is an arterial city road with junctions and signals, best known for the tech parks along it.

**Do I need to re-register my car when moving from Bengaluru to Hyderabad?**
Your driving licence stays valid anywhere in India. A car registered in Karnataka needs a Telangana registration if you keep it in Telangana for more than 12 months, unless it has a BH series plate. Check the current process with the Telangana RTA.

# Self-drive car rental in Hyderabad: how it works, from documents to returning the car

URL: https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/self-drive-car-rental-hyderabad.html
Category: Hyderabad roads · Published 2026-11-23 · Updated 2026-11-23

Self-drive car rental in Hyderabad works much as it does elsewhere: you book a car through an app or agency, show your licence and ID, pay the rent and usually a refundable deposit, and return the car with the agreed fuel, paying any tolls, fines and damage afterwards. The details that cost people money are the fuel policy, the damage terms and the check-out inspection, so read those closely.

This guide explains the process in general terms as of November 2026. It does not compare prices or recommend any company. Rental firms in Hyderabad range from app-based services, including marketplaces such as Zoomcar where individual hosts list their cars, to local agencies and fleet operators. Their terms differ, so treat this as a checklist rather than a rulebook.

## How does self-drive rental work in Hyderabad?

You book a car for a set period, collect it from a hub or have it delivered, drive it yourself and hand it back. The rent may be charged by the hour or the day, with or without a kilometre limit, and with or without fuel included.

### Key facts

| Item | What usually happens |
|---|---|
| Documents | Driving licence plus photo ID, verified online or at pick-up |
| Age | A minimum age set by the firm, commonly 21 or more |
| Deposit | Refundable, taken up front or offered as a no-deposit option at a higher price |
| Fuel | Either return as you got it, or fuel included in a per-kilometre price |
| Tolls | Paid by the car's FASTag, billed to you afterwards |
| Traffic fines | Passed on to you, sometimes deducted from the deposit |
| Damage | You pay up to a set limit or a damage fee, depending on the cover you choose |

Legitimate self-drive rental cars are registered as commercial vehicles, which in India usually means a black number plate with yellow characters. A private white-plate car offered for self-drive hire is a warning sign worth asking about.

## What documents do you need?

Every firm asks for a valid driving licence that covers cars, and most also want a government photo ID such as Aadhaar or a passport. Some ask for address proof or a selfie and document upload in the app before the booking is confirmed.

- **Your licence must be valid on every day of the booking.** An expired licence can void the insurance even if the firm did not notice.

- **Visitors from abroad** are typically asked for their home licence, an International Driving Permit and a passport. Some firms rent only to Indian licence holders. See our guide to driving in Hyderabad for NRIs and visitors (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/driving-in-hyderabad-for-nris-and-visitors.html).

- **Only the named driver may drive.** If someone else will share the driving, add them to the booking; an unlisted driver usually means no cover.

## How do deposits, fuel and kilometre limits work?

These three set the real cost of a rental, so understand them before you pay.

### Deposits

A refundable deposit is common, held on a card or paid by UPI or bank transfer. Firms deduct fuel shortfalls, tolls, challans, late fees and damage before returning it. Ask how many days the refund takes, and keep the receipt.

### Fuel policy

- **Same to same.** You return the car with the fuel level you received. Photograph the gauge at pick-up and refuel near the drop point.

- **Fuel included.** The price includes fuel for a set distance, and you pay per extra kilometre. Do not refuel at your own cost unless the firm tells you to.

- **Electric cars.** The battery level works like fuel. Check the charge at pick-up and know where you will charge. Our guide to electric cars in Hyderabad (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/electric-cars-in-hyderabad.html) covers charging.

### Kilometre limits

Some plans include unlimited kilometres; others cap the distance and charge for extra. A weekend trip out of the city on a capped plan can cost much more than you expect, so check before planning a long drive.

## What should you check before driving away?

Inspect the car properly, with the rental staff or host if possible, and record it. Most disputes come down to whether a scratch was there before you.

- **Walk round with your phone recording.** Film every panel, bumper, wheel and the windscreen in daylight, with the number plate in shot. Point out existing damage and make sure it is noted in the app or the form.

- **Check the tyres and the spare.** Look for bald patches and cuts, and confirm there is a spare, a jack and a wheel spanner.

- **Check the papers.** The registration certificate, insurance and a valid pollution certificate (PUC) should be in the car or available digitally.

- **Test the basics.** Lights, indicators, horn, wipers, brakes, air conditioning and the handbrake.

- **Note the fuel and odometer** on camera.

- **Check the FASTag.** Make sure a tag is fixed to the windscreen and ask whether it is active.

- **Save the helpline number** and ask what to do in a breakdown or accident.

If you are not used to the model, spend five minutes in the car park finding the gears, lights, wipers and hazard switch before you join traffic. If it is an automatic and you normally drive a manual, our guide to driving an automatic car (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/how-to-drive-automatic-car-india.html) helps.

## Who pays for tolls, fines and damage?

You do: tolls and fines follow the car, the rental firm passes them to you after the trip, and most firms make you liable for damage up to a set amount.

### FASTag, tolls and challans

- **FASTag.** FASTag is the normal way to pay tolls on national highways and the Outer Ring Road (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/hyderabad-outer-ring-road-guide.html). On a rental, tolls are paid from the car's tag and then billed to you. If the tag is not working, the toll plaza may charge more than the normal rate for paying another way.

- **E-challans.** Hyderabad issues many traffic fines from cameras, linked to the number plate. They can arrive weeks after you return the car, and the firm will charge them to the driver who had the car at that time. You can look up a vehicle's pending challans on the Telangana e-challan portal (https://echallan.tspolice.gov.in).

- **Parking.** Parking charges and towing fees during your rental are yours to pay.

### What happens if the car is damaged?

All rental cars carry the insurance the law requires, but that does not mean you pay nothing after damage. Some firms sell extra protection that lowers the amount you are liable for.

- **Read the exclusions.** Tyres, glass, the underbody, interior damage, driving on unpaved roads and driving under the influence are often excluded from the cover.

- **After an accident**, stop safely, make sure no one is hurt, call the firm's helpline and photograph the scene. For serious incidents, the insurer will usually need a police report.

- **Do not arrange your own repairs** or towing without the firm's approval, or you may end up paying for them.

## How do you return the car?

Return it on time, with the agreed fuel or charge, at the agreed place, and record it again.

- **Allow for traffic.** Late returns are usually charged by the hour. In the evening peak, the IT corridor and the central roads can add an hour to a short trip; see our guide to Hyderabad traffic hotspots and peak hours (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/hyderabad-traffic-hotspots-peak-hours.html).

- **Film the car again** at drop-off, including the fuel gauge and odometer.

- **Remove your belongings** and any FASTag or parking receipts you need.

- **Check the final bill** and the deposit refund. Query any deduction you do not understand with the photos and video you took.

## Get used to Hyderabad roads before you rent

If the city is new to you, or you have not driven for a while, the first hour in an unfamiliar rental car in Hyderabad traffic is the hardest. Sawari is a free browser driving simulator on five real Hyderabad routes, including Tank Bund, Necklace Road, the Charminar area, Cyber Towers to Jubilee Hills over the Durgam Cheruvu cable bridge, and Banjara Hills Road No. 1. It runs on a phone held sideways with an on-screen steering wheel, or on a tablet, laptop or PC, and lists your faults at the end of each drive. It will not teach you a particular car, but it can make the roads feel familiar before you set off.

Sawari is for practice only. It does not replace lessons with a licensed instructor or real driving experience. On the road, follow the signs, signals and instructions from the traffic police.

## Frequently asked questions

**What documents do I need for a self-drive car in Hyderabad?**
Usually a valid driving licence, a government photo ID such as Aadhaar or a passport, and sometimes address proof. Foreign licence holders are typically asked for an International Driving Permit and a passport. Each rental firm sets its own list, so check before you book.

**Is a security deposit required for self-drive cars?**
Many rental firms take a refundable deposit, while some offer bookings without one, often at a higher price or with conditions. Deposits are usually returned after the trip, minus any fuel, toll, challan or damage charges.

**Who pays tolls and traffic fines on a rental car?**
You do. Tolls are normally paid from the car's FASTag and charged to you afterwards, and e-challans issued during your booking are passed on to you, sometimes weeks later.

**Can I take a Hyderabad rental car to another state?**
Many firms allow outstation trips, but some charge extra, cap the distance or restrict certain states. Ask before you leave, because driving outside the allowed area can void the cover.

# The best time to drive in Hyderabad: by hour, day, area and season

URL: https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/best-time-to-drive-in-hyderabad.html
Category: Hyderabad roads · Published 2026-11-23 · Updated 2026-11-23

The best time to drive in Hyderabad is early morning, before about 8 am, and weekend mornings are the calmest of all; the worst times are weekday peaks, roughly 8.30 to 11 am and 5 to 9 pm, plus heavy rain and big festival days. The right answer also depends on where you are going, so this guide breaks it down by time, day, area and season.

Timings here come from Hyderabad and Cyberabad traffic police advisories and local news reports, as of November 2026. Traffic changes with road works and events, so always check a live traffic app and the latest Hyderabad Traffic Police (https://www.htp.gov.in) advisories before a long or important trip.

## What is the best time of day to drive?

Early morning is best, mid-afternoon is a reasonable second choice, and the two rush hours are the times to avoid.

| Time (weekdays) | What to expect |
|---|---|
| Before 8 am | Usually the lightest traffic of the day. Good for learners and long cross-city trips. |
| 8.30 to 11 am | Morning peak. Police advisories in 2026 ask commuters to avoid this window on affected roads. |
| 11 am to 4.30 pm | Steadier, though markets, schools and construction zones stay busy. |
| 5 to 9 pm | Evening peak, usually the worst of the day. Lakeside roads also fill with visitors. |
| After 9 pm | Lighter in most areas, but the IT corridor can stay busy until late, and night brings glare and faster drivers. |

The 8.30 to 11 am and 5 to 9 pm windows appear in Hyderabad Traffic Police advisories issued in 2026 for the Jubilee Hills and Banjara Hills flyover works, most recently in November 2026. Treat them as a sound guide for the city's busy corridors in general. If you drive at night, read our night driving tips (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/night-driving-hyderabad-tips.html) first.

## Which days are easiest?

Sunday morning is usually the easiest time of the whole week, and Saturday morning is close behind. Many offices are closed at weekends, so the commuter peaks largely disappear.

- **Weekend mornings** are the calmest, ideal for practice.

- **Weekend evenings** are busy around malls, Hussain Sagar, Necklace Road, temples and restaurant areas.

- **Monday mornings and Friday evenings** are often heavier than midweek, as people travel in and out of the city.

- **Days before long weekends and festivals** bring heavy traffic on roads out of the city and towards bus and railway stations.

## When should you drive in each area?

Each part of the city has its own rhythm, so plan by destination, not only by the clock.

### IT corridor: HITEC City, Madhapur and Gachibowli

Go early in the morning or in the middle of the day. Office start and finish times vary, so the evening rush here is long and can run late into the night. Cyberabad traffic police have repeatedly asked companies to stagger log-out times, especially on heavy rain days. Our guide to Hyderabad traffic hotspots and peak hours (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/hyderabad-traffic-hotspots-peak-hours.html) names the usual bottlenecks.

### Old City around the Charminar

Go early in the morning, before the shops open. Late mornings, evenings, weekends and festival days are much busier, with dense crowds on foot. During Ramzan the area stays busy late into the night: in 2026 the state government allowed shops to stay open until 5 am during the month. See our Charminar and Old City driving guide (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/charminar-old-city-driving-guide.html).

### Secunderabad

Avoid the peaks around Paradise Circle and the railway station, which jam badly on wet days. Elevated corridor works between Bowenpally and Paradise have caused long delays, so check diversions before you set off.

### To the airport

Plan backwards from your flight. The airport recommends arriving 120 minutes before a domestic flight and 180 minutes before an international one, so add your driving time and a generous margin if your trip crosses a rush hour. Late-night and very early trips on the PVNR Expressway or the Outer Ring Road are usually quick. Our guide to driving to Hyderabad airport (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/driving-to-hyderabad-airport.html) covers routes and drop-off rules.

## How do seasons and festivals change things?

Weather and festivals can make a normally easy drive slow, so check the calendar as well as the clock.

### Monsoon

The south-west monsoon usually brings rain from about June to September, and heavy showers can continue into October. A downpour floods low junctions and underpasses and can double journey times. If heavy rain is forecast, travel before it starts or wait until the water clears. Our monsoon driving guide (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/monsoon-driving-hyderabad.html) has the details.

### Summer heat

From about March to May, afternoons are very hot. Driving in the early morning or after sunset is more comfortable for you and easier on the car, and it is worth keeping water in the car and the tyres properly inflated.

### Festival periods

- **Ganesh festival and immersion.** Immersion processions head to Hussain Sagar, and Tank Bund, Necklace Road, NTR Marg and nearby roads are closed or restricted, sometimes for more than a day. In 2026 the main immersions fell in late September.

- **Bonalu.** During Ashada month, roughly July and August, police set diversions around the big temple celebrations at Golconda, Ujjaini Mahankali in Secunderabad and Lal Darwaza in the Old City.

- **Ramzan.** Evenings and nights around the Charminar and the Old City markets are very crowded, with extra restrictions for Friday prayers and Eid.

- **New Year's Eve.** On the night of 31 December 2025 police closed most flyovers except Begumpet and Tolichowki, and closed Tank Bund and Necklace Road to vehicles from 11 pm to 2 am. In past years the Outer Ring Road has also been closed to cars overnight. Expect drink-driving checks everywhere.

- **Sankranti and other long holidays.** Roads out of the city and towards bus and railway stations are very busy just before the holiday.

Before any festival day, check the advisories from Hyderabad Traffic Police, Cyberabad Police (https://www.cyberabadpolice.gov.in) and Rachakonda Police. They usually list closed roads, diversions and parking places a day or two in advance. The Hyderabad traffic helpline quoted in 2026 advisories is 9010203626.

## What is the best time for learners?

Early on a weekend morning, in dry weather and daylight, on a route you already know. That combination gives you light traffic, good visibility and nothing new to process except the driving itself.

- Start with weekend mornings on wide, steady roads such as Tank Bund Road or Necklace Road.

- Move to weekday mid-mornings or early afternoons once you are steady.

- Try the edge of a rush hour on a familiar route.

- Leave full peak hours, night driving, heavy rain and festival days until last.

Our honest guide to whether driving in Hyderabad is hard (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/is-driving-in-hyderabad-hard.html) sets out a fuller plan.

## Practising at any hour with Sawari

Sawari is a free browser driving simulator on five real Hyderabad routes, from Tank Bund Road and Necklace Road to the Charminar and Pathergatti. You can pick the time of day and how heavy the traffic is, so you can rehearse a busy route in dense traffic before you face it at rush hour. It runs on phones held sideways, tablets, laptops and PCs, and the debrief lists every fault at the end.

It has no rain and cannot predict a real jam, and it is practice only, not a substitute for lessons. Try Cyber Towers to Jubilee Hills (https://sawari.airacode.online/play.html?route=hitec-city) in dense traffic to get a feel for the IT corridor.

## Frequently asked questions

**What is the best time to drive in Hyderabad?**
Early morning, before about 8 am, is usually the easiest time, and weekend mornings are the calmest of all. Mid-afternoon on weekdays is often lighter than the morning and evening peaks.

**What are the peak traffic hours in Hyderabad?**
As of November 2026, Hyderabad Traffic Police advisories ask commuters to avoid 8.30 to 11 am and 5 to 9 pm on affected roads. On the IT corridor, evening traffic often stays heavy until late at night.

**Are Hyderabad roads closed on New Year's Eve?**
Usually some are. On the night of 31 December 2025 police closed most city flyovers except Begumpet and Tolichowki, and closed Tank Bund and Necklace Road to vehicles from 11 pm to 2 am. Check the advisory each year, because the list changes.

**When is the best time for a learner to practise driving in Hyderabad?**
Early on a weekend morning, in dry weather and daylight, on a wide road you already know. Avoid rush hours, heavy rain and festival days until you are more confident.

# A history of Hyderabad's roads: from the Charminar to the Outer Ring Road

URL: https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/history-of-hyderabad-roads.html
Category: Hyderabad roads · Published 2026-11-18 · Updated 2026-11-18

The history of Hyderabad's roads is a story of a city that kept adding new layers rather than replacing old ones. The narrow streets round the Charminar date from the 1590s; the road along Tank Bund sits on a sixteenth-century dam; Banjara Hills and Jubilee Hills were laid out on rock in the twentieth century; and HITEC City, the Outer Ring Road and the metro have pushed the city far to the west and beyond.

Knowing where each layer came from explains a lot about how the roads drive today: why the Old City is a maze of one-way lanes, why Tank Bund is so straight, and why your address in Jubilee Hills is a number.

## The Qutb Shahi city around the Charminar

Before Hyderabad there was Golconda, the fortified capital of the Qutb Shahi kings on its granite hill to the west. By the late sixteenth century the fort was crowded, and in **1591** Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah founded a new city on the south bank of the river Musi. The **Charminar**, built that year, stands at its centre.

The new city was planned around the monument, with main streets running out from it towards the points of the compass and markets along them. That is why so many Old City roads still meet at the Charminar, and why the streets around it feel like spokes of a wheel. Over four centuries the gaps filled in with houses, shops and lanes that were never meant for motor traffic. Today many are one-way, and the circle round the monument works like a crowded roundabout.

Our Charminar Old City driving guide (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/charminar-old-city-driving-guide.html) covers what those streets are like to drive now.

## Hussain Sagar and Tank Bund

Even before the city itself, the Qutb Shahis were shaping its geography. **Hussain Sagar** was created in the 1560s (most sources say 1562) during the reign of Ibrahim Quli Qutb Shah, by damming a tributary of the Musi. It is named after Hussain Shah Wali, who oversaw the work. For centuries the lake supplied drinking water to the city.

The embankment on its eastern side, the **Tank Bund**, became a natural road: a dry, level line across low ground between what grew into Hyderabad to the south and Secunderabad to the north. It was widened in 1946, and in the 1980s a row of statues of figures from Telugu history and culture was added along it. Necklace Road, which curves round the western and northern shores, came much later.

That history is why Tank Bund Road is so straight and so exposed to the lake. See our Tank Bund Road driving guide (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/tank-bund-road-driving-guide.html) for how it drives today.

## The Nizams, Secunderabad and a planned city

### Asaf Jahi rule and the cantonment

After the Mughal conquest of Golconda in 1687, Hyderabad passed in the eighteenth century to the Asaf Jahi dynasty, the Nizams. British influence grew, and in the early nineteenth century a large British military cantonment was set up on the land north of Hussain Sagar. It was named **Secunderabad** after Sikandar Jah, the third Nizam; most accounts date it to 1806.

Secunderabad grew as a separate town with its own grid of parade grounds, barracks, bazaars and, later, the railway. That is the origin of the "twin cities", and of the way traffic still funnels between them across a few links, Tank Bund among them.

### After the 1908 flood

On 28 September 1908 the Musi flooded catastrophically, killing thousands and destroying large parts of the city along its banks. The disaster changed how Hyderabad was planned. In **1912**, under the seventh Nizam, Mir Osman Ali Khan, a City Improvement Board was set up to rebuild and plan the city. Engineer M. Visvesvaraya advised on flood protection, which led to the Osman Sagar and Himayat Sagar reservoirs upstream.

The years that followed brought many of the grand public buildings beside the Musi, wider roads, and new planned neighbourhoods beyond the old walls. The city began to spread north and west, towards the rocky hills that would become Banjara Hills.

## The numbered roads of Banjara Hills and Jubilee Hills

West of Hussain Sagar the land rises into granite hills and boulders. As the city grew in the twentieth century, these hills were laid out as residential areas with wide plots, winding roads following the contours, and a plain naming scheme: the roads were simply numbered.

**Banjara Hills** came first. **Jubilee Hills**, further west, was developed largely from the 1960s through a cooperative housing society. In both, the numbers stuck. People still give directions as "Road No. 1", "Road No. 36" or "Road No. 45", and the roads still twist and climb the way the rock dictated. Banjara Hills Road No. 1 climbs steadily from Masab Tank, a legacy of the terrain rather than any plan.

Read more in our Banjara Hills Road No. 1 driving guide (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/banjara-hills-road-no-1-driving-guide.html).

## HITEC City, flyovers, the ORR and the metro

### Cyberabad

Hyderabad became the capital of Andhra Pradesh in 1956, and of Telangana in 2014. Its biggest change of direction came at the end of the 1990s. **Cyber Towers**, the first landmark building of HITEC City in Madhapur, was inaugurated on **22 November 1998**. The IT district that grew around it, often called Cyberabad, spread through Madhapur, Gachibowli, Kondapur and the Financial District.

The roads there are a different generation: wide, divided corridors built for office traffic, with big junctions and, more recently, the cable-stayed bridge over Durgam Cheruvu. Our HITEC City to Jubilee Hills drive (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/hitec-city-to-jubilee-hills-drive.html) follows one of these corridors from Cyber Towers back into the numbered roads of Jubilee Hills.

### Flyovers and the elevated expressway

As traffic grew, the city went up. Flyovers were built over the busiest junctions, and on **19 October 2009** the **P. V. Narasimha Rao Expressway**, an elevated road of about 11.6 km from Mehdipatnam to Aramghar, opened to traffic towards the new airport at Shamshabad. Many more flyovers and underpasses have followed. Our guide to driving on flyovers in Hyderabad (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/driving-on-flyovers-hyderabad.html) covers what they demand of a driver.

### The Outer Ring Road

The **Outer Ring Road**, an access-controlled expressway of about 158 km, loops right round the city. It was built in stages from the late 2000s and completed as a full ring by the end of the 2010s. It lets traffic between the highways bypass the centre and has drawn new development, from Gachibowli to Shamshabad, along its length.

### Hyderabad Metro

The first stretch of **Hyderabad Metro**, about 30 km from Miyapur to Nagole, was inaugurated on **28 November 2017**. Much of it runs on viaducts above the middle of main roads, which changed the look of many streets and left pillars in the median that drivers now steer round every day.

## Where Hyderabad's roads are heading

The pattern of adding layers continues. Further metro extensions have been planned, more flyovers and underpasses are being built at congested junctions, and a **Regional Ring Road** much further out has been proposed to take long-distance traffic round the wider region. Timelines for projects like these change, so treat any date you read as a plan rather than a promise.

What is unlikely to change is the city's character: a four-hundred-year-old core, a lakeside link between the twin cities, numbered hill roads and fast new corridors, all within a short drive of each other.

## Driving the layers in Sawari

Sawari's five routes happen to cut through most of these layers. The streets are rebuilt from OpenStreetMap (https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright) data, with real road layouts, one-way directions and flyovers:

- **Charminar and Pathergatti**: the 1591 city and its one-way lanes.

- **Tank Bund Road**: the road on the Qutb Shahi dam.

- **Necklace Road**: the later lakeside road round Hussain Sagar.

- **Banjara Hills Road No. 1**: the numbered hill roads.

- **Cyber Towers to Jubilee Hills**: the HITEC City era.

Shop fronts, stalls and many other details are estimated rather than copied, so treat it as realistic rather than exact. You can browse the route list (https://sawari.airacode.online/routes.html) or start a drive (https://sawari.airacode.online/play.html) free on a phone, tablet, laptop or desktop.

## Frequently asked questions

**How old is Hyderabad?**
Hyderabad was founded in 1591 by Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah, the fifth Qutb Shahi ruler, who moved his capital out from Golconda. The Charminar, built the same year, marks the centre of the new city.

**Why is it called Tank Bund?**
Tank Bund is the embankment, or bund, that holds back Hussain Sagar, the lake (tank) built in the 1560s under Ibrahim Quli Qutb Shah. The road along its top became the main link between Hyderabad and Secunderabad.

**Why are Banjara Hills and Jubilee Hills roads numbered?**
Both areas were laid out as planned residential layouts on rocky hills, and the roads were simply given numbers rather than names. The numbers stuck, so addresses there still read Road No. 1, Road No. 36 and so on.

**When did Hyderabad Metro open?**
The first stretch, about 30 km from Miyapur to Nagole, was inaugurated on 28 November 2017 and opened to the public the next day. More sections followed in later years.
