# Driving to Hyderabad airport: routes, timing, drop-off and parking at Shamshabad

URL: https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/driving-to-hyderabad-airport.html
Category: Hyderabad roads · Published 2026-11-18 · Updated 2026-11-18

Driving to Hyderabad airport, Rajiv Gandhi International Airport at Shamshabad, is straightforward once you know the three main ways in: the PV Narasimha Rao Expressway from Mehdipatnam, the Outer Ring Road from almost anywhere on the edge of the city, and NH 44 from the south of the old city. The harder parts are judging the time, and knowing the rules for the few minutes you spend at the terminal.

This guide covers the routes, how much time to allow, how drop-off, pick-up and parking work, and what changes when your flight leaves in the middle of the night.

## The main ways to drive to Hyderabad airport

The airport sits well south of the city, roughly 20 to 25 km from the centre depending on where you count from. Almost every drive ends on the airport approach road, which has its own speed limit and cameras. Which way you get there depends on where you start.

### PV Narasimha Rao Expressway

The PVNR Expressway is the elevated road that starts near the Sarojini Devi Eye Hospital at Mehdipatnam and runs for about 11.6 km to Aramghar, where it comes down to meet NH 44 heading south towards the airport. For anyone in Banjara Hills, Jubilee Hills, Masab Tank, Tolichowki or the central city, it is the usual route, because it lifts you over the busy road and junctions below it.

It is a long, raised road with no shops, no pedestrians and few places to stop. Keep left unless you are overtaking, hold a steady speed, and know which down ramp you need before you reach it. Ramps have been added and changed over the years, so follow the overhead signs rather than memory. Our guide to driving on flyovers in Hyderabad (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/driving-on-flyovers-hyderabad.html) covers joining, leaving and lane choice on raised roads.

### Outer Ring Road

The Outer Ring Road is the 158 km, eight-lane expressway round the city, and it has its own exit for Shamshabad and the airport. From Gachibowli, the Financial District, Kokapet, Patancheru, Medchal, Shamirpet or LB Nagar, joining the ORR and following it round is often simpler than crossing town, even when it is a longer distance on paper. It is tolled, so make sure your FASTag is working.

During heavy rain, Cyberabad traffic police have in the past advised airport traffic to take the ORR rather than parts of the older approach roads where water was flowing over the carriageway. Our Outer Ring Road guide (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/hyderabad-outer-ring-road-guide.html) explains exits, lane use and tolls.

### NH 44 through Aramghar and Shamshabad

NH 44, the old Bengaluru highway, runs south through Aramghar and past Shamshabad town towards the airport turn. If you start in the old city, Bahadurpura or anywhere south of the Musi, you may join it directly. It is a busy national highway with trucks, buses and local traffic, so it is slower than the expressway, but it is the road the expressway itself feeds into.

### The airport approach road

Whichever way you come, the final stretch is the airport approach road. Since February 2024 the airport has enforced a limit of 80 km/h along its whole length, with automatic speed enforcement and fines through the traffic police. It is tempting to speed up on a wide, empty road when you are late. Do not; the cameras are there for exactly that.

## How much time to allow

Work backwards from the airport's own advice. The airport recommends that you arrive 120 minutes before a domestic departure and 180 minutes before an international one, or whatever your airline tells you. International passengers with valid tickets can enter the terminal only three hours before departure, so there is little point arriving much earlier than that.

Then add:

- **Your driving time at that hour.** Check a live traffic app at the time you plan to leave, not the evening before. A drive that takes under an hour late at night can take much longer during the weekday evening peak.

- **A margin for the unexpected.** Rain, a breakdown on the expressway or a VIP movement can hold traffic for a long time. If you are flying out on a weekday evening or in heavy rain, be generous.

- **Time to park and walk.** If you are leaving the car at the airport, allow time to find a space and walk to departures with your bags.

Before festivals and long weekends, the airport sometimes issues its own advisory asking passengers to come earlier than usual. Look at the official Hyderabad airport website (https://www.hyderabad.aero) or its social media pages in the days before you fly.

## Drop-off, pick-up and the eight-minute rule

Hyderabad airport has a single terminal building for domestic and international flights. Departures and arrivals are on separate levels, each with its own ramp for vehicles.

### Dropping someone off

The departures ramp is for dropping passengers, not for waiting. At the time of writing (November 2026), the airport's parking page gives the first eight minutes on the ramp free, with charges after that and vehicles towed if they stay beyond fifteen minutes. The airport also says plainly that vehicles may pull up kerbside only to pick up or drop off passengers, and unattended vehicles at the kerb will be towed and fined.

Eight minutes is enough if you are organised. Have the bags ready to come out, say your goodbyes in the car before you arrive, and pull away as soon as the boot is shut. Two-wheelers and autos are not allowed on the ramps.

### Picking someone up

Do not circle the departures level or wait on the arrivals ramp for a flight that has only just landed. A passenger still at baggage reclaim can take a long time to come out. The calmer way is to wait in the car park, ask your passenger to call when they have their bags, then drive round to the arrivals ramp and collect them within the free window.

If you want to meet them inside, the airport has a paid Airport Village area outside the arrivals hall for people meeting passengers.

The ramps take payment by FASTag. A working FASTag on your car makes the barriers quicker, both at the ramps and at the car park.

## Parking at the airport

If you are leaving the car while you travel, or you need longer than a few minutes, use the airport car park rather than the ramps. The airport runs a car park with an automated entry and exit system, dedicated FASTag lanes and a valet option. Charges go up with the time you stay and are listed on the airport's parking page; rates change, so check them there before a long trip rather than relying on old figures.

Keep your parking ticket safe. The airport charges a separate fee for a lost ticket on top of normal parking. Take a photo of your bay number before you walk off, so you are not hunting for the car when you come back tired from a flight.

## Night flights and early departures

Many flights from Hyderabad leave late at night or before dawn, and that changes the drive.

- **The roads are faster, and so is everyone else.** An empty expressway at 2 am invites speed. Stick to the limits, especially on the airport approach road, where the cameras work at night too.

- **Watch for tiredness.** If you have been up all day before a late flight, or you are driving home after dropping someone at 4 am, tiredness is the real risk. Open a window, keep the music low and stop somewhere safe if your eyes start to close. Our night driving tips (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/night-driving-hyderabad-tips.html) go into this.

- **Expect trucks.** NH 44 and the ORR carry heavy goods vehicles through the night. Give them room and do not sit beside them for long.

- **Check for special closures.** On some nights, such as New Year's Eve, police have closed the ORR and the PVNR Expressway to cars late at night while still letting airport traffic through. Check Hyderabad and Cyberabad traffic police advisories if you fly on a festival night.

In the monsoon, low spots on some approach roads can flood quickly. See monsoon driving in Hyderabad (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/monsoon-driving-hyderabad.html) for what to do on a waterlogged road.

## Getting ready with Sawari

Sawari, our free browser driving simulator, does not have the airport, the expressway or the ORR. Its five routes are city streets, and it has no highways and no rain. What it can help with is the city part of the trip: the junctions, two-wheelers and lane changes you meet before you reach the fast roads.

If you start from the Masab Tank side, the Banjara Hills Road No. 1 route (https://sawari.airacode.online/routes.html#banjara-hills) is close to where many airport drives begin, with busy junctions and plenty of traffic. The Cyber Towers to Jubilee Hills route (https://sawari.airacode.online/play.html?route=hitec-city) covers the IT corridor roads many people drive before they turn towards the ORR. Use them to practise steady lane discipline and signalling, and use the night lighting to get used to reading the road in the dark. Then drive the real route with a calm passenger at a quiet time before you have a flight to catch.

Sawari is for practice only. It does not replace lessons with a licensed instructor. On the real road, follow the signs, the speed limits and any instructions from the traffic police and airport staff.

## Frequently asked questions

**How long is the free drop-off time at Hyderabad airport?**
At the time of writing, the airport's own parking page gives the first eight minutes on the terminal ramp free for quick pick-up and drop-off. After that charges apply, and vehicles left beyond fifteen minutes are towed. Check the airport website before you travel, because the rules can change.

**Which is the fastest way to drive to Hyderabad airport?**
From the central and western city, most drivers use the PV Narasimha Rao Expressway from Mehdipatnam and then the airport road. From the IT corridor and the outer suburbs, the Outer Ring Road is usually simpler. Check a live traffic app before you leave, because the best choice changes with the time of day and the weather.

**How early should I reach Hyderabad airport?**
The airport recommends arriving 120 minutes before a domestic flight and 180 minutes before an international one, or as your airline advises. Add your driving time, a margin for traffic and time to park on top of that.

**Can I wait at the kerb to pick someone up from Hyderabad airport?**
No. Vehicles may pull up kerbside only to pick up or drop off passengers, and unattended vehicles are towed and fined. If your passenger is not out yet, wait in the car park and drive to the ramp once they call.

---

# Electric cars in Hyderabad: road tax, charging and driving an EV in the city

URL: https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/electric-cars-in-hyderabad.html
Category: Hyderabad roads · Published 2026-11-18 · Updated 2026-11-18

Electric cars in Hyderabad make a strong case for city driving: short daily distances, slow traffic where an EV wastes little energy, and, at the time of writing, no road tax or registration fee in Telangana. The catch is planning: knowing when the tax waiver ends, where you will charge, and how heat and air conditioning affect your range.

This guide covers the rules and money first, then charging at home and in public, then what an EV is actually like to drive on Hyderabad's roads.

## EV road tax in Telangana: the waiver and its end date

Telangana brought out its Electric Vehicle and Energy Storage Policy in 2020. In November 2024 the state government issued a government order (widely reported as GO 41) giving a **100 per cent exemption from road tax and registration fee** for electric vehicles bought and registered in Telangana. It covers private electric cars as well as two-wheelers, autos, taxis, goods vehicles and buses.

The exemption is valid **until 31 December 2026**. At the time of writing (November 2026), no extension had been notified. That matters a great deal if you are buying in the next few weeks: road tax on a petrol or diesel car in Telangana is a significant share of the on-road price, and the saving only applies if the car is registered while the order is in force.

If you are buying close to the deadline, ask the dealer exactly when the car will be registered, not just invoiced, and confirm the current position with the Telangana Transport Department (https://www.transport.telangana.gov.in). Policies like this can be extended, changed or allowed to lapse.

### Green number plates

Battery electric vehicles in India carry green registration plates. Under a 2018 notification from the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, a private EV has white characters on green and a commercial EV has yellow characters on green. Hybrids are not battery electric vehicles and keep ordinary plates. Our guide to Telangana TG number plates (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/telangana-tg-number-plates-explained.html) explains the rest of the plate.

## Public charging for electric cars in Hyderabad

Public chargers come in two broad kinds, and it helps to know which your car accepts.

- **AC chargers.** These feed the car's own on-board charger, so the speed is limited by the car, typically a few kilowatts up to around 11 kW or more on some models. Most new cars sold in India use the Type 2 connector. AC charging suits a stop of a few hours: an office car park, a mall or a hotel.

- **DC fast chargers.** These charge the battery directly and are much quicker. Most current electric cars in India use the CCS2 connector. Expect to add a large share of your range in well under an hour, though charging slows as the battery fills, so stopping at around 80 per cent is usually the quickest way to get going again.

### Where you tend to find them

Chargers in Hyderabad cluster where people already park: malls, hotels, office campuses in HITEC City and the Financial District, some petrol stations, car dealerships and along the Outer Ring Road and highways out of the city. TGREDCO, the state's renewable energy agency, is the nodal agency for public charging and has been tendering new stations with private operators; a recent tender was reported to plan 200 stations in Hyderabad with a uniform tariff of Rs 13 per kWh. Coverage inside the older, denser parts of the city is thinner, partly because suitable land with a power connection is hard to find.

### Apps and payment

Each charging network usually has its own app for finding chargers, starting a session and paying, and there are aggregator apps that list several networks. Before relying on a charger, check in the app that it is working, that it has your connector, and what it costs per unit or per minute. Keep a second option in mind, because a charger shown as free can be occupied or out of order by the time you arrive.

## Home charging, including in apartments

For most owners, home charging does the bulk of the work. A car that covers a typical city day can be topped up overnight on a slow AC charger, which is gentler on the battery and far cheaper than public fast charging.

In an independent house it is fairly simple: an electrician checks your sanctioned load and wiring, and a wall box goes in near where you park. Apartments take more organising.

- **Talk to your residents' association first.** You will need permission to run a cable from your meter, or from a new connection, to your parking bay, and they will want to know who pays for the power.

- **Billing.** The cleanest arrangement is a separate connection or sub-meter for the charger, so your charging is not paid for out of the common-area bill. Ask your power distribution company (TGSPDCL for most of Hyderabad) what it offers for your building.

- **Safety.** Use a proper charger installed by a qualified electrician, with its own circuit and protection. Avoid long extension leads in a basement.

- **New buildings.** Telangana has been reported to be moving towards requiring charging points in new apartment buildings. If you are buying a flat, ask the builder what is provided.

## Range in Hyderabad traffic and heat

City driving is where an electric car does well. In stop-start traffic, a petrol engine burns fuel while idling and wastes energy every time you brake. An EV uses almost nothing while stationary, apart from the air conditioning, and recovers some energy when it slows down. So a slow crawl from Jubilee Hills to HITEC City at peak hour is less of a hit to range than the same time on an open highway.

The bigger factors in Hyderabad are heat and speed:

- **Air conditioning.** In April and May, the AC runs hard all the time. In slow traffic it becomes one of the largest uses of energy. Pre-cool the cabin while the car is still plugged in, and park in shade where you can.

- **Battery temperature.** Batteries prefer moderate temperatures. Modern EVs manage this themselves, but in strong heat the car may use energy to cool the battery and may limit fast-charging speed.

- **Highway speeds.** On the Outer Ring Road or a highway, steady high speed uses much more energy than city driving. If you are planning a longer trip, check where the fast chargers are before you go.

- **Daily charging habits.** Many manufacturers suggest charging to around 80 per cent for daily use and keeping 100 per cent for long trips. Follow your car's manual.

The range figure in the brochure is measured on a standard test cycle. Real-world range in Hyderabad will usually be lower, especially in summer with the AC on, so plan with some margin.

## Driving an EV on Hyderabad roads

### Regenerative braking and one-pedal driving

When you lift off the accelerator, an EV can use its motor to slow the car and put energy back into the battery. Many cars let you choose how strong this is, and some offer a "one-pedal" mode strong enough to bring the car almost to a stop. In Hyderabad traffic this is genuinely useful: you can ease off for a speed breaker, a slowing auto or a red light without touching the brake.

It takes a few days to get used to. Lifting off quickly in a strong regen mode slows the car harder than you may expect, and the driver behind cannot always tell, because brake lights may not come on unless the deceleration is strong enough. Lift off smoothly, keep a good gap, and still use the brake pedal for a proper stop. On a steep, wet descent, a gentler regen setting can feel more predictable.

### Quiet at low speed

An electric car is almost silent at walking pace. That is pleasant for you, but people in the road may not hear you coming. In the Old City lanes, in apartment car parks and near schools, assume that pedestrians, children and people stepping off the kerb have not noticed you. Newer EVs make an artificial sound at low speed for this reason, but it is quiet. Go slowly, cover the brake and give people time. The advice in our guide to sharing the road with autos, buses and two-wheelers (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/sharing-the-road-autos-buses-two-wheelers.html) applies with extra force.

### Instant pull

EVs deliver full pulling power from a standstill. That makes them quick away from a signal, but it can catch you out in a crowded junction or on wet roads. Squeeze the accelerator, do not stab it, especially during the monsoon (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/monsoon-driving-hyderabad.html).

### Waterlogging

Electric cars are sealed and tested against water, but the same rule applies as with any car: do not drive into water when you cannot see how deep it is. Underpasses in heavy rain are the usual trap.

## Practising city skills in Sawari

Sawari's player car behaves like a conventional automatic, not an EV, so it will not teach you one-pedal driving. What it can help with is the part that does not change with the powertrain: reading traffic, keeping a gap, signalling and taking speed breakers smoothly on real Hyderabad roads rebuilt from OpenStreetMap. The HITEC City to Jubilee Hills route (https://sawari.airacode.online/routes.html#hitec-city) is a good one to practise the kind of daily commute where many people in the city drive EVs. It is free in the browser on a phone, tablet, laptop or desktop.

Policies, tariffs and charger locations change often. Check the Telangana Transport Department and your charging operator for the current position before making a decision based on this guide.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is there road tax on electric cars in Telangana?**
Under a Telangana government order issued in November 2024, electric vehicles bought and registered in the state are fully exempt from road tax and registration fee until 31 December 2026. At the time of writing (November 2026) no extension had been notified, so check the Transport Department before you buy.

**How much does public EV charging cost in Hyderabad?**
Prices vary by operator and charger speed, and DC fast charging usually costs more per unit than AC charging. A state tender for new public stations in Hyderabad was reported to set a uniform tariff of Rs 13 per kWh, but always check the price in the operator's app before you plug in.

**Can I install an EV charger in my apartment parking?**
Usually yes, with the agreement of your residents' association, a safe wiring route to your parking bay and enough sanctioned load. Many owners ask the power distribution company about a separate connection or meter so that the charging is billed to them and not to the common area.

**Do electric cars lose range in Hyderabad's summer heat?**
Some. Running the air conditioning hard in slow traffic uses noticeable energy, and very high battery temperatures make the car protect itself. Parking in shade, pre-cooling while still plugged in and not charging to 100 per cent every day all help.

---

# Hyderabad Metro guide for drivers: the three lines, driving under the viaducts and park-and-ride

URL: https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/hyderabad-metro-guide-for-drivers.html
Category: Hyderabad roads · Published 2026-11-18 · Updated 2026-11-18

The Hyderabad Metro has three lines, Red, Blue and Green, running about 69 km on viaducts over the city's busiest roads. If you drive in Hyderabad, you spend a lot of time underneath it, so it helps to know where the Hyderabad metro lines run, how to drive safely below them, and when it makes sense to leave the car and take the train.

## The three Hyderabad metro lines

The first section opened in November 2017, and the three-line network was completed in February 2020. It was built by L&T Metro Rail (Hyderabad) under a concession with the state. In 2026 the Telangana government bought out L&T's stake, and the network is now under the state-owned Hyderabad Metro Rail Limited (HMRL).

| Line | From | To | Length (approx.) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Red Line | Miyapur | LB Nagar | 29 km |
| Blue Line | Nagole | Raidurg | 27 to 29 km |
| Green Line | JBS Parade Ground | MG Bus Station (MGBS) | 11 km |

- **The Red Line** runs north-west to south-east, from Miyapur through Kukatpally, Ameerpet, Lakdikapul, Nampally and Malakpet to LB Nagar.

- **The Blue Line** runs east to west, from Nagole through Uppal, Tarnaka, Secunderabad, Begumpet, Ameerpet, Jubilee Hills and Madhapur to HITEC City and Raidurg.

- **The Green Line** is the short one, from JBS Parade Ground in Secunderabad through Musheerabad to MGBS.

There are three interchanges: **Ameerpet** (Red and Blue), **MGBS** (Red and Green) and **Parade Ground** (Blue and Green).

For a driver, the useful way to think of it is this: if your road has a concrete viaduct running down the middle, you are probably on a metro corridor, and that road will have stations, buses and crowds of pedestrians at regular intervals.

## Driving under the metro viaducts

Most of the network runs on a viaduct above the middle of a main road, with the pillars in the median. That changes how the road below drives.

### Pillars and the median

- **Pillars hide things.** A row of thick pillars blocks your view of the opposite carriageway and of anyone stepping out from the median. Expect pedestrians, two-wheelers and even cattle to appear from between pillars, especially near stations and markets.

- **U-turns are under the viaduct.** Many median openings and U-turns on metro roads sit between pillars. Vehicles waiting to turn may be partly hidden, and they often nose out slowly. Our guide to U-turns in Hyderabad (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/u-turns-in-hyderabad.html) covers how to take one safely.

- **The right-hand lane is narrower than it looks.** Pillar bases and barriers can sit close to the fast lane. Keep a little space on your right and take care at night.

### Stations

Each elevated station spans the road, with stairs, lifts and escalators coming down to the footpaths on both sides. Around every station you can expect:

- Autos, cabs and share autos stopping in the left lane to pick up and drop off.

- Buses pulling in at nearby stops.

- People crossing the road to reach the stairs, often not at a crossing.

- Two-wheelers parked along the kerb and pulling out.

Slow down as you approach a station, cover the brake and watch the left lane carefully. Our post on sharing the road with autos, buses and two-wheelers (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/sharing-the-road-autos-buses-two-wheelers.html) has more on reading their moves.

### Light, rain and junctions

Under the deck the road is in shade by day and can be darker than the rest of the street at night, so pedestrians in dark clothes are harder to see. In heavy rain, water can collect where it runs off the viaduct. At big junctions where the metro crosses, the pillars and station structures can block your view of the signal and of traffic turning across, so approach slowly and look twice.

Never stop under a metro station to drop someone off in a live lane. Pull fully into the kerb where it is allowed, or use a proper pick-up point. Sudden stops near stations cause many rear-end bumps.

## Combining car and metro

For many trips, the fastest option is to drive part of the way and take the metro for the rest, especially into the busiest parts of the city where parking is hard.

### Park-and-ride

Some stations, especially at or near the ends of the lines, have parking areas for cars and two-wheelers. Stations in the city centre often have little or none. Capacity, charges and rules change, and popular car parks fill up early on weekdays, so check before you rely on one. The Hyderabad Metro Rail website (https://www.hmrl.co.in) is the place for current station information.

### When it makes sense

- **Commuting into Ameerpet, Punjagutta, Begumpet or HITEC City at peak hours.** Parking near offices and malls in these areas is scarce, and the roads below the viaduct are often slow.

- **Going to Secunderabad station or MGBS.** Both are on the network, and both are busy places to drive into.

- **Events and festivals.** When roads are closed or diverted, the metro often keeps running.

It makes less sense for trips well away from the lines, or when you are carrying heavy luggage, since many stations involve long stairs and walks.

## Phase 2 and the airport metro

Phase 2 is the plan to extend the network, and its status changes often, so this is the position at the time of writing (November 2026).

- The state approved a first set of corridors, often called Phase 2A, of about 76 km in late 2024 and sent it to the Centre. It includes extensions to the existing lines and a new line from **Nagole to Rajiv Gandhi International Airport** at Shamshabad.

- A further set of corridors, Phase 2B, was approved by the state in 2025.

- In May 2026 the Centre said it was ready to give in-principle support and to share costs equally with the state. At the time of writing (November 2026), final central approval for the first stage had been reported but not officially confirmed, so treat any completion date as provisional.

- No Phase 2 line is open, and timelines for metro projects often slip.

An earlier plan for an airport express line from Raidurg, through the Financial District, to the airport was dropped after the 2023 change of government in favour of the new Nagole route. Until a line opens, the airport is reached by road, mostly via the PV Narasimha Rao Expressway or the Outer Ring Road. See our ORR guide (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/hyderabad-outer-ring-road-guide.html) and our post on Hyderabad's flyovers and underpasses (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/hyderabad-flyovers-and-underpasses.html).

## Practising metro-corridor roads in Sawari

Sawari is a free browser driving simulator on five real Hyderabad routes, built from OpenStreetMap. It does not model the metro viaducts or stations, so it is not a replica of a metro corridor. What it does give you is busy multi-lane city traffic, with autos, buses and two-wheelers that pull in and out, and a debrief that shows every fault.

The Cyber Towers to Jubilee Hills route (https://sawari.airacode.online/routes.html#hitec-city) runs through the same part of the city as the western end of the Blue Line, and is good for practising lane choice and watching the left lane with traffic set to Busy or Dense. Use it to sharpen habits, then apply them on the real road with full attention. Sawari is for practice only and does not replace real lessons.

## Frequently asked questions

**How many metro lines are there in Hyderabad?**
Three: the Red Line from Miyapur to LB Nagar, the Blue Line from Nagole to Raidurg, and the Green Line from JBS Parade Ground to MGBS. Together they cover about 69 km, almost all of it elevated.

**Where can I change between Hyderabad metro lines?**
Ameerpet links the Red and Blue lines, MG Bus Station (MGBS) links the Red and Green lines, and Parade Ground links the Blue and Green lines.

**Is there a metro to Hyderabad airport?**
Not yet. As of November 2026 a Nagole to airport line is part of the Phase 2 plans, but it has not been built. The earlier plan for an airport express line from Raidurg was dropped in favour of the new proposal.

**Can I park my car at a Hyderabad metro station?**
Some stations, especially at or near the ends of lines, have parking, but many in the city centre have little or none. Capacity and charges change, so check at the station or with Hyderabad Metro Rail before relying on it.

---

# Hyderabad Outer Ring Road (ORR) guide: lanes, exits, tolls, speed limits and safety

URL: https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/hyderabad-outer-ring-road-guide.html
Category: Hyderabad roads · Published 2026-11-18 · Updated 2026-11-18

The Hyderabad Outer Ring Road (ORR), officially the Nehru Outer Ring Road, is a 158 km, eight-lane expressway that loops right round the city. It is the fastest way between the IT corridor, the airport and the highways out of Hyderabad, and it rewards drivers who keep to their lane, watch their speed and plan their exit early.

## What the Hyderabad ORR is

The ORR is an access-controlled expressway: you can only join or leave it at interchanges, there are no signals, no crossing traffic and no shops or houses opening onto it. It has four lanes in each direction, separated by a median, and along much of its length there are two-lane service roads on either side for local traffic.

It was built in stages by the Hyderabad Metropolitan Development Authority (HMDA). The first stretch, about 22 km from Gachibowli through Narsingi to Shamshabad, opened in November 2008 to serve the new airport. Further sections followed over the next decade, and the last gaps in the loop were closed by 2018.

The ring passes through, or close to, Gachibowli, Nanakramguda, Narsingi, Kokapet, Shamshabad, Pedda Amberpet, Ghatkesar, Keesara, Shamirpet, Medchal, Kandlakoya and Patancheru. It crosses or meets the main national highways leaving the city, including the roads towards Bengaluru, Vijayawada, Warangal, Nagpur and Mumbai.

## Exits and interchanges

There are roughly twenty interchanges on the ORR, and new ones have been added as the city has grown, so any count you read goes out of date quickly. Some of the ones Hyderabad drivers use most are:

- **Gachibowli and Nanakramguda**, for the Financial District, Gachibowli and HITEC City.

- **Kokapet and Narsingi**, for the newer western suburbs.

- **Shamshabad**, for Rajiv Gandhi International Airport and the Bengaluru highway.

- **Pedda Amberpet**, for the Vijayawada highway and the eastern side of the city.

- **Ghatkesar**, for the Warangal road.

- **Shamirpet and Medchal**, for the northern highways.

- **Patancheru**, for the Mumbai highway and the industrial area to the west.

Exits are numbered, and the overhead signs show both the number and the place names well in advance. On a road this fast, the numbers are easier to read and remember than the names. Before you set off, note the exit you want and the one before it, so you know when to start moving left.

If you miss your exit, carry on to the next one and come back. Never stop, reverse or cut across the chevrons at an exit. On the ORR, a missed exit costs a few kilometres, nothing more.

## Tolls and FASTag

The ORR uses **closed, distance-based tolling**. You pass a toll plaza when you join and when you leave, and the charge depends on the distance between those two interchanges, not on a fixed fee per plaza. Short hops cost little; a long run round half the ring costs more.

Since 2023 the tolling, operation and maintenance of the ORR have been run by IRB Golconda Expressway, a company of IRB Infrastructure, under a 30-year toll-operate-transfer agreement with HMDA. The road itself still belongs to the state.

- **Use a FASTag.** It is the normal way to pay, and FASTag lanes move far faster than cash. Make sure your tag is active, linked to the right vehicle and has enough balance before you join.

- **Pick the right lane at the plaza.** Lanes are marked overhead. Move into a FASTag lane early and slow down smoothly; plazas are where many low-speed bumps happen.

- **Check current rates** before you travel. Rates are revised periodically, so we do not list them here.

## Speed limits and lane discipline

The ORR has speed limits by lane. Since June 2023 the maximum in the **two lanes nearest the median** has been **120 km/h**, up from 100 km/h. The **two outer lanes** are limited to **80 km/h**, and are where heavy vehicles and slower traffic belong. Limits can be lower near interchanges, toll plazas and works, and they can be changed, so the signs on the road always come first. There is also a minimum speed in the fast lanes, so do not dawdle in them.

Lane discipline matters more here than anywhere else in the city, because speed differences between lanes are large.

- **Keep left unless overtaking.** In India we drive on the left, so the right-hand lanes are the faster ones. Overtake on the right, then move back.

- **Do not undertake.** Passing on the left at 100 km/h, where nobody is looking for you, is one of the most dangerous things you can do on the ORR.

- **Signal early and hold it.** Check your mirrors, check your blind spot, signal, and move one lane at a time. Our guide to indicators and lane discipline (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/indicators-and-lane-discipline.html) covers the routine.

- **Leave a big gap.** At 120 km/h you cover more than 30 metres a second. Keep at least a three-second gap, and more at night or in rain.

- **Watch lorries.** They are slow uphill, long to overtake and have large blind spots. Pass them decisively, do not sit alongside.

## Staying safe on the ORR

### Fatigue and monotony

The ORR is wide, straight for long stretches and much the same for many kilometres. That makes it easy to drift above the limit without noticing and easy to get drowsy, especially late at night or after a long day at work. If you feel your eyes getting heavy, open a window, leave at the next exit and rest. A short break is far safer than pushing on.

### Night driving

Much of the ORR is lit, but not every stretch, and lighting can be patchy near interchanges and works. Use dipped headlights, dip early for oncoming traffic on curves, and watch for unlit vehicles parked near the edge. Our night driving tips (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/night-driving-hyderabad-tips.html) have more.

### Rain

Heavy rain on a fast road brings spray, standing water and aquaplaning. Slow down well below the limit, keep further back and avoid sudden steering or braking. See our monsoon driving guide (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/monsoon-driving-hyderabad.html).

### Breakdowns

If your car develops a problem, signal and move left to the edge or shoulder as smoothly as you can, ideally onto an exit. Switch on your hazard lights. Get everyone out on the side away from traffic and stand behind the crash barrier if it is safe to do so. Do not stand in front of or behind the car, and do not try to change a tyre on the live lane side.

For an emergency, call 112. The ORR also has its own helpline and roadside SOS facilities; the numbers are shown on signboards along the road, so note them before you need them.

Never stop on the main carriageway to take a call, check directions or let someone out. Never walk across the ORR. Two-wheelers, autos and pedestrians are not allowed on the main carriageway for good reason.

## How the ORR changed Hyderabad

The ORR did more than speed up journeys. Before it, long-distance lorries had to pass through or near the city. Now much of that freight can go round, which takes heavy traffic out of inner roads.

It also reshaped where people live and work. The Financial District, Kokapet, Narsingi and Tellapur grew quickly because the ORR put them within easy reach of the airport and the IT corridor. Warehouses and logistics parks clustered round its eastern and northern interchanges. More than 30 radial roads link the ORR with the inner city, and the planned Regional Ring Road (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/hyderabad-regional-ring-road-rrr.html) is meant to do for the wider region what the ORR did for the city.

The flip side is that some interchanges, such as Gachibowli and Nanakramguda, now see heavy queues at peak hours, as the city has grown up to the edge of the ring.

## Practising high-speed habits in Sawari

Sawari does not include the ORR. It is a free browser driving simulator on five real Hyderabad routes, built from OpenStreetMap, and all five are city roads. What it can help with are the habits the ORR depends on: keeping to your lane, signalling every lane change, and planning moves early.

The Cyber Towers to Jubilee Hills route (https://sawari.airacode.online/routes.html#hitec-city) is the closest match. It has wide multi-lane stretches, flyover ramps and merging traffic, and Sawari's debrief flags every lane change or turn you made without signalling (`Q` and `E`). Set traffic to Busy or Dense to practise finding gaps. Read our HITEC City to Jubilee Hills guide (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/hitec-city-to-jubilee-hills-drive.html) first, then start the drive (https://sawari.airacode.online/play.html?route=hitec-city). Sawari is for practice only and is no substitute for real driving lessons.

For the latest official information on the ORR, see the HMDA website (https://www.hmda.gov.in).

## Frequently asked questions

**How long is the Hyderabad Outer Ring Road?**
The Nehru Outer Ring Road is about 158 km long. It is an eight-lane, access-controlled expressway with four lanes in each direction, circling the city through Gachibowli, Shamshabad, Pedda Amberpet, Ghatkesar, Shamirpet, Medchal and Patancheru.

**What is the speed limit on the ORR?**
Since 2023 the limit in the two lanes nearest the median has been 120 km/h, and the two outer lanes are limited to 80 km/h. Limits can change and differ near interchanges, so always follow the signs on the road.

**How does the ORR toll work?**
The ORR uses closed, distance-based tolling: you are charged for the distance between the interchange where you join and the one where you leave. FASTag is the normal way to pay. Rates are revised from time to time, so check the current rate before you travel.

**Can two-wheelers use the Hyderabad ORR?**
No. Two-wheelers and three-wheelers such as autos are not allowed on the ORR main carriageway. They can use the service roads that run alongside much of it.

# Hyderabad Regional Ring Road (RRR): route, northern and southern parts, and status in November 2026

URL: https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/hyderabad-regional-ring-road-rrr.html
Category: Hyderabad roads · Published 2026-11-18 · Updated 2026-11-18

The Hyderabad Regional Ring Road (RRR) is a planned second ring road around the city, far outside the Outer Ring Road. As of November 2026 it is still mostly a plan: the northern part has its land and is waiting to start construction, while the southern part's route has not yet been approved.

This is a fast-moving project. Everything below is as of November 2026, from official statements and news reports at the time of writing. Dates have slipped many times, so treat any target year as a hope rather than a promise.

## What the Hyderabad Regional Ring Road is

The Outer Ring Road (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/hyderabad-outer-ring-road-guide.html) now sits inside the built-up city in many places. The RRR is meant to be the next ring out: a high-speed road that links the district towns around Hyderabad, connects every national highway leaving the city, and lets long-distance traffic and freight avoid the metropolitan area entirely.

It is split into two halves, which are being handled very differently:

- **The northern part**, from Sangareddy round the north of the city to Choutuppal, about 161.5 km.

- **The southern part**, from Choutuppal round the south back to Sangareddy, reported at roughly 182 to 201 km depending on the alignment.

Together that is a ring of around 340 km or more, passing through parts of Sangareddy, Medak, Siddipet, Yadadri Bhuvanagiri, Nalgonda, Rangareddy, Vikarabad and neighbouring districts.

## The northern part: land done, construction waiting

The northern part is the one that is closest to becoming real. It has been approved by the Union Ministry of Road Transport and Highways as national highway **NH 161AA** under the Bharatmala Pariyojana programme, and it will be built by the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI).

### Route and design

The northern alignment runs through or near **Sangareddy, Narsapur, Toopran, Gajwel, Jagdevpur, Bhongir and Choutuppal**. It is planned as a **six-lane** road. In July 2026 the Union road transport minister, Nitin Gadkari, gave its length as 161.518 km and its estimated cost as about Rs 23,936 crore, to be built under the hybrid annuity model, where the government pays the builder in instalments over time.

Earlier reports said the design had been changed from a fully access-controlled expressway to a national highway with a lower design speed. The final details will only be clear once the road is built, so it is fair to say it will be a fast, six-lane highway rather than to promise a particular speed.

### Land and tenders

Land acquisition, often the slowest step for any Indian highway, is largely done. The minister's July 2026 statement said acquisition notices had been issued for about 99 per cent of the land needed. In October 2026 the Telangana Roads and Buildings minister said land acquisition for the northern part was complete, while another report that month put it at over 90 per cent. The state pays half the land cost, and the Centre pays the rest and the full construction cost.

The tenders have been the sticking point. NHAI invited bids for the northern part in late 2025, then extended the deadline again and again during 2026. At the time of writing, reports say the extensions are because the Union Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs has not yet given the final clearance needed to start the work. No construction contract had been reported as awarded as of November 2026.

## The southern part: still finding its route

The southern part is at a much earlier stage. Its job is to complete the ring through the southern districts and connect the RRR with the new developments south of the city, including the planned Bharat Future City, Pharma City and industrial parks.

- The state cabinet approved alignment options in mid-2025, and a revised alignment was sent to the Centre in February 2026.

- NHAI appointed a consultant for the detailed project report, which was still being prepared in 2026.

- In October 2026 the state handed the southern part to the Hyderabad Growth Corridor Limited (HGCL), the HMDA company that already works on the ORR and on land for Future City.

- The alignment has faced protests from farmers and landowners along the proposed route.

Reports describe it as a proposed six-lane road of about 201 km passing through areas such as Choutuppal, Amangal and Sangareddy. As of November 2026 the southern alignment had not been approved by the Centre, so there is no final route, cost or timetable to report.

## What is real and what is still a plan

| Item | Status, November 2026 |
|---|---|
| Northern part alignment | Approved (NH 161AA) |
| Northern part land | Reported complete or nearly complete |
| Northern part construction | Not started; tenders awaiting central clearance |
| Southern part alignment | Not yet approved by the Centre |
| Southern part project report | In preparation |
| Opening date for either part | None confirmed |

If you see adverts for plots that say the RRR is "under construction" or "opening soon", read them with care. Check the latest news, the official land notifications and the alignment maps yourself before deciding anything.

## What the RRR will mean for drivers

When it opens, the RRR should change journeys in a few clear ways.

- **Freight round, not through.** Lorries travelling between, say, the Mumbai highway and the Vijayawada highway could stay on the RRR instead of using the ORR. That should ease the heavy-vehicle lanes on the ORR.

- **Faster links between district towns.** Places like Sangareddy, Gajwel and Bhongir would be connected to each other directly, without going via Hyderabad.

- **New growth along the ring.** As the ORR did for Gachibowli and Kokapet, the RRR is expected to draw logistics parks, industry and housing to its interchanges.

- **Radial roads.** Plans link the RRR to the ORR and the city through a set of radial roads, some of which are being built or planned separately.

For drivers, the habits needed will be the same as on the ORR: lane discipline, long following gaps, early lane changes for exits and care around heavy vehicles. A new highway through farmland also means slow tractors, livestock and people crossing near villages in the early years, so it pays to stay alert even when the road is empty.

## Sawari and the RRR

Sawari does not include the RRR, which does not exist yet, or the ORR. It is a free browser driving simulator on five real city routes in Hyderabad, built from OpenStreetMap. What it is good for is building the basics that make highway driving safe: steady lane keeping, signalling every lane change and reading traffic ahead.

If you want to practise the merging and lane choice that ring roads demand, try the Cyber Towers to Jubilee Hills route (https://sawari.airacode.online/routes.html#hitec-city) with traffic set to Busy or Dense, and read our guide to indicators and lane discipline (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/indicators-and-lane-discipline.html). Sawari is for practice only and does not replace real lessons.

For official updates on national highway projects, see NHAI (https://nhai.gov.in) and the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (https://morth.nic.in).

## Frequently asked questions

**What is the Regional Ring Road in Hyderabad?**
It is a planned second ring road around Hyderabad, much further out than the Outer Ring Road, running through towns such as Sangareddy, Toopran, Gajwel, Bhongir and Choutuppal. It is in two parts, northern and southern, together about 340 to 360 km depending on the final southern alignment.

**Has construction of the Regional Ring Road started?**
As of November 2026, main construction has not started on either part. Land acquisition for the northern part has been reported as complete or nearly complete, but its construction tenders were still awaiting central clearance. The southern part's alignment had not been approved.

**How long is the northern part of the RRR?**
The northern part, from Sangareddy to Choutuppal, is about 161.5 km and is planned as a six-lane national highway, NH 161AA, to be built by NHAI under the Bharatmala programme.

**When will the Regional Ring Road be completed?**
There is no confirmed completion date. Dates in news reports have slipped several times. A realistic answer is that the northern part is years away from opening, and the southern part is further behind.

---

# Hyderabad flyovers and underpasses: the newer elevated roads that matter for daily drives

URL: https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/hyderabad-flyovers-and-underpasses.html
Category: Hyderabad roads · Published 2026-11-18 · Updated 2026-11-18

Hyderabad has built dozens of flyovers and underpasses in the last decade, and this list covers the ones that matter most for daily drives: what each one bypasses, where it lands and what to watch for. For how to drive any flyover well, from lane choice to merging, see our separate guide to driving on flyovers in Hyderabad (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/driving-on-flyovers-hyderabad.html); this post is about the roads themselves.

## Hyderabad flyovers and the SRDP

Most of the city's newer flyovers come from the **Strategic Road Development Plan (SRDP)**, a programme run through the Greater Hyderabad Municipal Corporation (GHMC) to take through traffic over the worst junctions. It covers flyovers, underpasses, road-over-bridges and steel bridges, and many of them are concentrated in the IT corridor around HITEC City, Gachibowli and Kondapur, and on the eastern side around LB Nagar.

The idea is the same everywhere: through traffic goes over or under the junction, while traffic that wants to turn uses the service road and the signal. That only works if you choose the right lane before the ramp, which is why knowing the city's main flyovers in advance is so useful.

## The big elevated roads

### PV Narasimha Rao Expressway

Opened in 2009 and about 11.6 km long, this is still Hyderabad's longest flyover. It runs on pillars from Mehdipatnam towards Aramghar, above the road below, and is the main route from the western and central city to Rajiv Gandhi International Airport. Exits are few, so plan which ramp you need before you join. Our flyover driving guide (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/driving-on-flyovers-hyderabad.html) covers the expressway's long ramps and merges.

### Aramghar to Zoo Park flyover

Opened in January 2025, this six-lane flyover is a little over 4 km long, making it the city's second longest. Built under SRDP, it lifts traffic over the junctions between Aramghar and the Nehru Zoological Park, including Shastripuram, on the busy southern approach to the city. It has been named after former Prime Minister Manmohan Singh. It is worth knowing if you drive between the airport side and the Old City or Bahadurpura.

## The IT corridor: HITEC City, Gachibowli and Jubilee Hills

### Shaikpet flyover

Opened on 1 January 2022, the Shaikpet flyover is a six-lane road about 2.7 km long, from Tolichowki towards Raidurg. It passes over several busy junctions, including Seven Tombs, Film Nagar Road and OU Colony, on one of the main links between the older western city and Gachibowli. It is long and busy at peak hours; get into your lane at Tolichowki and stay in it.

### Durgam Cheruvu cable bridge

The cable-stayed bridge across Durgam Cheruvu opened in September 2020. It links Jubilee Hills Road No. 45, via an elevated approach, with Madhapur and the HITEC City side of the lake. It has become a landmark, lit up at night, and that brings its own hazard: people stopping to take photos. Never stop on the carriageway; enjoy the view from the footpaths and viewpoints.

### Biodiversity Junction and Kothaguda

Two multi-level flyovers sort out some of the most complicated junctions in the IT corridor. The **Biodiversity Junction** flyovers, near Gachibowli, opened in stages in 2019 and 2020. The **Kothaguda** multi-level flyover opened on 1 January 2023, with a main flyover of about 2.2 km plus ramps, taking traffic over the Botanical Garden and Kothaguda junctions towards Kondapur and HITEC City.

Multi-level flyovers are the ones where wrong ramp choices happen most. The signs come thick and fast, and the ramps split close together. If you do this route daily, learn the layout once on a quiet day.

### Underpasses

The IT corridor also has several underpasses, such as the ones at **Ayyappa Society** and **Mindspace** junctions. Underpasses have their own risks: water collects at the lowest point in heavy rain, and the light changes sharply as you go in and out. Our monsoon driving guide (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/monsoon-driving-hyderabad.html) explains why you should never drive into a flooded underpass.

## Central and eastern Hyderabad

### Indira Park to VST steel bridge

Opened in August 2023, this four-lane, two-way steel flyover runs about 2.6 km from near Lower Tank Bund and Indira Park to VST, over the busy roads around Ashok Nagar and RTC X Roads. It is named after Nayani Narasimha Reddy. It saves several signals between the Tank Bund area and VST, and the newer layout catches out drivers who still expect the old junctions.

### Punjagutta steel bridges

Short steel bridges at Punjagutta, opened in 2020 and 2022, ease movements at one of the city's busiest junctions. They are short, but the ramps start and end close to other turns, so look well ahead.

### LB Nagar and the Vijayawada road

The LB Nagar area has a cluster of SRDP flyovers and underpasses, including flyovers at LB Nagar, Kamineni and Bairamalguda, many opened around 2020. Together they let through traffic on the Vijayawada highway skip a series of signals near the end of the metro's Red Line. Lanes split often here; read the overhead signs early.

## Tips for daily flyover routes

- **Learn your landing point.** For each flyover on your commute, know where it comes down and what is just after the landing: a junction, a bus stop, a speed breaker or a U-turn. Most surprises happen there.

- **Know your exit ramps.** On long elevated roads such as the PV Narasimha Rao Expressway, there are only a few ways off. Count them on your first few drives so you are never caught out.

- **Use the road below when you need to turn.** A flyover saves time only if you are going straight on. If your turn is at the junction it crosses, stay on the service road.

- **Check the map before new routes.** Recently opened flyovers may not yet appear in older maps or navigation data, and navigation apps sometimes confuse a flyover with the road beneath it. If the voice says "turn left" while you are on a flyover, carry on to the landing.

- **Leave more time in the monsoon.** The roads at the foot of ramps and in underpasses are the first to flood.

## Still being built

More projects are under way. A steel bridge from Malakpet towards Santosh Nagar, about 2.5 km long, was reported in February 2026 as under construction, with an expected opening around the end of 2026. Other flyovers and elevated corridors have been proposed or started across the city. Opening dates slip often, and roads near works have narrowed lanes, diversions and night closures, so allow extra time and follow the signs.

Flyovers in Hyderabad are sometimes closed at night, on special occasions such as New Year's Eve, or to certain vehicles. Closures are announced by the traffic police. Check the Hyderabad Traffic Police (https://www.htp.gov.in) for current advisories before late-night drives.

## Flyovers in Sawari

Sawari is a free browser driving simulator on five real Hyderabad routes, built from OpenStreetMap with real elevation, so its flyovers rise and fall as they do in life. Of the roads above, only the Durgam Cheruvu cable bridge and its approaches are in the game, on the Cyber Towers to Jubilee Hills route (https://sawari.airacode.online/routes.html#hitec-city), which also crosses flyover ramps and merges near Inorbit Mall. It is a good place to practise picking a lane before a ramp, with the blue lane band showing which way to go. Read our route guide (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/hitec-city-to-jubilee-hills-drive.html) and start the drive (https://sawari.airacode.online/play.html?route=hitec-city). Sawari is for practice and does not replace real lessons.

## Frequently asked questions

**What is the longest flyover in Hyderabad?**
The PV Narasimha Rao Expressway, about 11.6 km of elevated road from Mehdipatnam towards Aramghar, opened in 2009. The second longest is the Aramghar to Zoo Park flyover, a little over 4 km, opened in January 2025.

**What is SRDP in Hyderabad?**
SRDP is the Strategic Road Development Plan, a programme run through the GHMC to build flyovers, underpasses, road-over-bridges and steel bridges at the city's most congested junctions. Many of Hyderabad's newer flyovers were built under it.

**How long is the Shaikpet flyover?**
The Shaikpet flyover is about 2.7 km long and six lanes wide. It opened on 1 January 2022 and carries traffic from Tolichowki towards Raidurg, passing over several busy junctions on the way to Gachibowli and HITEC City.

**When did the Durgam Cheruvu cable bridge open?**
The Durgam Cheruvu cable-stayed bridge opened to traffic in September 2020. It links Jubilee Hills Road No. 45 with Madhapur and the HITEC City area across the lake.

# Hyderabad traffic hotspots and peak hours: where it jams, when, and how to plan around it

URL: https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/hyderabad-traffic-hotspots-peak-hours.html
Category: Hyderabad roads · Published 2026-11-18 · Updated 2026-11-18

Hyderabad traffic peak hours fall on weekday mornings, roughly 8 to 11 am, and evenings, roughly 5 to 9 pm, and the worst hotspots are the IT corridor, the Kukatpally and Ameerpet belt, Panjagutta, Mehdipatnam, LB Nagar and Secunderabad. Rain and road works can make any of them much worse. Knowing where and when the city jams lets you plan a drive that is shorter and far less stressful.

This guide is based on what Hyderabad and Cyberabad traffic police and local news have reported. We have not invented rankings; where we quote a figure, we say where it comes from.

## How bad is Hyderabad traffic?

Bad, but not the worst in India. In the TomTom Traffic Index for 2025, Hyderabad was ranked 47th among cities worldwide for congestion, behind several other Indian cities including Bengaluru and Pune. The same coverage reported a small improvement on the year before.

A city-wide number hides a lot, though. Hyderabad can feel easy on a Sunday morning and grind to a halt on a wet Wednesday evening. What matters to you as a driver is which roads you use and when.

## Hyderabad traffic peak hours

### Weekday mornings and evenings

The basic pattern follows the working day. Local reports on the IT corridor have quoted peak hours of about 8 to 11 am and 5 to 8 pm, and traffic police have quoted 8.30 to 11 am and 5 to 9 pm for the roads around KBR Park in Jubilee Hills. In practice, plan for the morning peak to run until late morning and the evening peak to last well past dark.

### The IT corridor runs late

The IT corridor has its own rhythm. Offices and shifts start and end at different times, so traffic officials have described heavy movement there in the morning and again in the evening, running to nearly midnight. Cyberabad traffic police have repeatedly asked IT companies to stagger log-out times, encourage carpooling and use company buses to spread the load.

### Weekends, festivals and events

Weekends are usually lighter in the morning but busy around malls, lakes and temples in the evening. Festivals, the Numaish exhibition, political rallies, cricket matches and Ganesh immersion bring diversions and heavy traffic to particular areas, usually announced in advance by the traffic police.

## Hyderabad's well-known traffic hotspots

### IT corridor: Gachibowli, HITEC City and Madhapur

The western IT district is the area most often reported as congested. Local reports have named Cyber Towers Circle as the main bottleneck linking Madhapur, HITEC City and Kukatpally, with IKEA junction, Wipro junction, Kothaguda and Bio-Diversity junction also slowing badly at busy times. The IIIT junction in Gachibowli has had traffic restrictions since April 2026 for flyover and underpass construction, and police advised avoiding it at peak hours where possible.

### Kukatpally and JNTU

The road from Kukatpally and JNTU towards HITEC City carries a heavy daily flow into the IT district. Cyberabad traffic police have been studying a dedicated carriageway from JNTU to Raidurgam, which tells you how much pressure that link is under.

### Ameerpet, Panjagutta and Khairatabad

The central belt between Ameerpet, Panjagutta and Khairatabad connects the west of the city to the old centre, and many cross-city trips pass through it. Rain-day reports have named Khairatabad, Raj Bhavan Road and Lakdi-ka-Pul among the stretches that jam. With flyover works narrowing roads near KBR Park, police have advised drivers heading towards Panjagutta and Ameerpet to use alternative roads.

### Jubilee Hills and Banjara Hills

The steel flyover works around KBR Park have narrowed the carriageway between Jubilee Hills Check Post and the Sagar Society side, and between TV9 junction and KBR Park. Traffic police have pointed drivers to Banjara Hills Road No. 1, Road No. 10 and Yusufguda as alternatives while the work goes on.

### Mehdipatnam

Mehdipatnam is where the PVNR Expressway to the airport begins and several busy roads meet, including the Masab Tank stretch. It is commonly named by motorists among the junctions that struggle at the busiest hours.

### LB Nagar, Secunderabad and Paradise

LB Nagar, on the eastern side, is where traffic from the Vijayawada highway and the eastern suburbs meets the city, and it is regularly named among the busy junctions. In Secunderabad, the roads around Paradise Circle and the railway station jam on wet days, and elevated corridor works between Bowenpally and Paradise have caused long delays. During those diversions, a traffic officer told reporters that jams were no longer limited to peak hours.

Other stretches come and go with construction and drainage works, so treat this as a guide to the usual suspects rather than a fixed list.

## Why these places jam

- **Office hours.** Huge numbers of people travel to the same few districts at the same times, especially the IT corridor.

- **Construction.** Flyovers, underpasses and elevated corridors are being built at several busy junctions. Barricades and machinery narrow the road for months, and traffic spills into neighbouring lanes and colony roads.

- **Junction design.** Many big roads meet at a few signalled junctions, with U-turns and free lefts nearby. Vehicles cutting across to reach a U-turn, or stopping in the free-left lane, slow everyone behind them. Our guide to U-turns in Hyderabad (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/u-turns-in-hyderabad.html) covers this.

- **Rain.** Even a drizzle slows Hyderabad down, and heavy rain floods low junctions. Local reports have described snarls across the city on consecutive days of rain.

- **Kerbside stopping.** Buses, autos and cabs stopping outside malls, metro stations and offices take a lane away exactly where traffic is heaviest.

## How to plan around Hyderabad traffic

### Change the time, not just the route

The most effective thing you can do is avoid the peaks. Leaving half an hour earlier in the morning, or waiting until after the evening rush, often saves more time than any shortcut. If your office allows flexible hours, use them.

### Check a live traffic app before you leave

Live traffic in map apps is the best guide to what the roads are doing right now. Check it just before you set off, not the night before, and let it suggest a route. Set your destination before you move and keep the phone mounted.

### Know your alternatives

For regular trips, learn one or two alternative routes in advance, so you are not trying new colony roads in the dark. Flyovers and the Outer Ring Road can take you round the worst junctions; our guide to driving on flyovers (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/driving-on-flyovers-hyderabad.html) helps with ramps and lane choice. Respect residential streets if the app sends you through them: slow down and watch for children and parked cars.

### Follow traffic police advisories

Diversions for construction, events and rain are announced by the Hyderabad Traffic Police (https://www.htp.gov.in) and, for the IT corridor and western suburbs, by Cyberabad traffic police, usually on social media. Check them on festival days and whenever heavy rain is forecast. If you are heading to the airport, see our guide to driving to Hyderabad airport (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/driving-to-hyderabad-airport.html).

### Be extra careful when it rains

Wet roads, flooded junctions and frustrated drivers are a bad mix. Leave much more time, avoid known flooding spots and never drive into water when you cannot see the road surface. Our monsoon driving guide (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/monsoon-driving-hyderabad.html) has the details.

Sitting in traffic is not wasted time if you use it well: keep a steady gap to the car ahead, stay in your lane and leave space for two-wheelers to pass. Constant lane hopping in a jam gains almost nothing and causes scrapes.

## Practising busy traffic in Sawari

Sawari is a free browser driving simulator on five real Hyderabad routes. It cannot predict a real jam and it has no rain, but it lets you practise driving in heavy traffic without any risk. The Cyber Towers to Jubilee Hills route (https://sawari.airacode.online/routes.html#hitec-city) runs from the IT corridor, over the Durgam Cheruvu cable bridge and along Road No. 45 and Road No. 36, so it covers roads mentioned in this guide. See our route guide (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/hitec-city-to-jubilee-hills-drive.html) for what to expect.

Set the traffic level to Dense and practise the habits that matter in a crawl: smooth braking, signalling with `Q` and `E`, checking around you with the mouse before a lane change, and leaving room for buses and autos that stop without warning. The debrief at the end lists every fault, so you can see whether you stayed calm and tidy.

Sawari is for practice only. It does not replace lessons with a licensed instructor. On the real road, follow the signs, signals and instructions from the traffic police.

## Frequently asked questions

**What are the peak traffic hours in Hyderabad?**
Weekday mornings from roughly 8 to 11 am and evenings from roughly 5 to 9 pm are the worst, with the IT corridor often slow well into the night. Exact times vary by area and change when it rains or when road works are under way.

**Which areas of Hyderabad have the worst traffic?**
The IT corridor around Gachibowli, HITEC City and Madhapur is the most often reported, along with Kukatpally and JNTU, Ameerpet, Panjagutta, Mehdipatnam, LB Nagar and Secunderabad. Areas with flyover or elevated corridor works can be slow at any hour.

**Where can I check Hyderabad traffic advisories?**
Hyderabad Traffic Police and Cyberabad Traffic Police publish diversions, closures and rain advisories on their websites and social media. Check them before festivals, rallies, big matches and on heavy rain days.

**Does rain make Hyderabad traffic worse?**
Yes, a lot. Waterlogged junctions slow everything down, and police have repeatedly asked IT companies to stagger or bring forward log-out times on heavy rain days to keep the roads moving.

---

# Telangana TG number plates explained: codes, HSRP, BH series and plate colours

URL: https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/telangana-tg-number-plates-explained.html
Category: Hyderabad roads · Published 2026-11-18 · Updated 2026-11-18

A TG number plate tells you a vehicle was registered in Telangana, and the two digits after it tell you which transport office registered it. This guide explains the change from TS to TG, what the Hyderabad codes mean, how the high-security plate (HSRP) rules apply in Telangana, how the BH series works and what each plate colour signals.

## How an Indian number plate is read

A standard Indian registration mark has four parts. Take **TG 09 AB 1234** as an example:

- **TG**: the state or union territory code, here Telangana.

- **09**: the code of the regional transport office (in Telangana, the RTA office or district) where the vehicle was registered.

- **AB**: a letter series, issued in sequence as numbers run out. Fancy numbers within a series are auctioned.

- **1234**: the number itself, from 0001 to 9999.

The office code shows where the vehicle was first registered, not where the owner lives now. A car registered in Khairatabad keeps its TG 09 number if the owner moves to Gachibowli.

## From TS to TG number plates: what changed in 2024

When Telangana was formed in June 2014, its vehicles were given the code **TS**. In March 2024 the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways issued a notification, dated 12 March 2024, changing Telangana's code to **TG**, and the Telangana Transport Department began registering new vehicles with TG from 15 March 2024.

Two points cause most of the confusion:

- **Existing TS plates stay valid.** The change applies only to vehicles registered after it came in. A car registered as TS 09 in 2022 remains TS 09; there is nothing to apply for.

- **Do not change TS to TG yourself.** Transport officials have warned owners against this. TS 09 AB 1234 and TG 09 AB 1234 can be two different vehicles, so altering your plate could give your car another vehicle's number. It is also not a legal registration mark for your vehicle.

Before 2014, Hyderabad vehicles were registered under Andhra Pradesh with the code AP, and you will still see a few on older vehicles.

## Telangana RTA codes for Hyderabad and around

Within Hyderabad, the transport department divides the city into zones, each with its own code. Around the city, the neighbouring districts have theirs. These are the codes you will see most often on Hyderabad roads:

| Code | Area |
|---|---|
| TG 07 | Ranga Reddy district |
| TG 08 | Medchal-Malkajgiri district |
| TG 09 | Hyderabad Central zone (Khairatabad) |
| TG 10 | Hyderabad North zone |
| TG 11 | Hyderabad East zone |
| TG 12 | Hyderabad South zone |
| TG 13 | Hyderabad West zone |

The same numbers were used with TS before March 2024, so TS 09 and TG 09 both mean the Central zone. Ranga Reddy (TG 07) and Medchal-Malkajgiri (TG 08) cover much of the growing west and north of the city, including large parts of the IT corridor and Kukatpally, so you will see plenty of both in HITEC City traffic.

Offices and the areas they serve can be reorganised, and each district has several offices. To find which office covers your address, check the Telangana Transport Department (https://www.transport.telangana.gov.in) website, which lists the state and district codes.

Registering a new vehicle is usually handled by the dealer, but the office that serves your address decides the code. If you are going for your own licence too, our guide to getting a driving licence in Hyderabad (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/how-to-get-driving-licence-hyderabad.html) covers the RTA process.

## High-security registration plates (HSRP) in Telangana

A high-security registration plate is an aluminium plate with a chromium hologram, a blue "IND" strip, a laser-etched serial number, and non-removable snap locks so it cannot be easily swapped. A third registration mark, a sticker on the windscreen, matches the plates.

### New vehicles

Under central rules, new vehicles sold in India since **April 2019** come with HSRP fitted by the manufacturer's dealer. If you bought your car new after that, you should already have them.

### Older vehicles

In April 2025 the Telangana government ordered that vehicles registered **before 1 April 2019** must also be fitted with HSRP, with a deadline of 30 September 2025, and said action would be taken under the Motor Vehicles Act for non-compliance. It applies to all classes of vehicle, including two-wheelers. At the time of writing (November 2026), check the Transport Department for the current position on enforcement and any later changes.

Fake websites offering HSRP booking have been reported in Telangana. Book only through the official portal linked from the Transport Department website, and never pay through a link sent by message.

## BH series: the Bharat registration

The **BH (Bharat) series** was introduced by the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways through a notification dated 26 August 2021, in force from 15 September 2021. It is meant for people who move between states for work, so they do not have to re-register their vehicle each time.

A BH plate reads like **24 BH 1234 AA**: the year of first registration, BH, a four-digit number and a letter series. There is no state or office code.

- **Who can apply:** it is voluntary and open to defence personnel, employees of central and state governments and their public sector undertakings, and employees of private companies with offices in four or more states or union territories.

- **Vehicles:** private, non-transport vehicles only.

- **Road tax:** paid for two years at a time (or multiples of two) instead of in one lump sum. The notified rates are 8 per cent for vehicles up to Rs 10 lakh, 10 per cent between Rs 10 lakh and Rs 20 lakh and 12 per cent above that, with 2 per cent less for electric vehicles. After the fourteenth year the tax becomes annual, at half the earlier rate.

Read the official Press Information Bureau release on the BH series (https://pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=1749764) for the full terms.

## Number plate colours and what they mean

| Plate | Meaning |
|---|---|
| White, black characters | Private, non-transport vehicle |
| Yellow, black characters | Commercial (transport) vehicle: taxis, autos, goods vehicles, buses |
| Green, white characters | Private battery electric vehicle |
| Green, yellow characters | Commercial battery electric vehicle |
| Black, yellow characters | Self-drive rental (commercial vehicle rented out without a driver) |
| Blue, white characters | Foreign diplomatic missions |

The green plates for electric vehicles come from a 2018 notification of the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways. Hybrids are not battery electric vehicles and keep ordinary white or yellow plates. If you are thinking of going electric, our guide to electric cars in Hyderabad (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/electric-cars-in-hyderabad.html) covers road tax and charging.

Plate colour matters to drivers too. A yellow plate warns you a vehicle may stop suddenly to pick up or drop passengers, as autos and cabs do all over the city; our post on sharing the road with autos, buses and two-wheelers (https://sawari.airacode.online/blog/sharing-the-road-autos-buses-two-wheelers.html) has more.

## Number plates in Sawari

The car you drive in Sawari carries a Telangana-style white plate, TS 09 EH 4521, with the blue IND strip of a high-security plate. In plate terms that is a private car registered at the Hyderabad Central zone before the 2024 change to TG. The number is invented, so it does not belong to any real vehicle. The traffic around you is generic, so look at the road, not the plates. You can start a drive (https://sawari.airacode.online/play.html) free on a phone, tablet, laptop or desktop.

## Frequently asked questions

**Do I need to change my TS number plate to TG?**
No. The TG code applies to vehicles registered from March 2024 onwards. Existing TS registrations remain valid, and owners must not change TS to TG on their own plates, because the result could clash with a different vehicle's genuine TG number.

**What does TG 09 mean on a number plate?**
TG 09 is the code for the Hyderabad Central zone, the regional transport office at Khairatabad. The other Hyderabad zones are TG 10 (North), TG 11 (East), TG 12 (South) and TG 13 (West).

**Is HSRP mandatory in Telangana?**
New vehicles across India have been fitted with high-security registration plates since April 2019. In April 2025 Telangana ordered HSRP for older vehicles registered before 1 April 2019 too. Book only through the official portal linked from the Transport Department website.

**Who can get a BH series number plate?**
The Bharat series is voluntary and open to defence personnel, central and state government and public sector employees, and employees of private companies with offices in four or more states or union territories. It is for private, non-transport vehicles.
